title: Uncomplicated malaria (adult)
presentation: Fever or history of fever in the last 48 hours.
Chills, rigors, headache, myalgia.
Recent travel to or residence in a malaria-endemic area.
redFlags: Repeated vomiting, inability to tolerate oral medication.
Severe anaemia or signs of shock.

management.detail: Do not treat empirically; treat only after a positive RDT or microscopy.
Six-dose regimen over three days, weight-banded; reinforce dosing with food.
Return immediately if fever persists or red flags appear.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the treatment of malaria

title: Hypertension, stage 1 (adult, non-emergent)
presentation: Office BP 140–159 / 90–99 mmHg on two separate occasions.
Often asymptomatic; may report headache, nocturia, palpitations.
redFlags: BP ≥ 180/120 with end-organ symptoms (chest pain, neurological deficit, dyspnoea) — hypertensive emergency.

diagnostics.test: Urinalysis + serum creatinine + fasting glucose + lipids
diagnostics.rationale: Screen for end-organ damage and concomitant risk factors.

management.detail: Salt reduction, weight management, physical activity, smoking cessation.
Per local formulary (e.g., amlodipine or hydrochlorothiazide); re-check in 4 weeks.
Monthly until controlled, then 3-monthly.

title: Type 2 diabetes, new diagnosis (adult)
presentation: Polyuria, polydipsia, unintentional weight loss, fatigue.
Often detected on opportunistic screening.
redFlags: Diabetic ketoacidosis symptoms (Kussmaul breathing, vomiting, abdominal pain).
Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state — altered mental status with severe hyperglycaemia.

diagnostics.rationale: ≥ 7.0 mmol/L on two occasions confirms diagnosis.
≥ 6.5% supports diagnosis and sets a baseline target.
Screen for nephropathy and lipid co-management.

management.detail: Self-monitoring, hypoglycaemia recognition, foot care, dietary counselling.
Metformin titrated from 500 mg daily, target 1 g BD as tolerated; re-check HbA1c at 3 months.
Blood pressure target < 140/90, statin if 10-year CV risk elevated.

title: Acute diarrhoea with dehydration (child <5 years)
presentation: Loose / watery stools >=3 times in 24 h.
Variable: vomiting, fever, reduced oral intake, decreased urine output.
Signs of dehydration depend on volume loss — see IMCI sign list.
redFlags: Lethargic or unconscious, unable to drink or drinks poorly.
Skin pinch goes back very slowly (severe dehydration).

diagnostics.rationale: Drives Plan A/B/C selection — no laboratory test is needed before initiating treatment.

diagnostics.test: Stool microscopy or PCR when persistent or dysenteric
diagnostics.rationale: Identifies Giardia / Entamoeba / Shigella / EHEC when first-line management fails.

management.detail: Use the IMCI sign rule: two or more severe signs -> Plan C; two or more some-dehydration signs -> Plan B; otherwise Plan A.
Extra fluids: ORS 50–100 mL per loose stool <2 y, 100–200 mL >=2 y. Zinc 10–20 mg daily for 10–14 days. Continue feeding, including breast milk. Counsel four return-immediately signs.
ORS 75 mL/kg over 4 h at the facility; reassess at 4 h. Continue breastfeeding. Escalate to Plan C if any danger sign appears.
Ringer's lactate or normal saline 100 mL/kg: 30 mL/kg in the first 30 min then 70 mL/kg over 2.5 h (infants 30 min + 5 h). Refer urgently if no IV available — give NG ORS while transferring.

Dysentery (visible blood): ciprofloxacin 15 mg/kg twice daily for 3 days where Shigella is sensitive. Cholera outbreak: doxycycline or azithromycin per local protocol. Routine antibiotics are NOT indicated for non-dysenteric diarrhoea.

references.label: WHO/UNICEF Joint Statement: Clinical management of acute diarrhoea (2004)

title: Pneumonia (child <5 years, IMCI)
presentation: Cough or difficult breathing.
Fast breathing relative to age: >=50/min (2–11 mo), >=40/min (12–59 mo).
Severe cases add chest indrawing, grunting, central cyanosis, stridor in a calm child, SpO2 <90%.

diagnostics.test: Clinical IMCI assessment with respiratory-rate count over a full minute
diagnostics.rationale: Bedside diagnosis — chest X-ray is NOT required to initiate treatment for non-severe pneumonia in IMCI.
SpO2 <90% reclassifies as severe and mandates oxygen + referral.

management.detail: Give first dose of injectable antibiotic: ampicillin 50 mg/kg + gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg IM/IV, or IM/IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg. Give oxygen if SpO2 <90%. Refer urgently.
Oral amoxicillin dispersible tablet 40 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days. Outpatient management. Counsel home care and return-immediately signs. Follow up in 3 days.
Soothe the throat with safe home remedies. No antibiotic. Return-immediately counselling. Follow up in 5 days if not improving.

title: Pulmonary tuberculosis (adult, new diagnosis)
presentation: Cough >=2 weeks (any duration in PLHIV).
Unintentional weight loss, drenching night sweats, fever.
Haemoptysis in advanced disease.
History of close contact with a confirmed TB case.

diagnostics.test: Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra on spot sputum (preferred)
diagnostics.rationale: WHO 2021 — initial diagnostic of choice; detects rifampicin resistance simultaneously.

diagnostics.test: Smear microscopy + culture where Xpert unavailable
diagnostics.rationale: Secondary path; treatment still requires bacteriological confirmation.
Mandatory at TB diagnosis per Kenya NTP — informs co-trimoxazole + ART decisions.
Supports diagnosis when bacteriology is negative or in extrapulmonary suspicion.

management.detail: Report to the Kenya NTP system. Begin contact tracing for household and close contacts.
Fixed-dose combination of HRZE (isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide + ethambutol) at weight-banded doses. Direct observation per local model.
HR (isoniazid + rifampicin). Total course 6 months for drug-susceptible TB.
Counsel on hepatotoxicity warning signs, peripheral neuropathy (give pyridoxine 25 mg daily), optic neuritis with ethambutol, and orange body fluids with rifampicin. Monitor LFTs if symptomatic.

Start ART within 2 weeks of TB therapy initiation (within 8 weeks if CD4 >=50). Start co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. Manage drug-drug interactions with rifampicin (e.g. switch to dolutegravir 50 mg twice daily during TB co-treatment).

references.label: Kenya National TB Programme — Tuberculosis Management Guidelines

title: HIV infection (adult, newly diagnosed)
presentation: Diagnosis confirmed by a sequential rapid-test algorithm or 4th-generation assay.
Patients vary from asymptomatic (most) to advanced HIV disease (CD4 <200 or WHO clinical stage 3/4).
redFlags: WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 features (oesophageal candidiasis, Kaposi sarcoma, recurrent bacterial pneumonia, etc.).
Cryptococcal antigen positive — pre-empt CNS disease.
Active TB symptoms (cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss).

diagnostics.rationale: Identifies advanced HIV disease and the need for OI prophylaxis bundle.
Baseline marker; repeated at 6 and 12 months for treatment monitoring.

diagnostics.test: TB symptom screen + Xpert when positive
diagnostics.rationale: TB is the leading OI; co-treatment timing depends on this.

management.detail: WHO recommends same-day or within-7-day initiation in patients without contraindications. First line per Kenya MoH: tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir (TLD) once daily.
Co-trimoxazole 960 mg daily; fluconazole pre-emptive therapy if cryptococcal antigen positive; isoniazid preventive therapy unless active TB suspected.
Counsel on lifelong daily medication, side effects of dolutegravir (insomnia, weight gain), partner notification options, condom use.
Viral load at 6 and 12 months, then annually if suppressed. Switch to second line on confirmed virological failure (two VL > 1,000 copies/mL with documented adherence).
Continue TLD across pregnancy. Mother stays on ART for life. Infant receives nevirapine prophylaxis for 6 weeks (or per current Kenya MoH protocol).

references.label: Kenya National AIDS & STI Control Programme (NASCOP) — ART Guidelines

title: Asthma (adult, stepwise long-term management)
presentation: Recurrent wheeze, chest tightness, cough — often nocturnal or with exertion.
Variable airflow obstruction reversible with bronchodilator.
Trigger pattern: cold air, infection, allergen, exercise, NSAIDs.
redFlags: Inability to complete sentences in one breath.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms reversible airflow obstruction; FEV1 increase >=12% and 200 mL after salbutamol.
Bedside tool — diurnal variability >10% supports diagnosis.

management.step: Step 1 — as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol (or SABA + low-dose ICS combo)
management.detail: GINA-aligned: avoid SABA-only therapy. Counsel inhaler technique and adherence.
Beclometasone 100–200 µg twice daily (or budesonide / fluticasone equivalent), plus as-needed reliever.

management.step: Step 3 — low-dose ICS / long-acting beta-2 agonist (LABA)
management.detail: Combination inhaler twice daily plus reliever. Re-check inhaler technique and adherence before escalating.
Twice daily; consider add-on tiotropium.
Biologic therapy, oral corticosteroid sparing, severe-asthma phenotyping.
Salbutamol 4–10 puffs via spacer every 20 min in the first hour; oral prednisolone 40–50 mg daily for 5–7 days; oxygen to target SpO2 93–95%. Refer if no response or any red flag.

references.label: GINA — Global Strategy for Asthma Management (2024)

title: Pre-eclampsia in pregnancy
presentation: New-onset hypertension (BP >=140/90 mmHg) after 20 weeks gestation.
Proteinuria (>=1+ on dipstick or >=300 mg/24 h).
May be asymptomatic at diagnosis; severe features develop later.
redFlags: Severe persistent headache, blurred vision, scotomata.
Right-upper-quadrant or epigastric pain (HELLP / hepatic capsule).

diagnostics.test: Repeated BP measurement on the same arm, seated, after 5 min rest
diagnostics.rationale: Confirms diagnosis on >=2 readings at least 4 h apart.
Significant proteinuria supports pre-eclampsia over gestational hypertension.
Daily kick chart; CTG / ultrasound where available.

management.detail: Mild / non-severe vs severe by BP threshold (160/110), severe symptoms, and laboratory features.

Magnesium sulphate loading dose 4 g IV slow over 5–10 min PLUS 10 g IM (5 g each buttock); maintenance 5 g IM every 4 h or 1 g/h IV infusion for 24 h after the last fit or delivery, whichever later. Control BP with IV labetalol 10–20 mg or oral nifedipine 10 mg immediate-release. Refer urgently; do not delay magnesium for transport.

Admit or daily clinic review. Start oral methyldopa 250 mg three times daily or labetalol 100 mg twice daily. Antenatal corticosteroids if <34 weeks. Plan delivery from 37 weeks or earlier with worsening features.
Weekly BP + dipstick. Start antihypertensive if BP persistently >=150/100. Reassess for pre-eclampsia at every contact.
BP can rise in the first 7 days post-partum — review at day 3 and day 7. Continue antihypertensive at least 6 weeks.

references.label: WHO Recommendations: Prevention and treatment of pre-eclampsia and eclampsia (2011)
Kenya MoH — Maternal and Newborn Health Quality of Care

title: Uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection (adult, non-pregnant female)
presentation: Dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency.
Suprapubic discomfort.
No fever, no flank pain, no vaginal symptoms.
redFlags: Failure of empirical therapy at 48–72 h.

diagnostics.rationale: Sufficient for empirical diagnosis in classic uncomplicated cases.

diagnostics.test: Urine culture only when red-flag features, recurrence, or treatment failure
diagnostics.rationale: Identifies resistance and guides second-line therapy; not routine for uncomplicated cases.

management.detail: Where sensitivities permit: nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days, OR co-trimoxazole 960 mg twice daily for 3 days. Avoid fluoroquinolones for uncomplicated UTI (AWaRe Watch — reserve).
Encourage fluids; paracetamol for pain. Phenazopyridine where licensed for 1–2 days only.
Complete the full course. Return if symptoms persist >48–72 h, develop fever or flank pain, or recur >=2 episodes in 6 months.

management.step: Recurrent UTI (>=2 per 6 months or >=3 per year)
management.detail: Investigate underlying cause (post-coital pattern, anatomy, residual urine). Consider prophylactic low-dose nitrofurantoin or post-coital single dose; refer if structural disease suspected.

title: Severe malaria (child <5 years)
presentation: Fever in a malaria-endemic area with one or more severe features.

Common severe features: lethargy / impaired consciousness, prostration, repeated convulsions, severe anaemia (palmar pallor, Hb < 5 g/dL), respiratory distress, hypoglycaemia, jaundice, dark/coloured urine, repeated vomiting, shock.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirm parasitaemia but DO NOT delay parenteral antimalarial waiting for confirmation.
Hypoglycaemia is common and lethal — treat with 5 mL/kg of 10% dextrose IV.

management.detail: Artesunate 3 mg/kg IM/IV at 0, 12, 24 h then once daily. If IV/IM unavailable, give artesunate suppository 10 mg/kg rectally as a single pre-referral dose.
Treat hypoglycaemia (10% dextrose 5 mL/kg IV); control convulsions (rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg or buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg); transfuse packed red cells if Hb <5 g/dL with respiratory distress.
Continue parenteral artesunate for at least 24 h and a minimum of 3 doses; transition to a full 3-day oral artemether-lumefantrine course once tolerating orally.

Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics (ampicillin + gentamicin or ceftriaxone) for any septic features; manage acidosis and dehydration cautiously per the FEAST trial principles (avoid rapid fluid boluses).

title: Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in children 6–59 months
presentation: MUAC < 11.5 cm, OR weight-for-height Z-score < -3, OR bilateral pitting oedema.
Visible severe wasting, baggy skin, prominent ribs.
May present with marasmus (severe wasting), kwashiorkor (bilateral oedema), or mixed picture.
redFlags: Appetite test failed (cannot finish 30 mL RUTF in 30 minutes).

diagnostics.rationale: Primary screening tool — single arm, mid-upper, taken to the millimetre.
Test on both feet for 3 seconds; even mild oedema classifies as SAM.
Hypoglycaemia and hypothermia are leading causes of death — screen at every visit.
Underlying conditions worsen prognosis; HIV care must be co-managed.

management.step: Triage to inpatient (complicated SAM) vs OTP (uncomplicated SAM)
management.detail: Any danger sign, failed appetite test, severe oedema (+++), bilateral oedema with marasmus, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, or sepsis → inpatient. Otherwise → OTP.

Initiate F-75 130 mL/kg/day in 8 meals over the first 1–2 days. Treat hypoglycaemia (5 mL/kg 10% dextrose), hypothermia (skin-to-skin), dehydration with ReSoMal (NOT standard ORS — risk of cardiac failure), and empirical antibiotics (ampicillin + gentamicin).
Move to F-100 or RUTF once oedema reduces and appetite returns; typically days 3–7. Increase intake by 10% per day.

RUTF 200 kcal/kg/day in divided doses, weekly review, amoxicillin per IMAM protocol, vitamin A on day 1, deworming after 2 weeks, immunisations updated. Exit criteria: MUAC > 12.5 cm + oedema free for 2 consecutive visits.
Counsel caregiver on nutrition and feeding practices; refer to community nutrition support; recheck MUAC at 1, 3 and 6 months post-discharge.

references.label: WHO Guideline: Updates on the management of severe acute malnutrition in infants and children (2013)
Kenya MoH — Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition (IMAM)

title: Adult community-acquired pneumonia
presentation: Acute cough with fever, sputum, dyspnoea or pleuritic chest pain.
Auscultation: focal crackles, bronchial breathing, dullness on percussion.
Severity varies — use CRB-65 (Confusion, RR >=30, BP <90/<=60, age >=65) for risk stratification.
redFlags: Failure to respond to first-line oral therapy at 48–72 h.

diagnostics.rationale: Identifies hypoxia and CRB-65 components at the bedside.
Confirms diagnosis, identifies complications (effusion, abscess, multilobar disease); not required for empirical outpatient treatment.

diagnostics.test: Sputum + blood cultures + Xpert MTB/RIF for severe / atypical / poor responders
diagnostics.rationale: Guides targeted antibiotics and rules out TB co-infection.

management.detail: Outpatient oral amoxicillin 500 mg–1 g three times daily for 5 days. Safety-net advice; review at 5–7 days.
Consider hospital-based assessment or short-stay observation. Add macrolide cover if atypical pathogens suspected.
Admit; start IV ceftriaxone 1–2 g daily + azithromycin 500 mg daily. Oxygen to target SpO2 94–98%. Consider sepsis bundle.
Reassess at 48–72 h; consider TB, viral pneumonia, abscess, empyema. Imaging + targeted microbiology.

references.label: BTS Guideline for the management of community acquired pneumonia in adults
WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Adults

title: Major depressive disorder (adult)
presentation: Persistent low mood and/or anhedonia for >=2 weeks.
Sleep, appetite, energy, concentration disturbance.
Feelings of guilt or worthlessness; psychomotor slowing or agitation.
Thoughts of self-harm or being better off dead (must be asked directly).
redFlags: Suicidal ideation with plan or intent.
Severe functional impairment (unable to care for self).

diagnostics.rationale: Validated 9-item severity instrument; item 9 is a direct suicide-risk gate.
Hypothyroidism, B12/folate deficiency, anaemia, HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder, post-stroke depression — screen with TSH, FBC, B12, HIV.
Alcohol or sedative dependence commonly co-exists and worsens prognosis.

management.detail: Ask directly about suicidal thoughts at every visit. For positive item 9 of PHQ-9 or any expressed ideation, develop a written same-day safety plan (warning signs, internal coping, social contacts, professional contacts, restricting access to means).
Brief structured psychological support per WHO mhGAP mhPP; lifestyle counselling; re-screen 2–4 weeks.
Initiate structured psychological therapy (problem-solving, behavioural activation). Consider SSRI (fluoxetine 20 mg daily first line per Kenya MoH). Review at 2 weeks.
Start SSRI alongside structured therapy. Review weekly initially; refer to mental-health specialist where capacity exists. Reassess for psychotic features.
Refer urgently for mental-health assessment; remove access to means; ensure responsible adult presence; document safety plan; follow up within 48–72 h.

references.label: Kenya MoH — Mental Health Policy and Treatment Guidelines
Kroenke K, Spitzer RL — PHQ-9 (J Gen Intern Med 2001)

title: Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH)
presentation: Blood loss >=500 mL after vaginal birth (>=1000 mL after caesarean), OR any blood loss with signs of haemodynamic compromise.
Causes (the 4 Ts): Tone (uterine atony — 70%), Trauma (genital tract injury — 20%), Tissue (retained products — 10%), Thrombin (coagulopathy).
redFlags: Tachycardia >120/min, hypotension <90 systolic, capillary refill >3 s.
Ongoing brisk haemorrhage despite uterine massage and uterotonics.

diagnostics.test: Visual estimation + drape collection of blood loss
diagnostics.rationale: Quantifies severity; under-estimation is common — use weighed gauze and calibrated drapes where available.
Shock index (HR / SBP) > 1.0 indicates significant volume loss before classic shock signs appear.
Identifies DIC; replace blood products empirically when assays unavailable.

management.step: Call for help — activate the obstetric haemorrhage protocol
management.detail: Two large-bore IV cannulae, bloods for crossmatch + FBC + clotting, give oxygen, keep the patient warm. Document time of onset and estimated loss.
10 IU IM stat OR 20–40 IU in 1 L normal saline at 60 mL/h. Heat-stable carbetocin 100 µg IM is a single-dose alternative where available.
If atony persists despite oxytocin, apply continuous bimanual compression while preparing further uterotonics.
Ergometrine 0.2 mg IM (avoid in hypertension / pre-eclampsia) OR misoprostol 800 µg sublingual OR carboprost 250 µg IM. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 h of onset reduces mortality (WHO 2017).
Examine for trauma and retained products under anaesthesia; apply intrauterine balloon tamponade; B-Lynch suture or hysterectomy at referral facility if conservative measures fail.
Crystalloid bolus 1 L; transfuse packed red cells early — use ratio resuscitation (FFP : platelets : red cells) for massive bleeding; correct hypothermia and acidosis.

references.label: WHO Recommendation on Tranexamic Acid for PPH (2017)
Kenya MoH — Maternal and Newborn Health Quality of Care

title: Anaemia in pregnancy
presentation: Often asymptomatic on routine screening.
Symptomatic: fatigue, breathlessness, palpitations, pallor (conjunctival, palmar).
Severe: dyspnoea at rest, ankle swelling, cardiac decompensation.
redFlags: Hb < 7 g/dL at any gestation — severe anaemia.
Active bleeding (antepartum haemorrhage, recent miscarriage, schistosoma haematuria).

diagnostics.test: Hb at booking and every trimester (Kenya MoH recommends 28 wk + 36 wk)
diagnostics.rationale: Defines severity band: mild 9–10.9, moderate 7–8.9, severe <7 g/dL.
Identifies hookworm and schistosomiasis (treatable causes in endemic areas).
Malaria is a leading cause of anaemia in pregnancy in endemic regions.

diagnostics.test: HIV test, sickle screen, blood film
diagnostics.rationale: Co-existing chronic disease changes the management.

management.detail: Daily oral iron 30–60 mg elemental + folic acid 400 µg from booking to 6 weeks post-partum (WHO 2016).
Treatment-dose oral iron 120 mg elemental daily in divided doses; treat malaria / hookworm if present; recheck Hb in 2–4 weeks.

Refer for inpatient assessment. IV iron sucrose 200 mg per session (or per local protocol) if oral iron failed or third trimester; transfuse packed cells if symptomatic, in heart failure, or actively bleeding.
Ensure Hb >=10 g/dL by 36 weeks; deliver at a facility with cross-matched blood available; AMTSL is mandatory.

references.label: WHO Guideline: Daily iron and folic acid supplementation in pregnant women (2016)
Kenya MoH — Maternal Nutrition Operational Guidance

title: Sickle cell disease — vaso-occlusive (painful) crisis
presentation: Severe deep bone pain (most commonly long bones, spine, chest).
Often a known sickle cell patient; may be precipitated by cold, dehydration, infection, hypoxia.
May present alongside acute chest syndrome, dactylitis (infants), splenic sequestration, stroke.
redFlags: Acute chest syndrome: fever, hypoxia, new infiltrate, chest pain (mortality emergency).
Sudden splenic enlargement with anaemia (sequestration crisis).
Severe anaemia (Hb >2 g/dL below baseline) or aplastic crisis (low reticulocytes).

diagnostics.rationale: Identifies aplastic crisis (low reticulocytes) or sequestration (drop from baseline).

diagnostics.test: Oxygen saturation + arterial blood gas if hypoxic
Chest X-ray when fever / hypoxia / chest signs
diagnostics.rationale: New infiltrate confirms acute chest syndrome.
Functional asplenia raises risk of invasive pneumococcal and salmonella infection.

management.detail: Mild pain: paracetamol 15 mg/kg + ibuprofen 10 mg/kg orally. Moderate–severe: IV morphine 0.1–0.15 mg/kg as starting bolus, then PRN with regular re-assessment. Continue until pain controlled; wean gradually.
Oral if tolerated; otherwise IV maintenance (1.5x maintenance only — avoid over-hydration, which worsens acute chest syndrome).

management.step: Oxygen if SpO2 < 95% on room air
management.detail: Maintain SpO2 >=95%. Otherwise oxygen is not routinely indicated.
Empirical antibiotics for fever (ceftriaxone covers most invasive pathogens in functional asplenia); incentive spirometry to prevent acute chest syndrome; warm environment.

management.step: Transfuse for severe anaemia / acute chest / stroke
management.detail: Simple transfusion for severe symptomatic anaemia; exchange transfusion for stroke, acute chest syndrome with hypoxia, or refractory priapism.
Hydroxyurea 15–20 mg/kg/day in those with >=3 crises/year or acute chest syndrome history. Penicillin V prophylaxis under 5 y; immunisations against pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus.

references.label: WHO — Sickle-cell disease and other haemoglobin disorders
British Society of Haematology — Management of the acute painful crisis in sickle cell disease (2015)
Kenya MoH — Standard Treatment Guidelines (Haematology chapter)

title: Acute bacterial meningitis
presentation: Acute headache, fever, neck stiffness, photophobia.
Altered mental status — drowsiness, confusion, coma.
Petechial / purpuric rash (meningococcal).
Infants: bulging fontanelle, lethargy, poor feeding, irritability.
redFlags: Glasgow Coma Scale <12 or rapidly declining.
Focal neurological deficit or new seizure.
Signs of raised intracranial pressure (papilloedema, Cushing response).

diagnostics.test: Blood cultures BEFORE first antibiotic dose (do not delay antibiotics waiting for LP)
diagnostics.rationale: Cultures remain positive briefly even after antibiotic; one set should be collected before treatment but should not delay it.

Confirms diagnosis (raised opening pressure, low glucose, high protein, neutrophil predominance) and identifies organism. Delay LP if focal neurology, GCS <12, coagulopathy, or signs of raised ICP — perform CT first.

diagnostics.test: CSF Gram stain + culture + glucose + protein + cell count + lactate
diagnostics.rationale: Bedside Gram stain guides initial antibiotic. CSF lactate >3.5 mmol/L supports bacterial cause.
Baseline for septic-screen workup; DIC frequently complicates meningococcaemia.

management.detail: Children and adults: IV ceftriaxone 2 g (50–100 mg/kg paediatric) BD. Add vancomycin if pneumococcal resistance prevalent. Add ampicillin in neonates and adults >50 y to cover Listeria. Do NOT delay for LP or imaging.
Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV given just before or with the first antibiotic dose reduces neurological sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis. Continue 6-hourly for 4 days only if pneumococcus confirmed.
Oxygen, IV fluids, vasopressors if shock; treat raised ICP (head-up 30°, mannitol if signs of herniation); manage seizures.
Meningococcal disease is notifiable. Close contacts receive ciprofloxacin 500 mg single dose (or ceftriaxone 250 mg IM if pregnant).
Hearing assessment + neurodevelopmental review at 4–6 weeks post-discharge in children. Vaccinate against pneumococcus / meningococcus / Hib if not already.

references.label: WHO — Standard Operating Procedures Surveillance Meningococcal Disease (2019)

title: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (newly diagnosed, adult)
presentation: Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss over weeks.
Often presents with diabetic ketoacidosis (50–80% of children, 20–30% of adults at diagnosis).
Younger age, lean body habitus, recent viral illness, autoimmune history.
redFlags: Diabetic ketoacidosis — Kussmaul respiration, dehydration, altered mental state, ketones in urine.
Severe hyperglycaemia with vomiting + abdominal pain.

diagnostics.test: Random plasma glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L plus symptoms
diagnostics.rationale: Single test sufficient with classical symptoms.

diagnostics.test: Fasting plasma glucose ≥ 7.0 mmol/L on two occasions

diagnostics.rationale: May be falsely low in haemolysis / blood loss / pregnancy.
Distinguishes T1DM (often ketotic at presentation) from T2DM.
Low in T1DM; supports immediate insulin therapy.

management.detail: Multiple-daily-injection (MDI) basal-bolus regimen: NPH (isophane) 0.2 U/kg at bedtime + soluble (regular) insulin 0.1 U/kg pre-meals, titrated to capillary glucose. Total ~0.5–1 U/kg/day.
≥ 4 capillary glucose checks/day (pre-meals + bedtime). Target fasting 4–7 mmol/L and 2-hour post-prandial < 10 mmol/L.
Insulin technique, hypoglycaemia recognition + treatment, sick-day rules, carbohydrate awareness, ID-bracelet, regular foot / eye review.
Endocrinology / paediatric diabetes clinic for ongoing optimisation; structured education programme (DAFNE-style).
Annual urine ACR + creatinine, fundoscopy / retinal photography, foot exam, lipid profile, BP, autoimmune screen (TSH + coeliac if symptoms).

references.label: WHO Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes
ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes 2024

title: Acute kidney injury (adult)
presentation: Oliguria (< 0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥ 6 h) or anuria.
Rising creatinine (≥ 26.5 µmol/L within 48 h, OR ≥ 50 % rise over 7 days — KDIGO).
Symptoms of uraemia in late presentations: nausea, fatigue, pruritus, asterixis.
May be triggered by hypovolaemia (diarrhoea, sepsis, haemorrhage), nephrotoxin exposure, or obstruction.

diagnostics.rationale: Stage AKI per KDIGO; potassium informs urgency.
Proteinuria, haematuria, casts suggest intrinsic renal disease; pyuria suggests infection.
Excludes obstruction (must be done within 24 h).
Confirms acidosis severity; lactate flags sepsis.

management.detail: ABC + IV crystalloid 500 mL bolus if volume-depleted, reassess; pause nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, ACE-i / ARB, aminoglycosides, IV contrast); treat sepsis with broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour if suspected.

K ≥ 6.0 with ECG changes → IV 10 mL of 10 % calcium gluconate over 10 min, insulin 10 U + 50 mL 50 % dextrose IV over 15 min, salbutamol 10 mg nebuliser; consider dialysis for refractory hyperkalaemia.
Hold metformin if eGFR < 30; reduce LMWH dose; avoid aminoglycosides / IV contrast.
Indications for urgent dialysis: refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, refractory fluid overload, uraemic complications, certain toxin ingestions (AEIOU).
Strict fluid balance, daily weight, electrolytes 12-hourly until stable.

references.label: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for AKI (2012, with 2024 update)

title: Iron deficiency anaemia (adult)
presentation: Fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, dizziness, palpitations.
Pallor (conjunctival, mucosal), tachycardia, systolic flow murmur.
Pica, restless legs, koilonychia in severe cases.
Common SSA causes: menstrual blood loss, pregnancy, hookworm, schistosomiasis, malaria, dietary inadequacy.
redFlags: Hb < 7 g/dL with symptoms — transfuse + admit.
Iron deficiency in a man or post-menopausal woman — investigate GI tract (colorectal cancer must be excluded).

diagnostics.rationale: Most useful test; < 30 ng/mL highly specific for iron deficiency. Acute-phase reactant — interpret with CRP.
< 16 % supports iron deficiency in inflammatory states with high ferritin.
Mandatory in men + post-menopausal women — rule out malignancy / coeliac.

management.detail: Deworm with albendazole 400 mg single dose where endemic, treat malaria, address menorrhagia (tranexamic acid, copper IUS), refer for GI workup where indicated.

Ferrous sulphate 200 mg (≈ 65 mg elemental iron) once daily on an empty stomach with vitamin C / orange juice; counsel dark stools, GI upset. Alternate-day dosing improves absorption + tolerability (WHO 2022). Continue 3 months after Hb normalises to replenish stores.
IV ferric carboxymaltose / iron sucrose for intolerance / malabsorption / severe deficiency / pregnancy beyond 14 weeks — single infusion replaces large dose.
Reserve for Hb < 7 g/dL with symptoms, ongoing bleeding, or imminent surgery.
Expect 1–2 g/dL rise; if no response → adherence, ongoing loss, malabsorption (coeliac), wrong diagnosis.

references.label: BSG Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia (2021)

title: Soil-transmitted helminthiasis in children (Ascaris, hookworm, Trichuris)
presentation: Often asymptomatic.
Hookworm: chronic iron-deficiency anaemia, fatigue, growth faltering.
Ascaris: abdominal pain, intermittent worms passed PR / by mouth; rarely bowel obstruction / biliary obstruction.
Trichuris (whipworm): chronic diarrhoea, rectal prolapse, dysentery in heavy infections.
redFlags: Bowel obstruction (Ascaris bolus) — vomiting, distension, no flatus.
Pulmonary symptoms during larval migration (Löffler syndrome).

management.detail: Albendazole 400 mg single dose (200 mg if 1–2 y) annually (or 2-yearly with prevalence ≥ 20 %). Equally effective for ascaris and hookworm; less effective for Trichuris (consider repeat dosing).
Mebendazole 500 mg single dose; or pyrantel pamoate 11 mg/kg single dose.
Ferrous sulphate where anaemic; bring forward MDA in high-risk school catchments.
Hand-washing, latrine use, wearing shoes, clean water, deworming campaigns through WASH programmes.

references.label: WHO Guideline on Preventive Chemotherapy for STH (2017)

title: Acute otitis media (child)
presentation: Ear pain (older child) or ear-pulling / irritability + fever (infant).
Reduced hearing.
Drainage from the ear (perforated drum).
Often follows URTI.
redFlags: Severe headache, neck stiffness, drowsiness (intracranial complication).
Recurrent AOM ≥ 3 episodes in 6 months → ENT review.

diagnostics.rationale: Bulging, opaque, erythematous tympanic membrane; OR pus in canal with confirmed perforation.

management.detail: Paracetamol 15 mg/kg every 6 h and / or ibuprofen 10 mg/kg every 8 h.

Age < 6 months OR < 2 y with bilateral / otorrhoea / severe symptoms → amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/day in 2 doses for 5 days (10 days if < 2 y or severe). Penicillin allergy → azithromycin or clindamycin.
Age ≥ 2 y, unilateral, non-severe, no otorrhoea — observe for 48–72 h with analgesia; reassess if not improving.
Co-amoxiclav for amoxicillin failure (no improvement at 48–72 h).
Mastoiditis, recurrent / persistent AOM, chronic suppurative OM, cholesteatoma suspected.

title: Urinary tract infection in pregnancy (including asymptomatic bacteriuria)
presentation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria — detected on routine ANC urine culture.
Cystitis — dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain, no systemic features.
Acute pyelonephritis — fever, loin pain, rigors, vomiting, often with cystitis symptoms.
redFlags: Preterm labour / preterm-premature rupture of membranes.
Renal abscess or obstruction suspected on ultrasound.

diagnostics.rationale: Culture mandatory in pregnancy; treat asymptomatic bacteriuria > 10⁵ CFU/mL.
If pyelonephritis or recurrent UTI — exclude obstruction / abscess.

diagnostics.test: FBC + CRP + U&E + blood cultures (if pyelonephritis)

management.detail: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg modified-release twice daily for 5–7 days (AVOID in last 4 weeks of pregnancy — neonatal haemolysis), OR cefalexin 500 mg three times daily for 7 days, OR amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily if sensitive. Avoid trimethoprim in first trimester (folate antagonist) and last trimester (kernicterus).
Admit. IV ceftriaxone 2 g once daily until afebrile + improving (typically 48 h), then complete 10–14-day oral course based on sensitivities. Maintain hydration; analgesia (paracetamol).
Repeat urine culture 1–2 weeks after completing treatment. Recurrent or relapsing → consider prophylactic nitrofurantoin 50 mg once nightly until delivery.
Adequate hydration, post-coital voiding, return-immediately signs: fever, loin pain, vomiting, reduced foetal movement, contractions.

references.label: WHO ANC Guidance — Antibiotics for asymptomatic bacteriuria

title: Scabies
presentation: Intense pruritus (worse at night).
Linear burrows in interdigital web spaces, wrists, elbows, axillae, periumbilical area, genitals, soles (infants).
Excoriations, pustular secondary infection (impetigo).
Crusted (Norwegian) scabies in immunocompromised — thick scaling, less itch.
redFlags: Secondary streptococcal infection → acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis or rheumatic fever risk.
Crusted scabies in HIV / immunocompromised — highly contagious, refer specialist.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical. Skin scraping with microscopy can confirm but is not required.

management.detail: Apply to entire body neck-to-toe (including face / scalp in infants and elderly), leave 8–14 hours, then wash off. Repeat in 7 days. Suitable from age 2 months and in pregnancy.
Alternative or for outbreak control / crusted scabies: 200 µg/kg orally on days 1 and 8 (and 15 for crusted). Avoid in pregnancy, breastfeeding (< 1 week post-partum), and children < 15 kg.
Even asymptomatic — re-infection is common otherwise.
Hot-wash (≥ 50 °C) or seal in plastic bag for 72 hours. Vacuum upholstery.
Itching often persists 2–4 weeks after successful treatment — antihistamines + emollients.

references.label: WHO Skin NTDs — Scabies and other ectoparasites
International Alliance for the Control of Scabies (IACS) 2020 criteria

title: Hyperlipidaemia + statin therapy (adult)
presentation: Asymptomatic — found on opportunistic lipid screen.
Xanthelasma, tendon xanthoma (familial hypercholesterolaemia).
May present after first CV event (stroke, MI, PAD).
redFlags: LDL > 4.9 mmol/L or total cholesterol > 8.0 → consider familial hypercholesterolaemia (Simon Broome / DLCN criteria).
Triglycerides > 10 mmol/L → pancreatitis risk; urgent fibrate / dietary intervention.
Statin myopathy: muscle pain + CK > 10× ULN → stop statin.

diagnostics.rationale: Diabetes is a major CV risk factor.
Hypothyroidism is a reversible cause; baseline before statin.
WHO/ISH or similar to guide initiation threshold.

management.detail: Diet — reduce saturated fat (< 7 % of energy), increase fibre, oily fish 2x/week, 30 min moderate exercise 5 days/week, smoking cessation, weight loss 5–10 % if overweight.
10-year CV risk ≥ 10 % (WHO/ISH high-risk band): atorvastatin 20 mg once daily.
After MI / stroke / PAD: atorvastatin 80 mg once daily (high-intensity), aim LDL < 1.8 mmol/L or > 50 % reduction.
Lipids at 3 months — expect ≥ 40 % LDL reduction. ALT baseline + 3 months + 12 months. Counsel statin-myopathy symptoms; check CK if myalgia.
Fibrate (fenofibrate 160 mg once daily) + dietary fat restriction if triglycerides > 10 mmol/L.

title: Acute bronchitis (adult, mostly viral)
presentation: Productive cough > 5 days, often after a URTI.
Low-grade fever, chest discomfort, wheeze.
Self-limiting — typically resolves in 3 weeks.
Sputum colour does NOT distinguish bacterial from viral aetiology.
redFlags: Pneumonia features — focal crackles, tachypnoea ≥ 22, fever ≥ 38.5, hypoxia.

diagnostics.rationale: No imaging required if no pneumonia features.
If pneumonia suspected (focal signs, hypoxia, elderly).
If cough > 14 days or TB risk factors.

management.detail: Paracetamol / ibuprofen for fever and pleuritic discomfort. Steam inhalation, honey + lemon, fluids. Smoking cessation.
AWaRe stewardship — antibiotics provide minimal benefit in acute bronchitis. Do NOT prescribe for sputum colour alone.
Salbutamol 100 µg, 2 puffs four times daily, only if wheeze or known asthma / COPD overlap.
Suspected pneumonia, COPD exacerbation with purulent sputum, frail elderly with comorbidities — amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days.
Return for fever > 5 days, breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis, or persistent cough beyond 3 weeks.

title: Neuropathic pain (adult)
presentation: Burning, shooting, or electric-shock pain in a dermatomal / peripheral-nerve distribution.
Hyperalgesia + allodynia (light touch or temperature painful).
Common causes: diabetic peripheral neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia, post-stroke pain, HIV-related neuropathy, trigeminal neuralgia, sciatica, chemotherapy-induced.
redFlags: Cauda equina syndrome — bilateral leg weakness, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention.
Acute compressive radiculopathy with progressive weakness.
Suicidal ideation in chronic pain — screen with PHQ-9 + item 9.

diagnostics.rationale: Distinguish neuropathic from nociceptive pain (≥ 4/10 on DN4 suggests neuropathic).

management.detail: Amitriptyline 10–25 mg at night, titrate to 75 mg (lower in elderly). OR gabapentin 300 mg three times daily, titrate to 1200 mg three times daily. OR pregabalin 75 mg twice daily (max 300 mg twice daily). OR duloxetine 30 mg daily (titrate to 60 mg). Start one at a time and titrate to effect or adverse effect over 4–8 weeks.
Opioids and NSAIDs are NOT first-line for chronic neuropathic pain. Tramadol may be considered short-term but carries dependence and serotonin-syndrome risk with SSRIs.
Capsaicin 0.075 % cream for localised post-herpetic neuralgia. Lidocaine 5 % patch for post-herpetic neuralgia.
Optimise glycaemic control in diabetes; antivirals for herpes (within 72 h); compression treatment for radiculopathy.
Pain clinic if uncontrolled at 12 weeks despite optimal pharmacotherapy. Mental-health support — depression / anxiety highly co-morbid (PHQ-9 + GAD-7).

references.label: NICE CG173 — Neuropathic pain in adults: pharmacological management (2013, updated)

title: Cellulitis (adult)
presentation: Localised painful, warm, erythematous, swollen skin with poorly demarcated edges.
Often on lower limb in adults; pre-existing skin breach (intertrigo, tinea pedis, ulcer).
Systemic features in moderate-severe: fever, tachycardia, malaise.
redFlags: Rapidly spreading erythema, severe pain disproportionate to findings (necrotising fasciitis).
Septic features (qSOFA ≥ 2, hypotension, altered mental state).
Periorbital / orbital cellulitis — refer ophthalmology + ENT urgently.

diagnostics.rationale: I = systemically well, II = systemically unwell, III = significant comorbidity / SIRS, IV = sepsis / necrotising.

diagnostics.test: FBC + CRP + lactate + blood cultures (if febrile / admitted)
Mark erythema border with skin pen

management.detail: Topical antifungal for tinea pedis (terbinafine), emollients for dry skin, ulcer care.

Flucloxacillin 500 mg orally four times daily for 5–7 days (or amoxicillin-clavulanate where staphylococcal cover unclear). Penicillin allergy: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily or clindamycin 300 mg four times daily.
IV flucloxacillin 1 g every 6 h (or cefazolin 1–2 g every 8 h). Step down to oral when clinical improvement + 48 h afebrile, complete 7-day course.
Surgical emergency. IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 h + clindamycin 900 mg every 8 h (toxin suppression). Urgent surgical debridement.
If erythema progresses or systemic features develop, escalate.

references.label: IDSA Skin and Soft Tissue Infections (2014)

title: Impetigo (child)
presentation: Non-bullous (more common): honey-crusted erosions on face / extremities.
Bullous: flaccid blisters that rupture leaving collarettes of scale.
Highly contagious — often clusters in schools / households.
Caused by Staphylococcus aureus and / or Streptococcus pyogenes.
redFlags: Post-streptococcal complications: acute glomerulonephritis (haematuria, periorbital oedema 1–3 weeks later).

diagnostics.rationale: No routine swabs needed unless treatment failure.

diagnostics.test: Urine dipstick at 2–4 weeks if streptococcal

management.detail: Topical fusidic acid 2 % cream three times daily for 5 days. Hygiene — gentle washing, separate towels, fingernail short, do not share.
Oral flucloxacillin 250–500 mg orally four times daily for 5 days (paediatric 12.5 mg/kg per dose). Penicillin allergy: clarithromycin / azithromycin.
Until lesions are crusted or 48 hours of antibiotic therapy completed (UK Health Security Agency guidance).

management.step: Treat household contacts with same lesions
management.detail: Symptomatic contacts only.

title: Peptic ulcer disease (adult)
presentation: Epigastric pain (gnawing / burning); duodenal ulcer pain typically relieved by food, gastric ulcer pain worsened.
Nausea, early satiety, weight loss (more concerning for gastric ulcer / cancer).
Risk factors: H. pylori, NSAID use, smoking, alcohol, stress (severe systemic illness).
redFlags: Haematemesis, melaena, coffee-ground vomit — refer for endoscopy.
Iron-deficiency anaemia in middle-aged or older patient.
Weight loss > 5 % / persistent vomiting / dysphagia (alarm features).

diagnostics.test: H. pylori test (stool antigen / urea breath test / serology)
diagnostics.rationale: Required before treatment; stop PPI 2 weeks beforehand.
All patients ≥ 55 with new dyspepsia + alarm features. Biopsy gastric ulcers to exclude malignancy.
Iron-deficiency anaemia from chronic blood loss.

management.detail: Where possible; substitute paracetamol. If NSAID essential (RA), co-prescribe PPI for gastric protection.

Triple therapy 14 days: omeprazole 20 mg twice daily + amoxicillin 1 g twice daily + clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily. Penicillin allergy: substitute amoxicillin with metronidazole 400 mg twice daily. Quadruple therapy for failures.
Omeprazole 20–40 mg once daily for 4 weeks (DU) or 8 weeks (GU). Add sucralfate for refractory cases.
Smoking cessation, alcohol moderation, smaller more frequent meals, avoid late-night eating, weight loss.
Mandatory for gastric ulcer (6–8 weeks) to confirm healing + biopsy. Not required for DU unless persistent symptoms.

references.label: NICE CG184 — Dyspepsia and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (2014, updated)
Maastricht V/Florence Consensus on H. pylori

title: Acute gout flare (adult)
presentation: Acute severe pain, swelling, erythema, warmth — usually monoarticular.
First MTP joint (podagra) most common; can affect ankle, knee, wrist.
Onset typically overnight; peak intensity at 12–24 h; self-resolves over 7–14 days untreated.
Triggers: alcohol (especially beer), red meat / shellfish, dehydration, diuretics, surgery, sepsis.
redFlags: Polyarticular flare with systemic features — exclude septic arthritis.
Fever / severely unwell — joint aspiration mandatory.
Recurrent flares / tophi / urolithiasis — start urate-lowering therapy.

diagnostics.rationale: Gold standard — negatively birefringent needle-shaped urate crystals. Also excludes septic arthritis (Gram stain, culture, WCC).
Often normal during the flare; check 2–4 weeks after to plan ULT (target < 360 µmol/L, or < 300 µmol/L if tophi).

management.detail: NSAID — naproxen 500 mg twice daily or ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for 5–7 days (avoid in CKD / heart failure / peptic ulcer).
Colchicine 500 µg orally twice or three times daily for 5–7 days (max 6 mg per course); reduce in renal impairment / CYP3A4 inhibitors.
Prednisolone 30–40 mg once daily for 5 days. Intra-articular methylprednisolone for monoarticular flare.

Start allopurinol 100 mg daily 2–4 weeks AFTER flare resolves; titrate to target urate < 360. Co-prescribe NSAID / colchicine cover for 6 months. Allopurinol hypersensitivity is more common in HLA-B*5801 (Han Chinese, Thai, Korean) — consider febuxostat alternative.
Weight loss, reduce alcohol (especially beer), low-purine diet, hydration, switch diuretic where possible (losartan reduces urate).

references.label: ACR Guideline for the Management of Gout (2020)
EULAR Recommendations for Management of Gout (2016)

title: Acute migraine (adult)
presentation: Unilateral throbbing headache lasting 4–72 hours.
Aggravated by activity, photophobia, phonophobia, nausea / vomiting.
Aura (visual scotoma, paraesthesiae, dysphasia) in 25 %; precedes headache by < 60 min.
Triggers: stress, sleep deprivation, dehydration, menstruation, certain foods.
redFlags: Thunderclap headache (peak severity < 1 min) — exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Sudden new headache > 50 years — exclude giant cell arteritis (ESR / CRP).
Focal neurological deficit beyond aura, fever, neck stiffness, papilloedema.
Aura > 60 min, change in aura pattern, aura without headache — investigate.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical; imaging only for red flags.

management.detail: Ibuprofen 400–600 mg orally + paracetamol 1 g orally + metoclopramide 10 mg orally (or aspirin 900 mg dispersible). Early treatment (within first hour) most effective.
Triptan (sumatriptan 50–100 mg orally, or 6 mg SC for severe attack). Avoid in coronary disease, uncontrolled hypertension, hemiplegic / basilar migraine.
Opioids and codeine — increase medication-overuse headache and rebound.
Paracetamol first-line; avoid NSAIDs in third trimester; triptans likely safe but limited data — counsel risk / benefit.
Propranolol 80 mg modified-release daily, OR amitriptyline 10–25 mg at night, OR topiramate 50–100 mg/day (avoid in pregnancy / weight-loss desired). Reassess at 8–12 weeks.
Headache diary, hydration, regular sleep, gradual caffeine cessation, identify + avoid triggers.

references.label: NICE CG150 — Headaches in over-12s: diagnosis and management (2021 update)

title: Acute hypoglycaemia (adult / child)
presentation: Capillary glucose < 4 mmol/L (< 3.0 in neonates).
Adrenergic phase: sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger (blunted by β-blockers).
Neuroglycopaenic phase: confusion, dysarthria, drowsiness, seizure, coma.
Causes: insulin / sulphonylurea overdose, missed meal, alcohol, sepsis, addisonian crisis, severe malaria in children.
redFlags: Recurrent within 24 h — sulphonylurea induced (long half-life) or insulinoma.
Hypoglycaemia in a non-diabetic adult — investigate Whipple's triad and refer.

diagnostics.test: Cause-directed: insulin level + C-peptide + sulphonylurea screen
diagnostics.rationale: If non-diabetic / unclear cause — distinguish exogenous insulin from endogenous.

diagnostics.test: U&E, malaria smear (children), TFT, AM cortisol (where Addison's suspected)

management.detail: Quick-acting carbohydrate 15–20 g (4–5 glucose tablets, 150 mL Coca-Cola, 1 small tube glucose gel). Recheck in 15 min; repeat once if still < 4. Then long-acting snack (sandwich, biscuit + milk).
Glucose gel applied to inside of cheek, OR 10 mL/kg of fruit juice. Then long-acting snack.
50 mL of 50 % dextrose IV in a large vein OR 100 mL of 10 % dextrose IV. Alternative — glucagon 1 mg IM (less reliable in malnourished / alcoholic / sulphonylurea-induced).
2 mL/kg of 10 % dextrose IV (NEVER 50 % in children — sclerosis risk).
Start 10 % dextrose infusion at maintenance + 50 % above. Sulphonylurea overdose → octreotide 50 µg SC 12-hourly + admit. Alcohol use → thiamine 100 mg IV before / with dextrose.
Identify cause, review insulin / sulphonylurea dose, missed meals, exercise, alcohol. Hypoglycaemia-awareness training; structured review with diabetes team.

references.label: JBDS-IP Management of hypoglycaemia in adults

title: Diabetic foot infection (adult)
presentation: Skin / soft-tissue infection of the diabetic foot — erythema, warmth, swelling, purulent discharge.
Often complicates a neuropathic ulcer (painless, plantar, weight-bearing) or ischaemic ulcer.
Probe-to-bone positive test (sterile probe through ulcer to bone) suggests osteomyelitis.
Septic features warn of severe / limb-threatening infection.
redFlags: Critical limb-threatening ischaemia (ABPI < 0.5, absent pulses, rest pain).
Crepitus / gas in tissues — necrotising fasciitis / gas gangrene.
Osteomyelitis (probe to bone, bone exposed in ulcer base).

diagnostics.rationale: Mild (skin only, ≤ 2 cm cellulitis), moderate (> 2 cm or deeper structures), severe (systemic features).

diagnostics.test: FBC, CRP, U&E, lactate, blood + tissue cultures (after debridement)

diagnostics.rationale: Osteomyelitis (cortical disruption, periosteal reaction); MRI most sensitive.
Exclude critical ischaemia — refer vascular surgery if abnormal.

management.detail: Outpatient flucloxacillin 500 mg orally four times daily for 1–2 weeks. Penicillin allergy: doxycycline.
IV amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2 g three times daily (or ceftriaxone + metronidazole); admit. Debridement of necrotic tissue. Off-loading (total contact cast / cast walker).
Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 8 h + clindamycin 900 mg every 8 h (toxin suppression). Urgent surgical debridement. ICU if sepsis.
IV antibiotics 6 weeks (or 2 weeks if all infected bone resected). Bone biopsy / culture-guided therapy preferred.
HbA1c target individualised; insulin often needed acutely during infection.
Podiatry, vascular surgery, endocrinology, infectious disease for moderate-severe infection. Long-term: foot care, custom footwear, smoking cessation.

references.label: IDSA / IWGDF Diabetic Foot Infection Guidelines (2023)
NICE NG19 — Diabetic foot problems (2015, updated)

title: Tetanus prophylaxis after wound (adult / child)
presentation: Risk assessment after any wound — penetrating, deep, contaminated with soil / faeces / saliva, devitalised tissue, animal bite, frostbite, burn, surgical wound.
Tetanus-prone wounds AND high-risk (heavy contamination, extensive devitalised tissue, surgery > 6 h after injury) need different management.
redFlags: Established tetanus — trismus, risus sardonicus, opisthotonus, autonomic instability → admit ICU.
Suspected infection at wound site → cellulitis / necrotising soft-tissue infection management.

diagnostics.rationale: Fully vaccinated = ≥ 3 documented doses; last dose < 10 years ago. Unsure / incomplete → assume non-immune.
Clean minor vs tetanus-prone vs high-risk.

management.detail: Up-to-date vaccination → no further action. < 3 doses or unknown → start / continue tetanus toxoid (Td or Td-IPV) 0.5 mL IM. Last booster > 10 y → Td 0.5 mL IM booster.

Up-to-date (≥ 3 doses, last < 5 y) → no further action. > 5 y or < 3 doses / unknown → tetanus toxoid PLUS consider tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG) 250 IU IM (500 IU if > 24 h since injury) if high-risk contamination / heavy soil / faecal.
TIG 500 IU IM in ALL non-fully-vaccinated patients (regardless of vaccination history if any doubt). Plus complete tetanus toxoid series.
Thorough irrigation, debridement of devitalised tissue, foreign-body removal. Do NOT suture heavily contaminated wounds.
Not routinely indicated unless clinical infection. For animal bites: amoxicillin-clavulanate 5–7 days. For human bites: amoxicillin-clavulanate + tetanus + HIV PEP risk assessment.

references.label: WHO Position Paper on Tetanus Vaccines (2017)
CDC ACIP — Tetanus prophylaxis after wound

title: Primary hypothyroidism (adult)
presentation: Fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, hoarse voice, menorrhagia.
Bradycardia, slow-relaxing reflexes, periorbital puffiness, goitre (Hashimoto's).
Subclinical: raised TSH with normal free T4 — often asymptomatic.
Pregnancy: any TSH > 4 mIU/L warrants treatment due to foetal CNS risk.
redFlags: Myxoedema coma — hypothermia, hyporeflexia, bradycardia, hypotension, altered consciousness (mortality 20–25 %).
Coexistent untreated adrenal insufficiency — treat adrenal first.

diagnostics.rationale: Most sensitive test; raised in primary hypothyroidism.
Low confirms overt hypothyroidism; normal with raised TSH = subclinical.
Confirms Hashimoto's; predicts progression in subclinical disease.

management.detail: Start 50 µg once daily (1.6 µg/kg) on empty stomach 30–60 min before food. Reduce to 25 µg in elderly / cardiac disease / coronary heart disease. Repeat TSH at 6–8 weeks and adjust by 12.5–25 µg.
Non-pregnant: 0.4–4 mIU/L (lower half of range in symptomatic). Pregnancy: TSH < 2.5 mIU/L in first trimester; increase levothyroxine by 25–30 % at confirmation of pregnancy.
Treat if TSH > 10, symptomatic, antibody-positive, or planning pregnancy. Otherwise monitor 6-monthly.
Lifelong therapy; same brand if possible (bioequivalence varies). Take separately from iron / calcium / soy / PPIs / coffee — separate by 4 hours.
ICU. IV levothyroxine 200–400 µg loading then 50–100 µg/day + IV hydrocortisone 100 mg every 8 h (treat presumed adrenal insufficiency first). Passive rewarming.

references.label: ATA Guidelines for the Treatment of Hypothyroidism (2014)

title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD, adult)
presentation: Heartburn — retrosternal burning, worse after meals / lying down / bending.
Acid regurgitation, sour taste, water brash.
Atypical: chronic cough, hoarseness, dental erosion, asthma.
Often associated with hiatus hernia, obesity, smoking, alcohol.
redFlags: Dysphagia, odynophagia → urgent endoscopy (stricture, Barrett's, cancer).
Weight loss > 5 %, anaemia, vomiting blood / melaena.
Persistent symptoms > 4 weeks despite optimal PPI in patients ≥ 55 years.
Family history of upper GI cancer.

diagnostics.rationale: Treat empirically; no investigation needed if no alarm features.
Where diagnosis uncertain and refractory to PPI.

management.detail: Weight loss (5–10 %), smoking cessation, avoid trigger foods (coffee, alcohol, fatty / spicy), elevate head of bed 15 cm, avoid lying flat for 3 h after meals, smaller more frequent meals.
Antacids (Mg/Al hydroxide) + alginate (e.g. Gaviscon) — useful for breakthrough symptoms during PPI therapy.
Omeprazole 20 mg once daily 30 min before breakfast, 4–8 weeks. Reassess: if controlled, step down to lowest effective dose; if relapses on stopping, long-term PPI.
Twice-daily PPI for 8 weeks; refer for endoscopy. Consider H. pylori test-and-treat in refractory dyspepsia.
Laparoscopic fundoplication for severe refractory disease or PPI-intolerance — specialist referral.

references.label: NICE CG184 — Dyspepsia and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease

title: Burns assessment + initial management (adult)
presentation: Thermal, chemical, electrical, radiation burn — site, depth, mechanism, time of injury.
Depth: superficial (erythema, dry), partial-thickness (blisters, painful, blanching), full-thickness (leathery, dry, painless, white / charred).
Total body surface area (TBSA) using Wallace 'rule of nines' or Lund-Browder chart (children).
Inhalation injury — facial burns, singed nasal hair, hoarseness, soot in sputum, stridor.
redFlags: Airway compromise (stridor, hoarseness, facial / oral burns) — intubate early.
Burn TBSA > 20 % adult / > 10 % child / > 5 % elderly → admit + fluid resuscitation.
High-voltage electrical burn → cardiac monitoring + rhabdomyolysis screen.
Chemical burn → continuous irrigation; identify agent.

diagnostics.rationale: Rule of nines or palm-method (palm = 1 % of TBSA in adult).

management.detail: Airway protection (intubate early if inhalation suspected — oedema progresses for 24 h). Oxygen 100 % for CO toxicity. Two large-bore IV cannulae (preferably through unburned skin).
Lactated Ringer's 4 mL × kg × % TBSA over 24 h, HALF in the first 8 hours from time of injury. Titrate to urine output 0.5 mL/kg/h (1 mL/kg/h electrical / paediatric / inhalation).
Cool burns with running water for 20 min within 3 hours of injury. Cover with cling film. Topical silver sulfadiazine for partial-thickness burns (not face / pregnancy). Tetanus prophylaxis.
IV opioid titrated (morphine 0.1 mg/kg). Avoid IM (poor absorption in shock + delayed peaks).
All full-thickness burns, hand / face / perineum / major joints, electrical / chemical, inhalation, > 10 % TBSA. NPO + NG decompression for major burns.

title: Acute low back pain (adult, non-specific)
presentation: Acute pain (< 6 weeks) in lumbosacral region, may radiate to buttock or thigh.
Often follows lifting / awkward movement / prolonged sitting.
Most cases (> 90 %) are non-specific musculoskeletal pain — self-limiting.
redFlags: Cauda equina: bilateral leg weakness, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention / incontinence, faecal incontinence → URGENT MRI + spinal surgery.
Spinal cord compression: progressive bilateral neurology, ataxic gait.
Malignancy: history of cancer, weight loss > 5 %, age > 50 with new back pain, night pain.
Infection: fever, IV drug use, immunocompromise, recent invasive spinal procedure.
Fracture: significant trauma, age > 65 with osteoporosis, chronic steroid use, severe localised midline pain.
Inflammatory: morning stiffness > 30 min, age < 45 at onset, alternating buttock pain, improved with exercise (axial spondyloarthritis).

diagnostics.rationale: Imaging NOT indicated for non-specific back pain in first 6 weeks.
Cauda equina, suspected malignancy / infection / spondyloarthritis.
Red flags only — exclude infection / malignancy.

management.detail: Most pain resolves within 6 weeks. Stay active — bed rest delays recovery. Continue working where feasible.
Paracetamol 1 g four times daily + NSAID (ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily) for 1–2 weeks.
Topical NSAID (diclofenac gel) for localised pain. Short-course diazepam 5 mg at night × 5 days for severe muscle spasm.
Refer if no improvement at 2 weeks. Includes core strengthening, exercise prescription, manual therapy.
Routine spinal imaging, opioids (except short course for severe pain), bed rest > 48 h, traction, TENS as first-line.
Same approach + gabapentinoids if neuropathic features predominate.

references.label: NICE NG59 — Low back pain and sciatica in over-16s (2016)

title: Asthma (paediatric, 5–11 years)
presentation: Recurrent wheeze, cough (often nocturnal / exertional), shortness of breath, chest tightness.
Variable airflow obstruction reversible with bronchodilator.
Triggers: viral URTI (most common), allergens (house dust mite, pet dander, pollen), exercise, cold air, smoke.
redFlags: Silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, altered mental state.
Inability to feed / speak in full sentences.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical in this age group; spirometry from age 5 where available.
Track personal best; > 20 % variability between best and worst is supportive.
Where atopic phenotype suspected and trigger identification helps.

management.detail: Salbutamol 100 µg inhaler, 1–2 puffs via spacer as needed. If used > twice / week, step up. AVOID nebulisers in primary care for routine acute attacks — pMDI + spacer equally effective.
Add low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (beclomethasone 100 µg twice daily via spacer) OR montelukast 5 mg chewable at bedtime.
Increase to medium-dose ICS, OR add LABA (formoterol 6 µg twice daily) in a combination inhaler from age 5+. Specialist review if not controlled at step 3.
Salbutamol 6–10 puffs via spacer every 20 min for 1 h, oral prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg (max 40 mg) for 3 days.
Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg + ipratropium 250 µg every 20 min × 3, IV magnesium sulphate 40 mg/kg over 20 min (max 2 g), IV hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg, oxygen target 94–98 %, admit.
Personalised asthma action plan, inhaler technique check, trigger avoidance counselling, smoking exposure cessation, review at 1 week.

references.label: GINA Global Strategy for Asthma — Children 5–11 (2024)
BTS / SIGN British Guideline on the Management of Asthma

title: Cardiac arrest — basic life support + early defibrillation (adult)
presentation: Unresponsive person with no breathing or only abnormal (agonal) breathing.
No palpable carotid / femoral pulse for ≥ 10 seconds (do not delay CPR while assessing).
Witnessed sudden collapse OR found unresponsive.
redFlags: Time-critical — survival falls 7–10 % per minute without CPR + defibrillation.
Witnessed VF / pulseless VT has highest survival with early defibrillation.
Hypothermic arrest may require prolonged CPR; do not declare death until rewarmed.

diagnostics.rationale: Shout-shake; no response → activate emergency response.
Look at chest for ≤ 10 sec; agonal gasps = arrest.
Only for trained rescuers; absence triggers CPR.
Shockable (VF / pulseless VT) vs non-shockable (asystole / PEA).

management.detail: Activate emergency response. Send second person for AED. Begin compressions while AED is fetched.
Depth 5–6 cm, rate 100–120/min, allow full recoil, minimise interruptions (< 10 sec). Compressions only if untrained / unwilling to do rescue breaths.
30 : 2 (single rescuer or 2-rescuer adult). Switch compressors every 2 min to prevent fatigue. Children: 30:2 single rescuer / 15:2 two rescuer.
Apply AED pads, follow prompts. Shock if VF / pulseless VT; resume CPR immediately for 2 min before pulse / rhythm check.
Hypoxia, Hypovolaemia, Hypo/hyperkalaemia, Hypothermia; Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thromboembolism (PE / coronary). Treat any identified cause concurrently.
On ALS team arrival, give SBAR + duration of CPR + rhythm history + drugs given.
Targeted temperature management 32–36 °C × 24 h, optimise oxygenation (94–98 %) + BP (MAP ≥ 65), 12-lead ECG for STEMI → cath lab if appropriate.

title: Hyperthyroidism / thyrotoxicosis (adult)
presentation: Weight loss with preserved appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, palpitations, anxiety, tremor.
Tachycardia (or atrial fibrillation), warm peripheries, fine tremor, lid lag, brisk reflexes.
Graves' disease: diffuse goitre + ophthalmopathy (proptosis, periorbital oedema, lid retraction) + pretibial myxoedema.
Toxic nodular goitre or single toxic adenoma in older patients.
redFlags: Thyroid storm — fever ≥ 39 °C, severe tachycardia, heart failure, agitation / delirium / coma, multi-organ dysfunction. Mortality 10–30 % untreated.
Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response.
Severe ophthalmopathy threatening vision (corneal exposure, optic-nerve compression).

diagnostics.rationale: Suppressed TSH with raised T4 / T3 confirms overt thyrotoxicosis.
Distinguish Graves' (diffuse uptake) from toxic adenoma (focal) vs thyroiditis (low uptake).

management.detail: Propranolol 20–40 mg orally three times daily until euthyroid (controls tremor, tachycardia, anxiety). Avoid in asthma.

Carbimazole 15–40 mg daily for 4–6 weeks until euthyroid, then maintenance 5–15 mg daily for 12–18 months. Pregnancy first trimester: switch to propylthiouracil (PTU) 100–200 mg three times daily — less teratogenic.
Radio-iodine ablation (avoid in pregnancy + breastfeeding; check pregnancy test before). Total thyroidectomy (if compressive goitre, severe ophthalmopathy, pregnancy + ATD intolerance).

Beta-blocker (propranolol 60–80 mg orally every 4 h OR IV esmolol). Antithyroid drug (PTU loading 600–1000 mg orally then 200–250 mg every 4 h). Iodine 1 h after PTU (Lugol's solution 8 drops every 6 h). Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 8 h (blocks T4→T3 conversion). Cooling, fluids, treat precipitant (infection, surgery, iodinated contrast).
Return for sore throat, fever, mouth ulcers, jaundice (agranulocytosis / hepatotoxicity from carbimazole / PTU). Smoking cessation reduces Graves' ophthalmopathy progression.

title: Acute otitis externa (adult / child)
presentation: Ear pain (often severe), itching, fullness, hearing loss, discharge.
Painful tragus / pinna manipulation (cardinal sign).
Otoscopy: erythematous, oedematous ear canal, ± debris / pus.
Risk factors: swimming, hot humid climate, hearing aids, cotton-bud use, eczema, diabetes.
redFlags: Malignant (necrotising) otitis externa — diabetic / immunocompromised + severe pain, granulation tissue in canal, cranial-nerve palsy → admit, IV ciprofloxacin, refer urgently.
Suspected tympanic-membrane perforation — avoid aminoglycoside drops.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms ear-canal inflammation; visualise drum where possible.
Only for refractory or recurrent — common: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus.

management.detail: Gentle dry-mopping / suction by ENT-trained clinician removes debris and improves topical drug delivery. AVOID syringing.
Ciprofloxacin 0.3 % + dexamethasone drops, 4 drops three times daily for 7 days. Alternative: gentamicin + hydrocortisone (avoid if perforation).
Paracetamol + ibuprofen at full doses for 5–7 days.
Keep ear dry (cotton-wool ball + Vaseline during showering, no swimming for 2 weeks). Avoid cotton buds. Treat eczema if present.
Ear wick to deliver drops to oedematous canal. ENT referral if not improving in 7 days, or for recurrent disease.

references.label: NICE NG138 — Otitis externa antimicrobial prescribing (2018)

title: Acute conjunctivitis (bacterial / viral / allergic)
presentation: Red eye, discomfort / gritty sensation, discharge, sometimes both eyes (sequentially).
Bacterial: purulent / mucopurulent discharge, eyelids stuck on waking; preserved visual acuity.
Viral: watery discharge, often associated URI, follicular conjunctiva, pre-auricular lymphadenopathy; highly contagious.
Allergic: itching is prominent, papillary conjunctiva, bilateral, history of atopy.
redFlags: Pain (vs discomfort), photophobia, reduced visual acuity → exclude keratitis / uveitis / acute angle-closure glaucoma — REFER same-day ophthalmology.
Contact-lens wearer with red eye → microbial keratitis until proven otherwise (Pseudomonas).
Hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis in neonate / adult → suspect gonococcal (especially if associated genital symptoms) — needs systemic antibiotic + ophthalmology.

diagnostics.rationale: For hyperacute, neonatal, severe / refractory — exclude N. gonorrhoeae / chlamydia.

management.detail: Self-limiting (7–14 days). Cool compress, lubricant drops, hand hygiene + separate towels. AVOID antibiotic drops. Counsel return if vision drops / severe pain.
Often self-limiting in 5–7 days; offer topical chloramphenicol 0.5 % drops every 2 h for 48 h then four times daily for 5 days (or fusidic acid 1 % gel twice daily) for severe / persistent cases.
Trigger avoidance + oral antihistamine + topical mast-cell stabiliser / antihistamine (sodium cromoglicate, ketotifen) up to 4 times daily during season.
Urgent referral. Empirical IV / IM ceftriaxone 25–50 mg/kg single dose for gonococcal + oral azithromycin / erythromycin for chlamydia. Saline irrigation. Test mother and infant.
Same-day ophthalmology + topical fluoroquinolone + culture. Remove contact lenses; do not wear until cleared.

title: Vulvovaginal candidiasis (thrush)
presentation: Vulvar itching, soreness, burning; thick white 'cottage-cheese' discharge.
Vulvar erythema, oedema, fissuring; vaginal mucosa erythematous.
Risk factors: recent antibiotics, diabetes, pregnancy, immunosuppression, oral contraceptives, tight synthetic underwear.
redFlags: Recurrent (≥ 4 episodes / year) — suspect uncontrolled diabetes or immunodeficiency (HIV).
Severe / unusual: dysuria, abdominal pain → consider PID / coexistent STI.
First episode in pregnancy — confirm diagnosis (swab) and check fasting glucose.

diagnostics.rationale: Empirical treatment is usually appropriate for first episode in a non-pregnant adult.
Confirms Candida species; identifies non-albicans (glabrata, krusei) — fluconazole-resistant.

management.detail: Fluconazole 150 mg orally single dose, OR clotrimazole 500 mg pessary single dose + 1 % cream applied twice daily for 7 days.
AVOID oral fluconazole. Use clotrimazole 500 mg pessary + 1 % cream (7-day course). Repeat at 7 days if symptoms persist.
Induction: fluconazole 150 mg orally on days 1, 4, 7. Maintenance: 150 mg orally once weekly for 6 months. Counsel diabetes / HIV workup.
Avoid douching / scented products. Cotton underwear. Probiotics evidence is weak. Treat sexual partner only if symptomatic.

title: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH, adult male)
presentation: Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS): hesitancy, weak stream, intermittency, terminal dribble, incomplete emptying, frequency, urgency, nocturia.
International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS): mild ≤ 7, moderate 8–19, severe 20–35.
Examination: enlarged smooth prostate on DRE; absence of nodules or asymmetry.
redFlags: Acute urinary retention (painful distended bladder) — catheterise + admit.
Haematuria — exclude bladder cancer (CT urogram + cystoscopy).
Hard nodular prostate on DRE / very high PSA — exclude prostate cancer.

diagnostics.rationale: Exclude UTI as cause of LUTS.
Age-stratified reference range; trend more useful than single value.

management.detail: Reduce evening fluid, caffeine, alcohol. Bladder retraining for urgency. Pelvic-floor exercises. Treat constipation. Review medications causing retention (anticholinergics, alpha-agonists).
Tamsulosin 400 µg once daily — works within 2 weeks. Counsel postural hypotension (especially first dose), retrograde ejaculation, floppy-iris syndrome at cataract surgery.
Finasteride 5 mg once daily — for large prostate (> 30 mL); takes 3–6 months to work; reduces PSA by 50 % (double measured value for cancer screening); sexual side effects, gynaecomastia.
Tamsulosin + finasteride for moderate-to-severe LUTS with large prostate.
Acute retention, chronic retention, refractory symptoms, complications (UTI, stones, AKI). Surgical options: TURP, laser enucleation, prostatic urethral lift.

references.label: EAU Guidelines on Management of Non-neurogenic Male LUTS
NICE CG97 — Lower urinary tract symptoms in men

title: Perinatal depression — EPDS screening + management
presentation: Depressed mood, anhedonia, poor sleep / energy, change in appetite, guilt / worthlessness, poor concentration during pregnancy or in the year after delivery.
Often masked by 'baby blues' (resolves day 10) — perinatal depression persists beyond 2 weeks.
Risk factors: previous depression, social adversity, intimate-partner violence, lack of support, preterm / sick baby, unwanted pregnancy.
redFlags: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) item 10 (self-harm thoughts) > 0 → same-day mental-health pathway.
Psychotic features (delusions, hallucinations) → puerperal psychosis — urgent admission.
Plans / means / preparatory acts of suicide.
Thoughts of harming the baby — safeguard mother + child.

diagnostics.rationale: 10-item, self-administered; total ≥ 13 = probable depression; item 10 (self-harm) any non-zero = immediate review.

diagnostics.test: Risk assessment (suicide, harm to baby, IPV)
diagnostics.rationale: Mandatory if EPDS ≥ 13 or item 10 positive.

diagnostics.test: TSH, FBC, glucose, vitamin D, B12

management.detail: Watchful waiting + supportive care; psychoeducation; sleep optimisation; partner / family involvement. Re-screen at 4 weeks.

Psychological therapy first-line (CBT, IPT, problem-solving therapy) — typically 8–16 sessions. Add sertraline 50 mg daily if psychological therapy unavailable / preference / severe. Sertraline preferred SSRI in pregnancy + breastfeeding (lowest breast-milk transfer).
Do not leave alone. Same-day mental-health pathway. Remove access to means. Mobilise family / partner support. Consider hospitalisation if active plan or psychosis.
Sertraline 50 mg → titrate to 100 mg over 2–4 weeks; review at 2, 4, 8 weeks. Continue ≥ 6–12 months after remission. Avoid paroxetine in first trimester (cardiac malformations).
Routinely include infant — depression impacts bonding and child development. Refer to community / health-visitor support, peer groups, infant-mental-health services.

references.label: WHO mhGAP — Maternal and Child Mental Health
NICE CG192 — Antenatal and postnatal mental health (2014, updated)

title: Epilepsy — chronic management (adult)
presentation: Recurrent unprovoked seizures (≥ 2 separated by > 24 h) OR single seizure with high recurrence risk (≥ 60 % at 10 years).
Seizure types: focal-onset (aware / impaired awareness), generalised onset (tonic-clonic, absence, myoclonic), unknown onset.
Common SSA causes: idiopathic / genetic, perinatal injury, neurocysticercosis, post-traumatic, post-meningitic, structural lesions (HIV-related).
redFlags: Sudden deterioration of seizure control — adherence, sleep, infection, alcohol, drug interaction (e.g. tramadol).
Pregnancy + valproate — major teratogen (10–11 % malformation, neurodevelopmental impact 30–40 %); switch to lamotrigine / levetiracetam pre-conception.
SUDEP risk — counsel adherence, nocturnal supervision in poorly controlled epilepsy.

diagnostics.rationale: Supports diagnosis and classifies syndrome; routine EEG normal in 50 % between seizures.
All new-onset adult epilepsy unless idiopathic generalised pattern + family history.

management.detail: Focal onset: lamotrigine (slow titration, rash risk) OR levetiracetam (first-line, fewer interactions). Generalised tonic-clonic: sodium valproate (avoid women of childbearing potential) OR lamotrigine OR levetiracetam. Absence: ethosuximide OR lamotrigine. Myoclonic: levetiracetam OR valproate.
Start one drug, titrate over weeks to maximum tolerated dose before declaring failure. If first AED fails, switch (do not add) before considering dual therapy.

Adherence (single dose missed = double-dose at next scheduled time only if within 12 h). Avoid alcohol > 2 units / day. Driving restrictions per local law (typically 1 year seizure-free for car licence). Swimming with supervision. Pregnancy planning + folic acid 5 mg pre-conception.
Failure of 2 appropriately chosen AEDs at adequate doses. Refer specialist for surgical evaluation (temporal lobectomy), VNS, ketogenic diet.
Consider after 2 years seizure-free; taper over 6–12 months. Risk of recurrence 30–40 % over 2 years; counsel + driving restrictions during taper.

references.label: NICE NG217 — Epilepsies in children, young people and adults (2022)

title: Rheumatoid arthritis (adult)
presentation: Symmetrical polyarthritis of small joints (MCP, PIP, wrists) > 6 weeks.
Morning stiffness > 30 minutes.
Fatigue, weight loss, low-grade fever in active disease.
Late: ulnar deviation, swan-neck / boutonnière deformities, rheumatoid nodules.
redFlags: Atlanto-axial subluxation — neck pain, paraesthesiae, hyperreflexia → urgent imaging.
Pericarditis, vasculitis, interstitial lung disease — severe extra-articular disease.
Felty syndrome — RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia → infection risk.
Methotrexate / biologic immunosuppression → severe infection / TB reactivation / opportunistic infection.

diagnostics.rationale: Anti-CCP highly specific (95 %); ESR / CRP track disease activity.
Periarticular osteopaenia, marginal erosions; baseline + 1 year.
Disease-activity assessment (joint count + ESR / CRP + global VAS); guides treatment escalation.
FBC, U&E, LFT, HBsAg / anti-HCV / HIV, chest X-ray, IGRA (latent TB), pregnancy test, varicella titre.

management.detail: DAS-28 < 2.6 (remission) or < 3.2 (low activity); review every 3 months in active disease; escalate if not at target.
Methotrexate 7.5–10 mg ONCE WEEKLY + folic acid 5 mg once weekly. Titrate to 25 mg/week. Add sulfasalazine + hydroxychloroquine (triple therapy) if DAS-28 not at target at 3 months.
After failure of 2 csDMARDs at maximally tolerated dose. Options: TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab), IL-6 (tocilizumab), JAK inhibitors (baricitinib, tofacitinib). Specialist input.

NSAID (ibuprofen / naproxen) for short-term flares with PPI cover. Low-dose prednisolone 5–10 mg daily as bridging in early disease; intra-articular methylprednisolone for mono-articular flares. AVOID long-term steroid where possible.

Stop methotrexate ≥ 3 months pre-conception (both partners). Sulfasalazine / hydroxychloroquine / TNF inhibitors generally safe in pregnancy. Disease flares are common postpartum — reinstate DMARD early.
Annual CV risk assessment (RA confers excess risk equivalent to diabetes); statin if QRISK > 10 %. Bone-density scan if chronic steroid > 3 months / postmenopausal.

references.label: EULAR Recommendations for management of RA (2022 update)
NICE NG100 — Rheumatoid arthritis in adults (2018)

title: Obesity (adult)
presentation: Body mass index ≥ 30 kg/m² (≥ 27.5 in South / East Asian descent — WHO 2004 modifier).
Increased waist circumference (≥ 102 cm men / ≥ 88 cm women) = central obesity.
Often co-exists with T2DM, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, MASLD, OSA, osteoarthritis, depression.
redFlags: Class III obesity (BMI ≥ 40) — high anaesthetic / perioperative risk.
Symptoms of secondary cause: hypothyroidism, Cushing's syndrome, hypothalamic disease, medication-induced (steroid, antipsychotic).
Severe obstructive sleep apnoea — daytime sleepiness, witnessed apnoeas, BP control resistant.

diagnostics.rationale: BMI for class; WC adds CV risk discrimination.

diagnostics.test: Fasting glucose / HbA1c + lipids + LFT + TSH + cortisol where indicated

management.detail: Energy-deficit diet (500–750 kcal/day below baseline). Mediterranean or low-carb pattern acceptable. ≥ 150 min/week moderate aerobic + resistance training 2 days/week. Behavioural therapy + group support increase success. Target 5–10 % weight loss in 6 months.

After 6 months of lifestyle. Options: orlistat 120 mg three times daily with meals (GI side effects); GLP-1 receptor agonists — liraglutide 3 mg SC daily or semaglutide 2.4 mg SC weekly (mean weight loss 10–17 %). Bupropion-naltrexone, phentermine-topiramate alternatives.

BMI ≥ 40 OR ≥ 35 with comorbidity (T2DM, OSA, HTN). Roux-en-Y gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy — average 25–30 % total weight loss + diabetes remission rates 40–80 %. Lifelong vitamin / mineral supplementation.
