Senna 7.5–15 mg nocte. Bisacodyl 5–10 mg nocte. Sodium picosulfate. Add to / instead of osmotic. Long-term safe contrary to old myth (no tolerance / colonic damage at standard doses).
Linaclotide 290 µg OD (chronic idiopathic / IBS-C) — guanylate cyclase agonist. Plecanatide 3 mg OD. Prucalopride 2 mg OD (5-HT4 agonist). Lubiprostone (chloride channel).

Prophylactic laxative on starting opioid (osmotic + stimulant). PAMORA (peripheral µ-receptor antagonist) — methylnaltrexone SC, naloxegol 25 mg OD PO, naldemedine — for refractory OIC; do not reverse analgesia.

Disimpaction first: phosphate enema (avoid in elderly / renal — phosphate overload), glycerin suppository, manual evacuation, oral high-dose macrogol (Movicol 8 sachets/day × 3 days). Then ongoing maintenance laxative.
Anorectal biofeedback (gold standard for pelvic floor dyssynergia — refer specialist). Pelvic floor physiotherapy. Botulinum toxin.
Fibre + fluid + exercise. Bulk-forming. Osmotic (macrogol / lactulose) safe. Senna acceptable. Avoid stimulants long-term + prolonged. Avoid mineral oil (impaired vit absorption).

title: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)
presentation: Rome IV — recurrent abdominal pain ≥ 1 day/week × 3 months associated with ≥ 2 of: defecation, change in stool frequency, change in stool form
Subtypes: IBS-C (constipation predominant), IBS-D (diarrhoea), IBS-M (mixed), IBS-U (unsubtyped)
Often associated with bloating, gas, mucus per rectum
Women > men 2:1; 10–15 % of adults
Bidirectional gut-brain axis — anxiety + depression + stress trigger
Post-infectious IBS — onset after gastroenteritis (campylobacter, salmonella, giardia in SSA)
redFlags: PR bleeding, weight loss, anaemia, nocturnal symptoms, family history CRC / IBD / coeliac → investigate
Significant impact on quality of life — multidisciplinary

diagnostics.test: Clinical diagnosis — Rome IV criteria + minimal investigation
diagnostics.rationale: positive diagnosis not exclusion of organic

diagnostics.test: FBC, CRP, ESR, coeliac serology, faecal calprotectin
Stool ova + cysts + parasites — endemic areas + travel
Lactose hydrogen breath test — if intolerance suspected

management.detail: Explain Rome IV-positive diagnosis (not exclusionary). Reassurance. Lifestyle: regular meals, slow eating, hydration. Exercise. Stress management. Sleep hygiene. Patient information leaflet.

management.step: Diet — low FODMAP first-line dietary intervention
management.detail: Low FODMAP (fermentable oligo-/di-/mono-saccharides + polyols) × 4–8 weeks, then re-introduce one group at a time to identify triggers. Requires dietitian. ~70 % respond. Avoid permanent low-FODMAP (microbiome concerns). Trial gluten-free if non-coeliac gluten sensitivity. Limit caffeine, alcohol, fizzy drinks, fatty meals.

Antispasmodic (hyoscine, mebeverine, peppermint oil) — for pain + cramps. Loperamide for diarrhoea. Macrogol or linaclotide for constipation. Tricyclic antidepressant (amitriptyline 10–30 mg nocte) — visceral analgesic + mood; first-line for moderate-severe IBS-D + pain. SSRI (citalopram 20 mg) for IBS-C + co-morbid depression / anxiety. Eluxadoline / ramosetron / alosetron for severe IBS-D (specialist).

CBT (gut-directed) — most evidence; reduces symptoms + improves QoL. Hypnotherapy + mindfulness-based stress reduction. Refer for moderate-severe + impacting QoL. App-based CBT (e.g. Mahana IBS) emerging.
Bifidobacterium infantis 35624 + multi-strain probiotics × 4 weeks trial; discontinue if no benefit.
Cholestyramine / colesevelam — for bile acid malabsorption (common in IBS-D). 25 % respond.

Multidisciplinary clinic — GI + dietitian + psychologist + gastroenterologist. Address comorbid mental health, fibromyalgia, chronic pelvic pain. Avoid unnecessary investigations + reassurance. Self-management apps + groups.

title: Neurocysticercosis
presentation: Most common cause of acquired epilepsy in Taenia solium-endemic SSA settings
New-onset focal or generalised seizures in a young adult is the classic presentation
Headache, raised intracranial pressure, focal deficits depending on cyst location/stage
Acquired by faecal-oral ingestion of T. solium eggs (human is the carrier of the adult tapeworm)
Cyst stages: vesicular, colloidal, granular-nodular, calcified
redFlags: Signs of raised ICP / hydrocephalus (vomiting, papilloedema, reduced GCS)

diagnostics.rationale: demonstrates cysts ± scolex; calcified lesions on CT; perilesional oedema staging
supports diagnosis; sensitivity falls with single/calcified lesions
exclude intraocular cysts (treatment can cause vision loss)

management.detail: Control seizures first (e.g. carbamazepine, phenytoin, levetiracetam); many patients need only ASM if lesions are calcified.
Start dexamethasone/prednisolone BEFORE and during antiparasitic therapy to limit inflammatory response to dying cysts.
For viable parenchymal cysts: albendazole 15 mg/kg/day (± praziquantel for multiple cysts) × 10–14 days, only after ophthalmic exam and steroid cover; NOT for calcified-only disease.
Neurosurgical referral for intraventricular cysts or hydrocephalus (endoscopic removal / shunt); avoid antiparasitics until CSF flow secured.
Treat taeniasis carriers, sanitation, pork inspection, mass deworming where endemic.

title: Amoebic liver abscess
presentation: Entamoeba histolytica; common in SSA with poor sanitation
Fever, right-upper-quadrant pain, tender hepatomegaly, often without diarrhoea
Usually a single abscess in the right lobe
May follow weeks-months after intestinal amoebiasis
redFlags: Rupture into peritoneum, pleura or pericardium
Sepsis / large abscess with impending rupture

management.detail: Metronidazole 750 mg three times daily (or tinidazole) × 7–10 days — first-line; rapid clinical response.
Follow with diloxanide furoate or paromomycin to clear intestinal carriage and prevent relapse.
Image-guided drainage if large (>5 cm), left-lobe, no response at 5–7 days, or impending rupture.
Analgesia, hydration; sanitation and contact stool testing.

title: Giardiasis
presentation: Giardia duodenalis; faecal-oral / contaminated water
Chronic or relapsing watery, foul-smelling diarrhoea with bloating and flatulence
Steatorrhoea, weight loss, lactose intolerance after infection
Common cause of malabsorption in children in SSA
redFlags: Failure to thrive / significant weight loss

diagnostics.rationale: if high suspicion with negative stool

management.detail: Tinidazole 2 g single dose (adult) or metronidazole 400 mg three times daily × 5–7 days.
Metronidazole 15 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses × 5–7 days; tinidazole 50 mg/kg single dose.
Nitazoxanide or albendazole for treatment failure / intolerance.
ORS as needed; treat household contacts, safe water and sanitation.

title: Strongyloidiasis
presentation: Strongyloides stercoralis; soil-transmitted, can autoinfect and persist for decades
Often asymptomatic; abdominal pain, intermittent diarrhoea, urticaria, larva currens (migratory serpiginous rash)
Eosinophilia is a common clue
Risk of hyperinfection with corticosteroids/HTLV-1/immunosuppression
redFlags: Hyperinfection / disseminated disease (sepsis, ileus, ARDS, Gram-negative/polymicrobial bacteraemia, meningitis)
Before starting corticosteroids or immunosuppression in an endemic-area patient — screen/treat first

management.detail: Ivermectin 200 µg/kg/day × 1–2 days is first-line and superior to albendazole.
Empirically treat at-risk patients from endemic areas before steroids/chemotherapy.
Daily ivermectin until stool negative ≥2 weeks, broad-spectrum antibiotics for translocation sepsis, ICU support.
Resolution of eosinophilia and negative follow-up stool/serology.

title: Loiasis (Loa loa)
presentation: Loa loa filaria transmitted by Chrysops (deer) flies in Central/West African rainforests
Calabar swellings (transient localised angioedema)
Subconjunctival migration of the adult worm ("eye worm")
Eosinophilia; many co-endemic with onchocerciasis/LF
redFlags: High microfilarial load (>30,000 mf/mL) — risk of fatal encephalopathy with ivermectin/DEC

diagnostics.rationale: sheathed microfilariae; quantify load before treatment
screen for onchocerciasis and LF before microfilaricidal therapy

management.detail: Mandatory before treatment — high loads contraindicate standard ivermectin/DEC due to encephalopathy risk.
Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) curative for adult worms; albendazole to slowly reduce high loads first.
Pre-treat with albendazole ± apheresis to lower load before DEC, under specialist care.
Surgical removal under topical anaesthetic if accessible plus systemic therapy.

title: Trachoma
presentation: Chlamydia trachomatis (serovars A–C); leading infectious cause of blindness, hyperendemic in parts of SSA
Active disease: follicular/intense inflammation of the upper tarsal conjunctiva (children)
Cicatricial disease: conjunctival scarring, trichiasis, corneal opacity (adults, women > men)
Spread by eye-seeking flies, fomites, fingers in dry crowded settings
redFlags: Trichiasis (in-turned lashes touching the globe) — sight-threatening, urgent surgery

diagnostics.test: WHO simplified grading (TF, TI, TT, TS, CO)

management.detail: WHO programme: Surgery for trichiasis, Antibiotics, Facial cleanliness, Environmental improvement.
Bilamellar tarsal rotation for trichiasis to prevent blindness.
Azithromycin 20 mg/kg single oral dose (max 1 g) for the individual and mass drug administration where TF prevalence ≥5%; tetracycline eye ointment as alternative.
Promote face-washing and access to water/sanitation, reduce fly breeding.

title: Vitamin A deficiency / xerophthalmia
presentation: Leading cause of preventable childhood blindness in SSA
Night blindness is the earliest symptom
Conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spots, corneal xerosis progressing to keratomalacia
Associated with measles, diarrhoea, malnutrition and increased mortality
redFlags: Corneal ulceration/keratomalacia — ocular emergency, risk of permanent blindness

diagnostics.rationale: night blindness, Bitot's spots, corneal involvement
confirms deficiency where available (not required to treat)

management.detail: WHO schedule: age <6 m 50,000 IU, 6–11 m 100,000 IU, ≥12 m 200,000 IU orally on day 1, day 2 and day 14.
Manage measles, diarrhoea and malnutrition concurrently; protect/lubricate the cornea.
Routine vitamin A supplementation programmes, dietary diversification, fortification, breastfeeding.
Urgent ophthalmology for corneal involvement.

title: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency
presentation: X-linked enzymopathy; high prevalence in malaria-endemic SSA (offers some malaria protection)
Episodic acute haemolysis triggered by oxidant drugs, infection, or fava beans
Triggers: primaquine/tafenoquine, dapsone, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, naphthalene
Neonatal jaundice; usually asymptomatic between crises
redFlags: Severe haemolysis with haemoglobinuria, acute kidney injury, profound anaemia
Before prescribing primaquine/tafenoquine or dapsone — test G6PD status

diagnostics.rationale: diagnose deficiency; may be falsely normal during acute haemolysis (test after recovery)

management.detail: Stop the oxidant drug; counsel on lifelong avoidance list and fava beans.
Hydration, monitor Hb and renal function; transfuse for severe symptomatic anaemia.
Confirm G6PD status before primaquine/tafenoquine radical cure of P. vivax/ovale; weekly primaquine regimen where mild deficiency.
Phototherapy/exchange transfusion per bilirubin thresholds.

title: Measles (clinical)
presentation: Highly contagious paramyxovirus; recurrent SSA outbreaks where coverage is low
Prodrome: high fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis (the 3 C's), Koplik spots
Maculopapular rash from day 3–4 spreading cephalocaudally
Immunosuppression predisposes to complications

management.detail: Give vitamin A on day 1 and day 2 to all children with measles (age-based dosing) — reduces mortality.
Antipyretics, fluids/ORS, nutrition; treat secondary bacterial pneumonia/otitis with antibiotics.
Airborne precautions; notify public health, ring vaccination of contacts.
Two-dose measles vaccination; post-exposure MMR within 72 h or immunoglobulin for vulnerable contacts.

title: Pertussis (whooping cough)
presentation: Bordetella pertussis; most severe in unimmunised infants
Catarrhal stage then paroxysmal coughing fits with inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting
Infants may present with apnoea and cyanosis rather than whoop
Cough may persist for weeks ("100-day cough")
redFlags: Apnoea, cyanosis or bradycardia in an infant

diagnostics.rationale: marked lymphocytosis supports diagnosis in infants

management.detail: Azithromycin (or clarithromycin/erythromycin) — most effective in the catarrhal phase; reduces transmission even if cough persists.
Monitoring for apnoea, oxygen, feeding support; ICU for severe cases.
Macrolide for close contacts, especially infants/pregnant women in the household.
Primary DTP/pentavalent immunisation and maternal pertussis vaccination in pregnancy.

title: Diphtheria
presentation: Corynebacterium diphtheriae; outbreaks where immunisation coverage falls
Sore throat with an adherent grey pseudomembrane on the tonsils/pharynx that bleeds when scraped
Bull-neck cervical lymphadenopathy
Toxin causes myocarditis and neuropathy; cutaneous form in the tropics
redFlags: Airway obstruction from the membrane — emergency
Any clinical suspicion — isolate and treat without waiting for culture

diagnostics.rationale: do not delay antitoxin for laboratory confirmation

management.detail: Give equine diphtheria antitoxin urgently on clinical suspicion (after hypersensitivity testing) — neutralises unbound toxin; benefit falls with delay.
Benzylpenicillin or a macrolide × 14 days to eradicate the organism and stop toxin production.
ENT/ICU for airway compromise; telemetry for myocarditis.
Strict isolation, notify, antibiotic prophylaxis + vaccination of contacts, immunise the patient on recovery.

title: Yellow fever
presentation: Flavivirus transmitted by Aedes/Haemagogus mosquitoes; endemic in tropical SSA
Acute phase: fever, headache, myalgia, conjunctival injection, relative bradycardia (Faget sign)
Toxic phase (~15%): jaundice, haemorrhage, renal failure, high mortality
Vaccine-preventable

diagnostics.rationale: confirm; cross-reacts with other flaviviruses — confirm with PRNT
assess hepatic, renal and bleeding severity

management.detail: No specific antiviral — fluids, correct coagulopathy, manage renal failure, ICU for toxic phase.
Bleeding risk; use paracetamol for fever/pain.
Bed nets/vector control during viraemia to prevent transmission.
Single-dose yellow fever vaccine gives lifelong immunity; outbreak response vaccination and vector control; notify WHO/IHR.

title: Brucellosis
presentation: Brucella spp. from unpasteurised dairy or contact with infected livestock; common in pastoralist SSA communities
Undulating fever, drenching sweats, arthralgia, fatigue, hepatosplenomegaly
Focal disease: sacroiliitis/spondylitis, orchitis, endocarditis, neurobrucellosis
Often chronic/relapsing

diagnostics.rationale: definitive but low yield; alert lab to suspicion (biohazard)

diagnostics.test: Imaging (MRI spine, echo) for focal disease

management.detail: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily × 6 weeks PLUS either streptomycin/gentamicin (first 2–3 weeks) or rifampicin × 6 weeks — combination reduces relapse.
Prolonged (≥3 months) triple therapy; surgery for endocarditis/abscess; specialist input.
Rifampicin-based regimens (avoid doxycycline/aminoglycoside in pregnancy).
Pasteurisation, animal vaccination, protective equipment for abattoir/farm workers.

title: Cutaneous anthrax
presentation: Bacillus anthracis from contact with infected livestock/hides; commonest anthrax form in SSA
Painless papule → vesicle → black necrotic eschar with marked surrounding non-pitting oedema
Regional lymphadenopathy, low-grade fever
History of contact with sick/dead animals or animal products
redFlags: Extensive oedema of head/neck threatening the airway
Systemic features / suspected inhalational or GI anthrax

diagnostics.test: Gram stain + culture of lesion fluid / blood
diagnostics.rationale: Gram-positive boxcar rods; alert lab (biohazard) before antibiotics

management.detail: Uncomplicated cutaneous: oral ciprofloxacin or doxycycline × 7–10 days; switch to IV combination therapy if systemic/extensive.
Surgery worsens outcomes; allow the eschar to separate.
IV ciprofloxacin + clindamycin/linezolid (± antitoxin) and supportive care for systemic anthrax.
Notify, investigate animal source, vaccinate/treat at-risk handlers, safe carcass disposal.

references.label: WHO Anthrax in humans and animals guidance

title: Plague (Yersinia pestis)
presentation: Yersinia pestis; endemic foci in SSA (notably Madagascar, DRC)
Bubonic: sudden fever with a tender, swollen lymph node (bubo) after a flea bite
Septicaemic: sepsis, DIC, acral gangrene
Pneumonic: rapidly fatal pneumonia, person-to-person spread
redFlags: Pneumonic plague — droplet isolation, public-health emergency

diagnostics.rationale: bipolar "safety-pin" Gram-negative bacilli; alert lab (high biohazard)

management.detail: Streptomycin or gentamicin first-line; alternatives ciprofloxacin or doxycycline — start within hours of suspicion.
Droplet precautions for suspected/confirmed pneumonic plague until 48 h of effective therapy.
Fluid resuscitation, manage DIC and shock.
Notify immediately, post-exposure prophylaxis (doxycycline/ciprofloxacin) for contacts, flea/rodent control.

title: Hydatid disease (cystic echinococcosis)
presentation: Echinococcus granulosus larval cysts from dog tapeworm eggs; common in livestock-rearing SSA regions
Slow-growing cysts, most often in the liver then lung; often asymptomatic for years
Hepatomegaly, RUQ pain, or chest symptoms with lung cysts
Anaphylaxis risk if a cyst ruptures
redFlags: Cyst rupture → anaphylaxis or secondary dissemination

diagnostics.rationale: characterises liver cysts and stage (active vs inactive)
supports diagnosis; negative does not exclude

management.detail: Match treatment to cyst stage: PAIR/surgery for active cysts, watch-and-wait for inactive (CE4/CE5).
10–15 mg/kg/day; alone for small cysts and as peri-procedural cover (start before and continue after PAIR/surgery to prevent spillage recurrence).
Puncture-Aspiration-Injection-Reaspiration for suitable hepatic cysts under albendazole cover.
For large/complicated/superficial cysts; meticulous technique to avoid spillage; treat anaphylaxis if rupture.

title: Tungiasis (jiggers)
presentation: Tunga penetrans sand flea burrows into the skin, usually of the feet; a poverty-related NTD in SSA
Itchy/painful papule with a central black dot, on toes/soles/periungual skin
Multiple lesions cause inflammation, fissures, difficulty walking
Affects mainly children and the elderly in resource-poor settings
redFlags: Secondary bacterial infection, abscess, or ascending cellulitis
Auto-amputation/deformity of digits with heavy infestation

diagnostics.rationale: characteristic lesion with central punctum on the feet

management.detail: Sterile extraction of the flea or topical dimeticone occlusion; keep wounds clean.
Treat secondary bacterial infection; ensure tetanus prophylaxis.
Closed footwear, treat household/animal reservoirs, improve flooring/hygiene.
Community-level control reduces reinfestation.

title: Podoconiosis
presentation: Non-filarial elephantiasis from long-term barefoot exposure to irritant red-clay volcanic soils; endemic in SSA highlands
Bilateral but often asymmetric lower-leg lymphoedema, usually below the knee and ascending
Itching, burning, 'mossy' papillomatous skin changes; NOT caused by filaria
Strong familial/genetic susceptibility; affects barefoot farming communities
redFlags: Recurrent acute dermatolymphangioadenitis (painful 'acute attacks' with fever)

diagnostics.rationale: distinguish from lymphatic filariasis (geography, bilaterality, foot-onset)

management.detail: Daily washing, drying, emollients, elevation and compression bandaging/stockings — mainstay that reverses early disease.
Consistent shoe-wearing is preventive and therapeutic.
Rest, elevation, analgesia and antibiotics for superimposed bacterial infection.
Nodulectomy for advanced 'mossy' disease in selected patients; community-based morbidity management.

title: Cataract
presentation: Leading cause of blindness in SSA, largely from a surgical backlog
Painless, gradual, progressive blurring of vision and glare
Lens opacity on a white/reduced red reflex
Age-related most common; also diabetic, traumatic, congenital, steroid-induced
redFlags: Congenital/paediatric cataract — urgent referral to prevent amblyopia
Sudden vision change suggesting another pathology

diagnostics.rationale: grade the cataract, assess the posterior segment / red reflex

management.detail: Definitive treatment — small-incision cataract surgery (SICS) or phacoemulsification with intraocular lens; high-volume programmes address the SSA backlog.
Operate bilateral/severe cases first; manage expectations and biometry.
Topical steroid/antibiotic, monitor for endophthalmitis and posterior capsule opacification.
Optimise diabetes; protect against UV; review steroid use.

references.label: WHO Blindness and vision impairment guidance

title: Chronic suppurative otitis media
presentation: Persistent (≥2 weeks) ear discharge through a perforated tympanic membrane; common in SSA children
Painless or mildly painful otorrhoea, conductive hearing loss
Often follows untreated/recurrent acute otitis media
Cholesteatoma may complicate longstanding disease
redFlags: Intracranial spread (meningitis, brain abscess, sinus thrombosis) — headache, fever, neurological signs
Cholesteatoma (foul discharge, attic crust) — surgical referral

diagnostics.rationale: perforation, discharge, granulation, attic crust suggesting cholesteatoma
guides therapy in non-resolving cases (Pseudomonas, Proteus, Staph)

management.detail: Regular dry mopping/wicking is the cornerstone — keep the ear dry.
Topical ciprofloxacin drops (quinolones preferred — non-ototoxic) outperform systemic antibiotics for uncomplicated CSOM; WHO advises against routine systemic antibiotics.
Systemic antibiotics + urgent ENT/surgery (mastoidectomy/tympanoplasty) for complications or cholesteatoma.
Audiology and hearing rehabilitation; prompt treatment of acute otitis media, keep water out of the ear.

references.label: WHO Chronic suppurative otitis media guidance

title: Epistaxis (nosebleed)
presentation: Most bleeds are anterior from Little's area (Kiesselbach plexus)
Posterior bleeds (older, hypertensive, anticoagulated patients) are heavier and harder to control
Precipitants: trauma/nose-picking, dry air, hypertension, anticoagulants, coagulopathy, tumours
redFlags: Haemodynamic compromise / large-volume or posterior bleed
Bleeding on anticoagulants or with a known coagulopathy
Recurrent unilateral epistaxis with nasal obstruction (exclude tumour, e.g. nasopharyngeal carcinoma/angiofibroma)

diagnostics.rationale: identify the bleeding point (often anterior septum)
if heavy, recurrent, anticoagulated or coagulopathy suspected

management.detail: Sit forward, pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for 10–15 minutes, ice/cold; avoids swallowing blood.
Topical anaesthetic/vasoconstrictor then silver-nitrate cautery of an identified anterior bleeding point.
Anterior packing (e.g. nasal tampon) if cautery fails; posterior packing/balloon for posterior bleeds — admit.
ENT referral for endoscopic control, sphenopalatine artery ligation or embolisation; correct coagulopathy and reverse anticoagulation as needed.

title: Bell's palsy
presentation: Acute idiopathic lower-motor-neuron facial (VII) palsy, likely post-viral (HSV reactivation)
Rapid (<72 h) unilateral facial weakness INCLUDING the forehead
Loss of nasolabial fold, incomplete eye closure, drooling
May have post-auricular pain, altered taste, hyperacusis
redFlags: Forehead sparing or other cranial nerve/limb signs → suspect a central (stroke) lesion — urgent
Vesicles in the ear/palate (Ramsay Hunt — herpes zoster oticus)
Bilateral palsy or systemic features (Lyme, GBS, sarcoid, parotid tumour)
Inability to close the eye — corneal protection needed

diagnostics.rationale: LMN pattern with forehead involvement and no other neurology
exclude Ramsay Hunt and parotid mass

management.detail: Prednisolone (e.g. 50–60 mg/day × 10 days, ideally within 72 h of onset) improves recovery.
Add aciclovir/valaciclovir for severe palsy or suspected Ramsay Hunt (with steroids).
Lubricating drops by day, ointment + taping/eye patch at night to prevent exposure keratopathy — essential while the eye cannot close.
Most recover in weeks–months; refer if no improvement by 3 weeks, atypical features, or incomplete recovery for physiotherapy/specialist review.

title: Dementia (including Alzheimer's disease)
presentation: Progressive decline in memory and ≥1 other cognitive domain impairing daily function
Alzheimer's: insidious memory-led decline; vascular: stepwise with vascular risk factors; also Lewy body and frontotemporal
Behavioural and psychological symptoms (agitation, depression, psychosis) are common
Rising prevalence in SSA; under-diagnosed
redFlags: Rapid progression or young onset — investigate for reversible/secondary causes
Delirium superimposed (acute change) — find the precipitant
Safety risks: wandering, driving, self-neglect, falls
Severe behavioural disturbance or risk to self/others

diagnostics.test: Cognitive testing (MMSE/MoCA or culturally validated tools)

diagnostics.rationale: TFTs, B12/folate, calcium, glucose, HIV, syphilis serology where relevant
exclude tumour/SDH/NPH and assess vascular/atrophy pattern
confirm decline and impact on ADLs

management.detail: Correct B12/thyroid/depression, optimise vascular risk factors, review deliriogenic drugs.
Donepezil/rivastigmine/galantamine for mild–moderate Alzheimer's/Lewy body; memantine for moderate–severe or as add-on.
Cognitive stimulation, structured routine, caregiver education and support, advance care planning.
First-line non-drug strategies; reserve low-dose antipsychotics for severe agitation/psychosis with risk, time-limited (caution: stroke/mortality risk, avoid in Lewy body).

title: Parkinson's disease
presentation: Progressive neurodegenerative disorder from dopaminergic nigrostriatal loss
Cardinal features: bradykinesia plus resting tremor and/or rigidity, usually asymmetrical onset
Postural instability later; non-motor features: hyposmia, constipation, REM-sleep disorder, depression
Good initial response to levodopa supports the diagnosis
redFlags: Early falls, symmetrical signs, rapid progression or poor levodopa response — suspect atypical parkinsonism
Neuroleptic malignant / sudden withdrawal of dopaminergic therapy

diagnostics.test: Clinical diagnosis (UK Brain Bank / MDS criteria)

diagnostics.rationale: exclude vascular/structural mimics (DaT scan where available)

management.detail: Most effective symptomatic therapy; first-line where disability affects function — titrate to response.
Options in younger patients or as adjuncts; weigh impulse-control and neuropsychiatric side effects.

management.step: Do not abruptly stop dopaminergic drugs
management.detail: Risk of akinetic crisis / NMS-like state; maintain dosing including during illness/admission.
Physiotherapy, OT, speech/swallow therapy; treat non-motor symptoms (constipation, depression, psychosis with caution).

references.label: MDS Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for PD

title: Pellagra (niacin deficiency)
presentation: Niacin (vitamin B3)/tryptophan deficiency; seen with maize-dependent diets, alcoholism, malabsorption, isoniazid use
Classic triad — the 4 D's: Dermatitis, Diarrhoea, Dementia (and Death if untreated)
Photosensitive, symmetrical, pigmented dermatitis (Casal's necklace) on sun-exposed skin
Glossitis, neuropsychiatric changes (confusion, irritability)
redFlags: Coexisting severe malnutrition or alcoholism with Wernicke risk

diagnostics.rationale: thiamine, B12, folate, zinc — common in malnutrition

management.detail: Nicotinamide (preferred — no flushing) 100 mg three times daily orally, or IV in severe disease, until resolution.
Balanced diet, B-complex, manage alcoholism/malabsorption; review isoniazid (give pyridoxine).
Skin protection from sunlight, rehydration, nutritional rehabilitation.
Dietary diversification and fortification in maize-dependent populations.

references.label: WHO Pellagra prevention and control in emergencies

title: Dengue fever
presentation: Flavivirus transmitted by Aedes aegypti; rising arboviral burden in urban SSA
High fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia/arthralgia ('breakbone'), rash
Critical (defervescence, days 3–7) phase: plasma leakage → warning signs/shock; thrombocytopenia
Severe dengue more likely with secondary heterotypic infection
redFlags: Warning signs: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, hepatomegaly, rising HCT with falling platelets
Severe dengue: shock, severe bleeding, organ impairment

diagnostics.rationale: confirm; NS1 best in first days

management.detail: Outpatient if no warning signs; admit warning signs; ICU for severe dengue.
Oral fluids if tolerating; judicious isotonic crystalloid for warning signs/shock guided by HCT and urine output — avoid both under- and over-resuscitation.
Bleeding risk; use paracetamol for fever/pain.
Serial HCT/platelets and vitals through the critical phase; mosquito avoidance/source reduction; notify.

references.label: WHO Dengue guidelines for diagnosis, treatment, prevention and control

title: Rabies (clinical disease)
presentation: Lyssavirus from a bite/scratch of an infected animal (mostly dogs in SSA); essentially 100% fatal once symptomatic
Prodrome: fever, paraesthesia/pain at the bite site
Furious rabies: hydrophobia, aerophobia, agitation, autonomic instability
Paralytic rabies: ascending flaccid paralysis
redFlags: Any symptomatic rabies — palliative focus; near-universally fatal
Prevention is the priority: a fresh bite is an emergency for post-exposure prophylaxis (see rabies PEP)

diagnostics.test: Antemortem testing (saliva RT-PCR, nuchal skin biopsy)
diagnostics.rationale: where available; do not delay decisions

management.detail: Once symptomatic, survival is exceptional — emphasise PEP after any exposure: wound washing, rabies immunoglobulin + vaccine series.
Sedation (benzodiazepines/opioids), quiet environment, treat agitation and autonomic storms; involve family.
Standard/barrier precautions; PEP for exposed carers/contacts.
Notify; promote dog vaccination and bite-prevention programmes (target: zero dog-mediated human rabies by 2030).

title: Scorpion sting envenomation
presentation: Neurotoxic envenomation; severe in young children (notably Androctonus/Leiurus species in North/Sahelian Africa)
Local: intense pain, paraesthesia at the sting site
Systemic autonomic storm: sweating, hypersalivation, vomiting, hypertension/tachycardia then hypotension
Severe: pulmonary oedema, myocarditis, neuromuscular signs
redFlags: Cardiorespiratory: pulmonary oedema, cardiogenic shock, myocarditis

management.detail: Pain control (local anaesthetic infiltration/systemic analgesia), reassurance, wound care, tetanus prophylaxis.
Species-specific scorpion antivenom where available for systemic/severe cases, especially children — give early.
Prazosin (alpha-blockade) for the autonomic syndrome/pulmonary oedema; supportive cardiorespiratory care and ICU for severe cases.
Observe systemic cases for cardiorespiratory deterioration; avoid atropine unless symptomatic bradycardia.

title: Primary open-angle glaucoma
presentation: Chronic progressive optic neuropathy; a leading cause of irreversible blindness in SSA (often advanced at presentation)
Painless, insidious loss of peripheral vision; central vision preserved until late
Raised intraocular pressure is the main modifiable risk factor (but can be normal-tension)
Optic disc cupping (increased cup-to-disc ratio)
redFlags: Advanced field loss / very high IOP at presentation
Acute angle-closure (painful red eye, haloes) — different emergency

diagnostics.rationale: raised pressure; baseline for treatment targets

diagnostics.test: Dilated optic disc exam / cup-to-disc ratio

management.detail: Prostaglandin analogue (e.g. latanoprost) once at night — most effective; alternatives/add-ons: beta-blocker (timolol — caution in asthma/COPD), carbonic-anhydrase inhibitor, alpha-agonist.
Selective laser trabeculoplasty as primary or adjunct therapy where available.
Trabeculectomy (or drainage device) for progression despite maximal medical therapy.
Regular IOP, disc and field review; emphasise adherence; screen first-degree relatives.

references.label: ICO Guidelines for Glaucoma Eye Care

title: Corneal ulcer (microbial keratitis)
presentation: Sight-threatening corneal infection; often follows trauma (vegetative/agricultural injury — fungal common in SSA)
Painful red eye, photophobia, watering, reduced vision, white corneal infiltrate/ulcer
Hypopyon (layered pus in the anterior chamber) in severe cases
Causes: bacterial, fungal (Fusarium/Aspergillus), Acanthamoeba (contact lens), herpetic
redFlags: Any corneal ulcer is an emergency — risk of perforation and blindness
Hypopyon, large/central or rapidly enlarging ulcer

diagnostics.rationale: stains the epithelial defect; characterise size/depth

management.detail: Same-day specialist care; do NOT patch an infected eye; stop contact-lens wear.
Hourly broad-spectrum topical antibiotic (e.g. fluoroquinolone or fortified cefuroxime+gentamicin); add topical antifungal (natamycin) for suspected fungal keratitis.
Can worsen fungal/herpetic disease — specialist decision only.
Cycloplegia for pain, treat raised IOP, daily review; corneal gluing/graft for impending/actual perforation.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the management of corneal ulcer

title: Pterygium
presentation: Fibrovascular conjunctival growth onto the cornea, usually nasal; linked to chronic UV/dust exposure — common in equatorial SSA outdoor workers
Often asymptomatic; redness, irritation, foreign-body sensation
Astigmatism or visual-axis encroachment with growth
redFlags: Growth threatening or crossing the visual axis
Atypical/rapidly growing lesion (exclude ocular surface neoplasia)
Significant astigmatism or restricted eye movement

diagnostics.rationale: characteristic triangular fibrovascular lesion; document size and corneal encroachment

management.detail: Lubricants and short topical anti-inflammatories for irritation; UV-protective sunglasses and dust avoidance.
For visual-axis threat, marked astigmatism, recurrent inflammation or cosmesis — autograft markedly lowers recurrence vs bare-sclera.
Adjuncts (e.g. mitomycin-C) in selected/recurrent cases; continued UV protection.
Monitor for recurrence and astigmatic change.

title: Ophthalmia neonatorum (neonatal conjunctivitis)
presentation: Conjunctivitis in the first 28 days of life; gonococcal and chlamydial forms are sight-threatening
Gonococcal (days 2–5): hyperacute, profuse purulent discharge, marked lid oedema — corneal perforation risk
Chlamydial (days 5–14): mucopurulent, may be associated with pneumonia
Acquired during passage through an infected birth canal
redFlags: Hyperacute purulent discharge / corneal involvement (gonococcal) — emergency, perforation risk

diagnostics.test: Conjunctival swab — Gram stain, culture, NAAT

management.detail: Single dose ceftriaxone (e.g. 25–50 mg/kg IM/IV, max 125 mg) PLUS frequent saline eye irrigation; admit — sight-threatening.
Oral erythromycin (or azithromycin) × 14 days (topical alone is insufficient; covers associated pneumonia).
Treat mother and partners for the relevant STI.
Routine neonatal ocular prophylaxis (e.g. tetracycline/erythromycin ointment) and antenatal STI screening/treatment.

title: Sigmoid volvulus
presentation: Twisting of a redundant sigmoid colon causing closed-loop large-bowel obstruction; disproportionately common in SSA (high-fibre diet, megacolon)
Gross abdominal distension, absolute constipation, colicky pain, vomiting (late)
Often older or institutionalised patients; recurrent episodes
Plain film: 'coffee-bean'/inverted-U loop arising from the pelvis
redFlags: Peritonism, fever, tachycardia → ischaemia/perforation — emergency laparotomy

diagnostics.rationale: classic coffee-bean sign of a dilated sigmoid loop
assess for ischaemia and resuscitation needs

management.detail: IV fluids, nasogastric decompression, correct electrolytes, analgesia.
Flexible sigmoidoscopy/rigid scope decompression with a flatus tube if no signs of ischaemia — relieves the acute obstruction.
Elective sigmoid colectomy after successful decompression (high recurrence); emergency resection (± Hartmann's) if ischaemia/perforation or failed detorsion.
For recurrence and signs of bowel compromise post-decompression.

title: Acute intestinal obstruction
presentation: Mechanical blockage of the bowel; SSA causes include hernias (commonest), adhesions, volvulus, TB, ascariasis, malignancy
Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distension, absolute constipation (no flatus/faeces)
High obstruction → early vomiting; low obstruction → marked distension, later vomiting
Examine all hernial orifices (obstructed hernia is a leading SSA cause)
redFlags: Peritonitis, fever, tachycardia, raised lactate → strangulation/perforation — emergency surgery

diagnostics.rationale: dilated loops, air-fluid levels; small- vs large-bowel pattern
site, cause, and signs of ischaemia

management.detail: IV fluids, correct electrolytes, NG tube ('drip and suck'), urinary catheter, analgesia, antiemetics.
Reduce/repair an obstructed hernia, detort a volvulus, deworm for ascaris bolus; trial conservative management for adhesional SBO without ischaemia.
Laparotomy for strangulation, perforation, complete/closed-loop obstruction, or failed conservative therapy — resect non-viable bowel.
Broad-spectrum cover for strangulation/perforation; serial examination.

title: Incarcerated / strangulated hernia
presentation: A hernia (inguinal commonest) that cannot be reduced; strangulation = compromised blood supply to its contents
Painful, tense, irreducible groin/abdominal-wall lump, often with overlying erythema
May present as bowel obstruction (vomiting, distension)
Untreated inguinal hernia is a major cause of preventable obstruction/death in SSA
redFlags: Strangulation: severe pain, tenderness, erythema, systemic toxicity → emergency surgery
Features of bowel obstruction or peritonitis

diagnostics.rationale: tense irreducible mass; assess for tenderness/skin changes and obstruction

management.step: Do NOT force reduction if strangulated
management.detail: Forced reduction of compromised bowel risks reducing dead bowel into the abdomen.

management.step: Gentle reduction of an incarcerated, non-strangulated hernia
management.detail: Analgesia, Trendelenburg and gentle taxis may reduce an early incarceration; then plan early elective repair.
Resuscitate then operate urgently — assess viability, resect non-viable bowel, repair the defect.
Broad-spectrum cover if strangulated/resection; tension-free repair; promote timely elective repair to prevent emergencies.

title: Acute urinary retention
presentation: Sudden painful inability to pass urine with a palpable/tender distended bladder
Commonest in older men from benign prostatic enlargement; also drugs, constipation, UTI, neurological causes, post-operative
Suprapubic pain and distension relieved by catheterisation
redFlags: High-pressure chronic retention with renal impairment / hydronephrosis
Neurological cause — cauda equina (back pain, saddle anaesthesia, bowel/bladder dysfunction) — emergency

diagnostics.test: Clinical exam (palpable bladder) + post-catheter residual volume

diagnostics.rationale: assess BPE/prostate; neurological exam if cauda equina suspected

management.detail: Urethral catheterisation (suprapubic if urethral fails/contraindicated); record drained volume.
Start an alpha-blocker (e.g. tamsulosin) in men before a trial without catheter; treat UTI/constipation, review precipitating drugs.
After high-volume/high-pressure retention — watch fluid/electrolyte balance and renal recovery.
Trial without catheter; urology referral for BPE management/surgery; urgent imaging/neurosurgery if cauda equina.

title: Paraphimosis
presentation: A retracted foreskin trapped behind the glans causing a constricting band, oedema and pain
Often iatrogenic (foreskin not replaced after catheterisation/examination)
Progressive glans swelling; risk of ischaemia if prolonged
redFlags: Glans ischaemia/necrosis with prolonged constriction — emergency reduction

diagnostics.rationale: swollen glans with a constricting band of retracted foreskin

management.detail: Compress the oedematous glans (with local/penile block) and reduce the foreskin over it — first-line and usually successful.
Iced glove, osmotic agents (granulated sugar/gauze), or multiple puncture technique before reduction.
Dorsal slit if manual reduction fails or ischaemia threatens — urgent.
Always replace the foreskin after procedures; consider elective circumcision for recurrent cases.

title: Epididymo-orchitis
presentation: Inflammation/infection of the epididymis ± testis; STI organisms in younger men, coliforms/UTI in older men
Gradual-onset unilateral scrotal pain, swelling and tenderness; positive Prehn sign (relief on elevation)
May have dysuria/urethral discharge (STI) or LUTS/UTI symptoms
redFlags: Cannot exclude testicular torsion (sudden severe pain, younger patient) — torsion is the surgical emergency
Abscess formation, sepsis, or Fournier's gangrene

diagnostics.rationale: increased flow (vs absent in torsion); exclude abscess — when torsion cannot be excluded

diagnostics.test: STI testing (urethral/urine NAAT) or MSU culture
diagnostics.rationale: guide antibiotic choice by likely organism

management.detail: If torsion cannot be confidently excluded → urgent surgical exploration; do not delay for imaging.
Treat for gonorrhoea + chlamydia (e.g. ceftriaxone IM single dose + doxycycline 100 mg twice daily × 10–14 days); treat partners.
Fluoroquinolone or other culture-guided antibiotic × 10–14 days.
Analgesia, scrotal support, rest; review; drain abscess/urology referral for complications.

title: Febrile seizure
presentation: Seizure with fever in a child 6 months–5 years without CNS infection or a defined cause
Simple: generalised, <15 minutes, once in 24 h; complex: focal, prolonged, or recurrent within 24 h
Common, usually benign; family history frequent
Must exclude meningitis/encephalitis as the cause of the fever+seizure
redFlags: Features of meningitis/encephalitis (neck stiffness, bulging fontanelle, rash, drowsiness)
Prolonged seizure / status epilepticus (>5 minutes — treat)
Age <6 months or >5 years, or first complex seizure — investigate further

diagnostics.test: Identify and assess the fever source

diagnostics.rationale: if any features of CNS infection, especially <12–18 months or incompletely vaccinated

diagnostics.test: Bloods/urine as indicated by the focus

management.detail: Most stop spontaneously; if >5 minutes give a benzodiazepine (rectal diazepam/buccal midazolam) and follow the status protocol.
Antipyretics for comfort (do not prevent recurrence), manage the source (e.g. malaria, otitis, pneumonia).
Explain the benign nature of simple febrile seizures and recurrence risk; teach first aid and when to return.
Complex features, diagnostic uncertainty, <18 months, or suspected CNS infection.

title: Birth asphyxia / hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy
presentation: Perinatal hypoxia-ischaemia causing neonatal encephalopathy; a leading cause of SSA neonatal death and disability
Failure to initiate/sustain breathing at birth, low Apgar, need for resuscitation
Encephalopathy: altered tone/consciousness, poor feeding, seizures (Sarnat staging)
Multi-organ involvement (renal, cardiac, hepatic)
redFlags: No breathing/heart rate at birth — immediate resuscitation

diagnostics.rationale: document severity of perinatal depression and acidosis

management.detail: Warmth, stimulation, airway, bag-mask ventilation within 'the golden minute'; the single highest-impact intervention.
Maintain normoglycaemia, normothermia (avoid hyperthermia), normal ventilation/perfusion; treat seizures (phenobarbital).
For moderate–severe HIE in term infants where cooling protocols and monitoring exist (improves outcome); avoid passive overcooling without monitoring.
Skilled birth attendance, partograph use, prompt management of obstetric emergencies; developmental follow-up for survivors.

references.label: WHO Guidelines on basic newborn resuscitation

title: Neonatal omphalitis (umbilical infection)
presentation: Bacterial infection of the umbilical stump and surrounding tissue; an important SSA neonatal-sepsis source where cord care is poor
Periumbilical redness, induration, discharge, foul smell
May progress rapidly to sepsis, necrotising fasciitis, or portal pyaemia
redFlags: Spreading erythema/induration, crepitus → necrotising fasciitis — surgical emergency
Signs of sepsis (poor feeding, temperature instability, lethargy)

diagnostics.rationale: measure periumbilical erythema/induration; assess for systemic sepsis

management.detail: Admit and start IV broad-spectrum cover (e.g. ampicillin + gentamicin; add anti-staphylococcal/anaerobic cover for severe/necrotising disease).
Urgent debridement if necrotising fasciitis suspected.
Thermoregulation, feeding/fluids, glucose, monitor for sepsis.
Clean cord care; WHO chlorhexidine 7.1% cord application in high-mortality settings; promote hygienic delivery.

references.label: WHO Newborn cord care / chlorhexidine guidance

title: Cerebral palsy
presentation: Permanent, non-progressive disorder of movement and posture from an early brain insult (antenatal, perinatal asphyxia, kernicterus, neonatal infection)
Delayed motor milestones, abnormal tone (spasticity commonest), persistent primitive reflexes
Subtypes: spastic, dyskinetic, ataxic, mixed; often with comorbidities (epilepsy, intellectual disability, feeding/communication problems)
A common SSA childhood disability, frequently linked to preventable perinatal events
redFlags: Regression/loss of skills (suggests a progressive disorder — re-evaluate)
Severe feeding difficulty / aspiration / faltering growth
Hip subluxation, contractures, or severe spasticity affecting function

diagnostics.rationale: identify the underlying lesion / exclude progressive pathology
vision, hearing, feeding, seizures, cognition, hips

management.detail: Physiotherapy, occupational and speech/feeding therapy; positioning, mobility aids and orthoses — the cornerstone of care.
Stretching/splinting, oral agents (baclofen), botulinum toxin to targeted muscles; orthopaedic/neurosurgical input for severe cases.
Antiepileptics for seizures, nutrition support, vision/hearing aids, communication support.
Caregiver training, school inclusion, community-based rehabilitation; prevention through perinatal care and jaundice/infection management.

title: Clubfoot (congenital talipes equinovarus)
presentation: Congenital foot deformity (equinus, varus, adductus, cavus); common and very treatable if started early
Rigid inward/downward-turned foot from birth, uni- or bilateral
Idiopathic most common; may be syndromic/neurogenic
Untreated clubfoot is a major preventable cause of physical disability in SSA
redFlags: Associated neuromuscular condition (e.g. spina bifida) — assess

management.detail: Serial weekly plaster casts to correct the deformity, usually with a percutaneous Achilles tenotomy — corrects most idiopathic clubfeet without major surgery.
Boots-and-bar bracing after casting (full-time then night-time for years) — essential to prevent recurrence; emphasise adherence.
Start within the first weeks of life for best results; established Ponseti programmes exist across SSA.
Soft-tissue/bony procedures when casting is insufficient or for late presentation.

title: Intestinal amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery)
presentation: Entamoeba histolytica colitis; faecal-oral, common with poor sanitation in SSA
Gradual-onset bloody, mucoid diarrhoea with cramps and tenesmus; fever often mild/absent
Spectrum from asymptomatic carriage to fulminant colitis
Can disseminate to cause amoebic liver abscess
redFlags: Fulminant/necrotising colitis, toxic megacolon or perforation

diagnostics.rationale: trophozoites with ingested red cells (or cysts); differentiate from Shigella
distinguishes E. histolytica from non-pathogenic E. dispar

management.detail: Metronidazole (or tinidazole) for invasive disease — 7–10 days; faster symptom control with tinidazole.
Follow with diloxanide furoate or paromomycin to eradicate intestinal cysts and prevent relapse/transmission (also treat asymptomatic cyst passers in non-endemic settings).
ORS/IV fluids for fluid losses.
Safe water, sanitation, hand hygiene; investigate for concurrent liver abscess if RUQ symptoms.

title: Taeniasis (intestinal tapeworm)
presentation: Adult Taenia solium (pork) or T. saginata (beef) tapeworm from undercooked meat
Often asymptomatic; mild abdominal discomfort, passage of motile proglottids in stool
T. solium carriers are the source of human cysticercosis/neurocysticercosis — a key public-health link
Eosinophilia may be present
redFlags: T. solium taeniasis (cysticercosis transmission risk to self/others)

diagnostics.rationale: diagnose; species often indistinguishable by eggs

management.detail: Single-dose praziquantel (5–10 mg/kg) or niclosamide eliminates the adult worm.
Speciate where possible; counsel on cysticercosis risk and hygiene to prevent autoinfection/transmission.
Meat inspection, thorough cooking, sanitation, treat carriers; consider neurocysticercosis screening in symptomatic patients.
Confirm clearance.

title: Chikungunya
presentation: Alphavirus transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes; outbreaks across SSA
Abrupt high fever with severe, often symmetrical polyarthralgia/arthritis and rash
Arthralgia can persist for weeks–months (chronic phase)
Co-circulates with dengue — distinguish (chikungunya: more joint pain; dengue: more haemorrhage/leakage)
redFlags: Severe disease in neonates (vertical transmission), elderly, comorbidities

diagnostics.rationale: lymphopenia; platelets less reduced than dengue

management.detail: Rest, fluids, paracetamol for fever/pain; no specific antiviral.
Bleeding risk if dengue; then NSAIDs may help arthralgia.
Analgesia, physiotherapy; rheumatology input for persistent arthritis.
Mosquito avoidance, source reduction; notify for outbreak response.

title: Relapsing fever (louse-/tick-borne)
presentation: Borrelia spp.; louse-borne (B. recurrentis — epidemic, crowding/displacement in the Horn of Africa) or tick-borne (endemic)
Recurring episodes of high fever lasting days separated by afebrile intervals
Headache, myalgia, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, bleeding
Spirochaetaemia detectable during febrile episodes
redFlags: Severe disease: myocarditis, hepatic failure, bleeding, splenic rupture
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction after the first antibiotic dose (can be life-threatening)

management.detail: Single-dose (louse-borne) or short-course (tick-borne) doxycycline; erythromycin/penicillin alternatives — highly effective.
Observe closely after the first dose; supportive care for rigors/hypotension.
Fluids, manage bleeding/organ dysfunction.
Delousing/hygiene for louse-borne epidemics, tick avoidance for endemic disease; notify.

title: Female genital schistosomiasis
presentation: Schistosoma haematobium egg deposition in the female genital tract; highly prevalent yet under-recognised in endemic SSA
Bloody/abnormal vaginal discharge, post-coital bleeding, pelvic pain, dyspareunia, contact bleeding
Characteristic 'sandy patches'/grainy lesions on the cervix/vagina at speculum exam
Associated with infertility and increased HIV acquisition risk
redFlags: Symptoms mimicking cervical cancer/STI — examine and screen

diagnostics.rationale: sandy patches, grainy/rubbery lesions, abnormal vessels on cervix/vagina

diagnostics.test: Urine microscopy for S. haematobium eggs
diagnostics.rationale: supports diagnosis (may be negative despite genital disease)
VIA/cytology/HPV and STI testing — overlapping presentation

management.detail: Praziquantel 40 mg/kg (single or split dose) treats the schistosome infection; earlier treatment limits irreversible genital damage.
Treat co-infections/STIs; counsel on infertility risk and HIV prevention; established lesions may not fully reverse.

management.step: Integrate with cervical screening + HIV services
management.detail: Examine and screen opportunistically in endemic areas.
Mass drug administration and WASH in endemic communities; treat girls before genital damage develops.

references.label: WHO Female genital schistosomiasis: a pocket atlas

title: Haemorrhoids
presentation: Symptomatic engorgement of the anal vascular cushions; very common, aggravated by constipation, straining, pregnancy
Bright-red rectal bleeding (on the paper/coating stool), pruritus, prolapse, perianal lump
Internal graded I–IV by prolapse; external can thrombose causing acute pain
redFlags: Rectal bleeding with red-flag features (weight loss, change in bowel habit, age >50, anaemia) — exclude colorectal cancer
Acute thrombosed/strangulated haemorrhoid with severe pain

diagnostics.rationale: confirm and grade; visualise internal haemorrhoids
colonoscopy/FBC if red-flags or age >50 — never attribute bleeding to piles without examining

management.detail: High-fibre diet, fluids, stool softeners/laxatives to avoid straining; topical agents for symptom relief; perianal hygiene.
Rubber-band ligation (grade I–III) or sclerotherapy for persistent internal haemorrhoids.
Haemorrhoidectomy for grade III–IV/large external or failed conservative therapy.
Within 48–72 h consider excision for rapid pain relief; otherwise conservative with analgesia and stool softeners.

title: Anal fissure
presentation: Linear tear of the anoderm, usually posterior midline, often after passing hard stool
Severe sharp pain on defecation with bright-red bleeding; anal spasm
Chronic fissure (>6 weeks) has a sentinel pile/skin tag and exposed internal sphincter fibres
redFlags: Atypical/lateral or multiple fissures — exclude Crohn's, TB, HIV, syphilis, malignancy

diagnostics.rationale: visualise the fissure (often posterior midline); avoid painful PR/proctoscopy acutely

diagnostics.test: Consider underlying disease for atypical fissures

management.detail: High-fibre diet, fluids, laxatives and sitz baths break the pain–spasm cycle — most acute fissures heal.
Topical GTN or diltiazem to lower sphincter tone and promote healing (headache common with GTN).
Chemical sphincterotomy for chronic fissures failing topical therapy.
Lateral internal sphincterotomy for refractory chronic fissures (small incontinence risk).

references.label: ASCRS Practice Parameters for anal fissures

title: Perianal abscess and fistula-in-ano
presentation: Infection of the anal glands forming a perianal/ischiorectal abscess; may evolve into a fistula-in-ano
Throbbing perianal pain, swelling, redness, fever; fluctuant tender mass
Recurrent discharge from an external opening suggests a fistula
Consider Crohn's, TB and HIV in recurrent/complex disease
redFlags: Spreading sepsis / necrotising perineal infection (Fournier's gangrene) — emergency

diagnostics.rationale: locate and define the abscess; examination under anaesthesia for deep/complex collections
delineate complex fistula tracks before surgery
Crohn's/TB/HIV in recurrent or complex cases

management.detail: Definitive treatment for an abscess — drain without waiting for 'pointing'; antibiotics alone are insufficient.
Add antibiotics for cellulitis, sepsis, immunocompromise or diabetes.
Lay open simple low fistulae; seton/staged procedures for complex/high tracks to protect continence.
Crohn's-related disease needs combined medical–surgical care; urgent debridement for Fournier's gangrene.

references.label: ASCRS anorectal abscess and fistula guidance

title: Perforated appendicitis with peritonitis
presentation: Progression of appendicitis to perforation, more common with late presentation (typical in SSA)
Migratory RIF pain becoming generalised, high fever, vomiting, generalised peritonism
May form an appendix mass/abscess; sepsis/shock in advanced cases
redFlags: Generalised peritonitis, sepsis or shock — emergency laparotomy
Extremes of age with diagnostic delay

management.detail: IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone + metronidazole) before theatre.
Open or laparoscopic with peritoneal lavage for perforation/peritonitis.
Consider antibiotics ± image-guided drainage with interval appendicectomy in selected stable patients.
Continue antibiotics per severity, monitor for collection/ileus, sepsis source control.

references.label: WSES Jerusalem guidelines for acute appendicitis

title: Perforated peptic ulcer
presentation: Full-thickness perforation of a gastric/duodenal ulcer causing chemical then bacterial peritonitis
Sudden severe epigastric pain becoming generalised, board-like rigidity
Risk factors: H. pylori, NSAIDs, smoking; free air under the diaphragm on erect film
redFlags: Generalised peritonitis, sepsis, shock — surgical emergency

management.detail: IV fluids, NG decompression, analgesia, broad-spectrum antibiotics, PPI.
Omental (Graham) patch repair and peritoneal lavage; open or laparoscopic.
Eradicate H. pylori, stop NSAIDs, acid suppression; biopsy gastric ulcers to exclude malignancy.
Sepsis monitoring, nutrition, confirm H. pylori eradication.

title: Kwashiorkor (oedematous severe acute malnutrition)
presentation: Oedematous severe acute malnutrition from inadequate protein/energy intake, often with infection
Bilateral pitting oedema (feet→legs→face), apathy/irritability, 'flaky-paint' dermatosis, sparse depigmented hair, hepatomegaly
Weight may be masked by oedema; appetite poor
High mortality without careful, phased re-feeding
redFlags: Hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration/shock, severe anaemia, infection (often hidden)
Failed appetite test / complications → inpatient care

diagnostics.rationale: diagnose and grade SAM; oedema defines kwashiorkor

diagnostics.test: Blood glucose, infection screen, electrolytes, Hb

management.detail: Stabilisation: treat/prevent hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration (ReSoMal, NOT standard ORS), electrolytes, infection; cautious feeding (F-75).
Start low-energy F-75 then transition to catch-up F-100/RUTF only after oedema resolves and appetite returns — avoid refeeding syndrome and fluid overload.
Vitamin A, folate, zinc and a multivitamin; withhold iron until the recovery (catch-up) phase.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics routinely in complicated SAM; sensory stimulation; transition to outpatient therapeutic feeding and monitor.

references.label: WHO Management of severe acute malnutrition guidance

title: Nutritional rickets
presentation: Defective bone mineralisation in growing children from vitamin D and/or calcium deficiency
Bowing of legs, widened wrists/ankles, rachitic rosary, frontal bossing, delayed fontanelle closure/dentition
Growth faltering, bone pain, hypotonia; risk factors include exclusive breastfeeding without supplementation and limited sun exposure
redFlags: Consider renal/hepatic or genetic causes if refractory

diagnostics.test: Serum calcium, phosphate, ALP, 25-OH vitamin D, PTH

diagnostics.rationale: exclude renal causes in refractory cases

management.detail: Treatment-dose vitamin D (cholecalciferol/ergocalciferol) with adequate dietary/supplemental calcium per age — corrects biochemistry and heals bone.
IV/oral calcium for symptomatic hypocalcaemia (seizures/tetany).
Continue maintenance vitamin D and calcium; promote sunlight and dietary sources.
Routine infant vitamin D supplementation, especially exclusively breastfed infants; follow-up biochemistry/radiology and orthopaedic review for residual deformity.

references.label: Global Consensus on Prevention and Management of Nutritional Rickets

title: Developmental dysplasia of the hip
presentation: Spectrum of abnormal hip development from dysplasia to dislocation; better outcomes with early detection
Neonate: positive Barlow/Ortolani, asymmetric thigh creases, limited abduction
Older infant/child: leg-length discrepancy, painless limp, toe-walking
Risk factors: breech, female, family history, oligohydramnios
redFlags: Late diagnosis (walking age) — worse outcomes, may need surgery

diagnostics.rationale: imaging of choice before ossification; for risk factors/abnormal exam

management.detail: Abduction harness for infants <6 months maintains reduction and promotes normal acetabular development — high success when started early.
For later presentation/failed harness, under anaesthetic with arthrogram.
For irreducible or late-presenting dislocations.
Targeted screening of at-risk infants; monitor acetabular development radiologically.

title: Trigeminal neuralgia
presentation: Paroxysmal, severe, electric-shock-like unilateral facial pain in trigeminal nerve territory
Triggered by light touch, chewing, talking, cold air; brief stabs with refractory periods
Usually idiopathic (neurovascular compression); secondary causes include MS and tumours
redFlags: Sensory loss, bilateral symptoms, deafness or other neurology — suspect a secondary cause (MS/tumour) → image
Severe weight loss from inability to eat

diagnostics.rationale: characteristic paroxysmal trigeminal pain with triggers and normal exam
for atypical features/young patients/sensory signs — exclude secondary causes and assess neurovascular compression

management.detail: Carbamazepine (or oxcarbazepine) titrated to effect markedly reduces attacks; monitor for rash/hyponatraemia/blood dyscrasia.
Add/switch to lamotrigine, baclofen or gabapentin for inadequate response/intolerance.
Neurosurgery — microvascular decompression (durable) or ablative procedures (radiofrequency, balloon, gamma knife).
Nutrition support during severe flares; treat any identified secondary cause.

title: Ascariasis (roundworm)
presentation: Ascaris lumbricoides, the largest and one of the commonest soil-transmitted helminths in SSA
Often asymptomatic; heavy load causes abdominal pain, malnutrition, growth faltering in children
Larval lung migration → Loeffler syndrome (cough, wheeze, transient infiltrates, eosinophilia)
Worms may be passed/vomited
redFlags: Intestinal obstruction from a worm bolus (children)
Severe respiratory symptoms in Loeffler syndrome

management.detail: Albendazole 400 mg single dose (or mebendazole) clears the infection; pyrantel is an alternative.
Conservative management ± piperazine for partial obstruction; surgery/endoscopy for complete obstruction or biliary ascariasis.
Nutritional support, iron as needed.
WHO preventive chemotherapy (deworming) of at-risk groups, sanitation and hygiene.

title: Hookworm disease
presentation: Necator americanus / Ancylostoma duodenale; major cause of iron-deficiency anaemia in SSA
Larvae penetrate skin (ground itch) → lung migration → intestinal attachment with chronic blood loss
Fatigue, pallor, breathlessness from anaemia; epigastric pain; growth/cognitive impact in children
Eosinophilia, hypoproteinaemia in heavy infection
redFlags: Faltering growth / cognitive impairment in children

management.detail: Albendazole 400 mg single dose (or mebendazole) — high cure rates.
Treat iron-deficiency anaemia with oral (or IV) iron; transfuse only for severe symptomatic anaemia.
Deworm after the first trimester per WHO and treat anaemia.
WHO preventive chemotherapy, footwear, sanitation and hygiene to interrupt transmission.

title: Acute otitis media (childhood)
presentation: Acute middle-ear infection, very common in young children, often after a viral URTI
Ear pain, fever, irritability, ear-tugging in infants; bulging/red tympanic membrane
Otorrhoea if the drum perforates; usually self-limiting
Recurrent/persistent disease can cause hearing loss and CSOM
redFlags: <6 months, or bilateral with significant illness

diagnostics.rationale: bulging, erythematous, immobile tympanic membrane ± effusion/perforation

management.detail: Paracetamol/ibuprofen for pain and fever — the priority for comfort.
Many cases resolve without antibiotics; offer delayed/no antibiotic for mild disease in older children.
Amoxicillin first-line (high-dose) for <6 months, bilateral in <2 years, otorrhoea, or severe/persistent illness; co-amoxiclav for failure.
Review persistent effusion/hearing; pneumococcal vaccination; manage recurrent disease/refer for grommets if needed.

title: Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
presentation: Immune-complex nephritis 1–3 weeks after streptococcal throat or skin infection; common in SSA children
Nephritic syndrome: haematuria (cola-coloured urine), oedema (periorbital), hypertension, oliguria
Usually self-limiting in children with good recovery
Low complement (C3) that normalises by ~8 weeks
redFlags: Acute kidney injury / fluid overload / pulmonary oedema

diagnostics.rationale: renal function; low C3 supports diagnosis

diagnostics.test: Evidence of streptococcal infection (ASOT/anti-DNase B, throat/skin swab)

management.detail: Salt and fluid restriction; treat the streptococcal infection (penicillin) to limit spread (does not alter the nephritis course).
Loop diuretics (furosemide) for oedema/hypertension; antihypertensives for severe hypertension.
Treat hyperkalaemia/acidosis; dialysis rarely needed for severe AKI.
Monitor BP, renal function and urinalysis until C3 and urine normalise; most children recover fully.

title: African tick-bite fever (rickettsiosis)
presentation: Rickettsia africae from Amblyomma tick bites; common in rural/savannah SSA and travellers
Fever, headache, myalgia with one or more inoculation eschars (tache noire) and regional lymphadenopathy
Maculopapular/vesicular rash variable; usually milder than Mediterranean spotted fever
Often multiple eschars (clustered tick bites)

diagnostics.rationale: characteristic tache noire is a strong clue

diagnostics.test: Serology / PCR of eschar where available

management.detail: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for ~7 days (or until afebrile several days) — rapid response; first-line.
Macrolide (azithromycin) in pregnancy/children where doxycycline is avoided.
Antipyretics, hydration; most cases are self-limiting and respond quickly.
Tick avoidance, protective clothing, repellents and prompt tick removal.

title: Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis
presentation: Most acute sinusitis is viral; bacterial infection suggested by persistence/worsening
Facial pain/pressure, nasal obstruction, purulent discharge, hyposmia, worse on bending forward
Bacterial features: symptoms >10 days, 'double-sickening', high fever with purulence
Maxillary sinus most often involved
redFlags: Orbital cellulitis/abscess (eye swelling, proptosis, painful/restricted eye movement, visual change) — emergency

diagnostics.rationale: duration and pattern distinguish bacterial from viral; examine for complications
only if complications suspected or recurrent/refractory

management.detail: Analgesia, saline irrigation, intranasal corticosteroid, decongestants short-term — sufficient for most (viral) cases.
Reserve amoxicillin (or co-amoxiclav) for persistent >10 days, worsening, or severe disease; doxycycline/macrolide if penicillin-allergic.
IV antibiotics + ENT/ophthalmology/neurosurgery for orbital or intracranial complications.
ENT referral and assessment for underlying allergy/anatomy.

title: Allergic / vernal keratoconjunctivitis
presentation: Chronic, often seasonal, bilateral ocular allergy; vernal form severe in children in hot dry climates (common in SSA)
Intense itching, redness, watering, photophobia, ropy mucoid discharge
Giant 'cobblestone' papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva; limbal Horner-Trantas dots in vernal disease
Risk of vision-threatening corneal involvement (shield ulcers) in severe vernal disease
redFlags: Corneal involvement / shield ulcer — vision-threatening, refer

diagnostics.rationale: tarsal papillae, limbal changes, corneal involvement

management.detail: Reduce triggers (dust, pollen), lubricants and cold compresses for symptom relief.
Dual-action agents (e.g. olopatadine) or mast-cell stabilisers for maintenance control.

management.step: Topical steroids / immunomodulators for severe disease
management.detail: Short steroid pulses (specialist, monitor IOP) and topical ciclosporin/tacrolimus for vernal disease to spare steroids.
Manage shield ulcers and prevent scarring with ophthalmology input.

title: Acute bacterial parotitis
presentation: Ascending Staphylococcus aureus infection of the parotid gland, classically in dehydrated/elderly/post-operative patients
Acute painful swelling over the parotid, worse with eating; fever
Pus expressible from Stensen's duct on gland massage
Dehydration and poor oral hygiene are key risk factors
redFlags: Spreading infection / abscess, airway compromise from neck swelling

diagnostics.rationale: purulent discharge from Stensen's duct confirms

diagnostics.test: Pus culture + blood culture if septic

management.detail: Correct dehydration, oral care, sialogogues (sour sweets) and gland massage to promote salivary flow.
Empirical anti-staphylococcal therapy (e.g. flucloxacillin; cover MRSA where prevalent) adjusted to culture.
Incision and drainage/aspiration for an abscess not responding to antibiotics.
Hydration and oral hygiene, especially peri-operatively and in the elderly.

references.label: ENT/IDSA head and neck infection guidance

title: Tension pneumothorax
presentation: Severe respiratory distress and tachypnoea, often after chest trauma or positive-pressure ventilation.
Tracheal deviation away from the affected side, absent breath sounds and hyper-resonance on that side.
Distended neck veins, hypotension and tachycardia (obstructive shock).
redFlags: Cardiovascular collapse / cardiac arrest — needle decompression must not wait for imaging.
Rapidly rising ventilation pressures in an intubated patient.

diagnostics.rationale: Decompress on clinical grounds; do NOT delay for a chest X-ray in an unstable patient.
Absent lung sliding supports the diagnosis when available and time permits.
Confirmatory only AFTER decompression in a stabilised patient.

management.detail: Large-bore cannula in the 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line OR 4th/5th space anterior axillary line; a hiss of air confirms.
Insert an intercostal drain (5th space, anterior axillary line) after decompression and connect to an underwater seal.
Treat shock, give oxygen, and address the underlying cause (trauma, barotrauma).

references.label: ATLS Advanced Trauma Life Support — thoracic trauma
WHO Integrated Management for Emergency & Essential Surgical Care (IMEESC)

title: Open (compound) fracture
presentation: Fracture with an overlying wound communicating with the bone or fracture haematoma.
Visible bone, exposed fat, or bleeding consistent with a deep wound over a fracture.
High-energy mechanism with significant soft-tissue injury.
redFlags: Absent distal pulses or signs of vascular injury — surgical emergency.
Gross contamination, devitalised tissue or established infection.

diagnostics.rationale: Document distal pulses, capillary refill, sensation and motor function before and after any manipulation.
Define fracture configuration and joint involvement.
Guides antibiotic choice, debridement urgency and prognosis.

management.detail: Give IV antibiotics within 1 hour (e.g. a first-generation cephalosporin; add gentamicin and metronidazole for higher-grade/contaminated wounds).
Assess immunisation status; give tetanus toxoid +/- immunoglobulin per wound risk.
Remove gross contamination, cover with a saline-soaked sterile dressing, photograph once, then splint and analgese; do not repeatedly expose.
Refer for theatre debridement and skeletal stabilisation; timing depends on contamination and limb viability.

title: Acute compartment syndrome
presentation: Pain out of proportion to the injury, worsening despite analgesia.
Pain on passive stretch of the muscles in the affected compartment.
Tense, swollen compartment, often after fracture, crush, reperfusion or tight casting.
redFlags: Paraesthesia, paralysis and pulselessness are LATE signs — do not wait for them.
A tight cast or dressing — split/remove immediately.
Rising creatine kinase / myoglobinuria suggesting muscle necrosis.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; the earliest reliable sign is escalating pain and pain on passive stretch.
A delta pressure (diastolic BP − compartment pressure) < 30 mmHg supports the diagnosis where monitoring is available.
Detect rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury.

management.detail: Split or remove any cast/dressing down to skin; keep the limb at heart level (not elevated).
Definitive treatment is urgent surgical fasciotomy of all involved compartments — do not delay for investigations.
Oxygen, analgesia, IV fluids to protect kidneys from myoglobinuria; correct hyperkalaemia.

references.label: BOAST Diagnosis & Management of Compartment Syndrome of the Limbs

title: Blunt splenic injury
presentation: Left upper quadrant pain and tenderness after blunt abdominal trauma; left lower rib fractures raise suspicion.
Referred left shoulder-tip pain (Kehr sign).
Signs of hypovolaemia: tachycardia, hypotension after a high-energy mechanism.
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability not responding to resuscitation — needs immediate laparotomy.

diagnostics.rationale: Detects free intraperitoneal fluid at the bedside in the unstable patient.
Grades injury and identifies active extravasation in the stable patient.
Monitors for delayed bleeding during non-operative management.

management.detail: Two large-bore cannulae, balanced resuscitation, activate major haemorrhage protocol and crossmatch.
Haemodynamic instability → laparotomy (splenectomy/repair). Stable patients with lower-grade injury → non-operative management +/- angioembolisation.
If splenectomy performed, vaccinate against encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, Hib, meningococcus) and counsel on overwhelming post-splenectomy infection.

references.label: WSES classification & guidelines for splenic trauma

title: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)
presentation: Lower abdominal/pelvic pain, often bilateral, in a sexually active woman.
Abnormal vaginal/cervical discharge, deep dyspareunia, intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding.
Cervical motion, adnexal or uterine tenderness on bimanual examination.
redFlags: Fever, rigors, severe pain or signs of pelvic peritonitis (possible tubo-ovarian abscess).
Pregnancy — exclude ectopic, and treat as complicated.
Failure to improve at 72 hours on oral therapy.

diagnostics.rationale: Always exclude ectopic pregnancy in a woman with pelvic pain.

diagnostics.test: NAAT for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis
diagnostics.rationale: Identifies the commonest causative organisms; do not delay treatment for results.
Indicated if a tubo-ovarian abscess is suspected or the patient is severely unwell.

management.detail: Treat on clinical suspicion to preserve fertility, e.g. IM ceftriaxone plus oral doxycycline and metronidazole; tailor to local guidance.
Admit for IV therapy if pregnant, severely unwell, tubo-ovarian abscess, or failed oral therapy.
Treat sexual partners, advise abstinence until both treated, offer HIV/syphilis screening and contraception review.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the management of STIs

title: Puerperal (postpartum) sepsis
presentation: Fever, lower abdominal pain and offensive lochia within 6 weeks of delivery or abortion.
Uterine tenderness, sub-involution of the uterus.
Tachycardia, malaise, may progress to septic shock.
redFlags: Hypotension, altered mental state, lactate ≥ 2 — manage as septic shock (sepsis six).
Severe abdominal pain or peritonism (retained products, uterine perforation, abscess).
Group A streptococcal infection — rapidly progressive, high mortality.

diagnostics.rationale: Take before antibiotics where possible; lactate guides resuscitation.
Detects retained products of conception or pelvic collection.

management.detail: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, IV fluids, oxygen; take cultures, lactate and monitor urine output.
Evacuate retained products, drain collections; consider hysterectomy in life-threatening uterine infection.
Cover Gram-negative, anaerobes and streptococci (e.g. broad-spectrum beta-lactam + metronidazole; add clindamycin if invasive GAS suspected for toxin suppression).

references.label: WHO recommendations for prevention and treatment of maternal peripartum infections
RCOG Green-top Guideline — sepsis in pregnancy/puerperium

title: Obstructed labour
presentation: Failure of labour to progress despite good contractions; prolonged labour.
Maternal exhaustion, dehydration, maternal tachycardia and pyrexia.
Excessive moulding, caput, a Bandl ring, or oedematous vulva/cervix.
redFlags: Continuous lower abdominal pain with cessation of contractions and a tender abdomen — impending/actual uterine rupture.
Foetal distress or absent foetal heart.
Haematuria or signs suggesting fistula formation from prolonged pressure.

diagnostics.rationale: Crossing the action line signals obstruction needing intervention.
Assess descent, presentation, moulding, caput and a possible Bandl ring.
Identifies foetal compromise requiring expedited delivery.

management.detail: IV fluids, correct dehydration, analgesia, antibiotics; insert a urinary catheter.
Caesarean section is usually required; symphysiotomy or assisted delivery only where appropriate and CS is unavailable.
Active management of the third stage (PPH risk), monitor for fistula, sepsis and uterine rupture.

references.label: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth (MCPC)

title: Umbilical cord prolapse
presentation: Cord palpable or visible below the presenting part after rupture of membranes.
Sudden foetal bradycardia or variable decelerations after membrane rupture.
Risk factors: malpresentation, prematurity, polyhydramnios, high presenting part.
redFlags: Foetal bradycardia — obstetric emergency requiring immediate delivery.
Cord compression / vasospasm with deteriorating foetal heart trace.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms cord presentation and assesses cervical dilatation for mode of delivery.

management.detail: Elevate the presenting part manually; place the mother knee-chest or in steep head-down/left-lateral position; consider bladder filling. Minimise cord handling and keep it warm.
Category-1 caesarean section unless vaginal delivery is imminent and faster.
Summon obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams immediately.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 50 — Umbilical Cord Prolapse

title: Placental abruption
presentation: Sudden constant abdominal pain with or without vaginal bleeding after 20 weeks.
A tense, tender, 'woody-hard' uterus; uterine hypertonus.
Bleeding may be concealed — shock may be out of proportion to visible blood loss.
redFlags: Maternal shock, foetal distress or absent foetal heart.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical; ultrasound is insensitive and must not delay management.
Detect anaemia and DIC; prepare for transfusion.
Quantifies feto-maternal haemorrhage to guide anti-D dosing.

management.detail: Large-bore IV access, balanced transfusion, activate major haemorrhage protocol, monitor closely.
