presentation: Often asymptomatic; muscle weakness, cramps, fatigue and constipation as potassium falls.
Causes: diuretics, GI losses (vomiting/diarrhoea), hyperaldosteronism, refeeding.
Severe: arrhythmia and paralysis.
redFlags: ECG changes (U waves, flattened T waves) and arrhythmia — life-threatening.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms hypokalaemia, detects cardiac effects; magnesium must be corrected for potassium to respond.

management.detail: Oral replacement for mild cases; cautious IV potassium with cardiac monitoring for severe/symptomatic hypokalaemia.
Replace magnesium concurrently — hypokalaemia is refractory until this is corrected.
Adjust diuretics, treat GI losses or hyperaldosteronism; recheck levels.

title: Biliary colic / symptomatic gallstones
presentation: Episodic severe right-upper-quadrant/epigastric pain, often after fatty meals, lasting up to a few hours.
Pain may radiate to the right scapula; associated nausea.
Between episodes the patient is well; no fever (distinguishes from cholecystitis).
redFlags: Fever and persistent RUQ pain (acute cholecystitis).
Jaundice with pain and fever (ascending cholangitis).
Epigastric pain radiating to the back (gallstone pancreatitis).

diagnostics.rationale: First-line to detect gallstones and assess the gallbladder wall and bile ducts.

management.detail: Analgesia for acute pain; advise a low-fat diet.
Refer for laparoscopic cholecystectomy for recurrent symptomatic stones.
Escalate promptly if features of cholecystitis, cholangitis or pancreatitis develop.

title: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
presentation: Re-experiencing a traumatic event (flashbacks, nightmares, intrusive memories).
Avoidance of reminders, hyperarousal (hypervigilance, startle, sleep disturbance) and negative mood/cognitions.
Symptoms persisting beyond a month after trauma.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical; screening tools support case finding.

management.detail: Trauma-focused CBT or EMDR is first-line treatment.
An SSRI (or SNRI) where psychological therapy is declined, ineffective, or for comorbid depression.
Address sleep, substance use and social support; manage suicide risk.

title: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)
presentation: Recurrent intrusive obsessions (thoughts, images, urges) causing anxiety.
Compulsions (repetitive behaviours/mental acts) performed to reduce distress.
Time-consuming (>1 hour/day) and impairing; insight is usually retained.
redFlags: Severe functional impairment or suicide risk.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical; assess severity and impact (e.g. Y-BOCS).
Screen for depression and suicide risk.

management.detail: CBT with exposure and response prevention is first-line.
An SSRI (often at higher doses and longer trials than for depression); clomipramine as an alternative.
Combine therapy and medication for moderate-severe disease; refer refractory cases for specialist augmentation.

references.label: NICE OCD and body dysmorphic disorder guideline

title: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura)
presentation: Palpable purpura over the buttocks and extensor surfaces of the legs in a child.
Arthralgia/arthritis, colicky abdominal pain, and renal involvement (haematuria/proteinuria).
Often follows an upper respiratory infection.

diagnostics.rationale: Characteristic purpura with normal platelets in a well child usually suffices.
Detect and monitor renal involvement (the main determinant of long-term outcome).

management.detail: Most cases are self-limiting; rest, hydration and simple analgesia.
Serial urinalysis and BP for weeks–months; refer significant nephritis to nephrology.
Corticosteroids for severe abdominal pain or significant renal/other organ involvement (specialist-guided).

references.label: EULAR/PRINTO/PRES criteria and management guidance for IgA vasculitis

title: Abnormal uterine bleeding (heavy menstrual bleeding)
presentation: Excessive menstrual blood loss affecting quality of life, with or without irregular bleeding.
Possible symptoms of anaemia (fatigue, breathlessness).
Causes structured by PALM-COEIN (structural vs non-structural).
redFlags: Risk factors for endometrial cancer (obesity, unopposed oestrogen, age).

diagnostics.rationale: Assess anaemia and exclude pregnancy-related bleeding.
Identify structural causes and exclude malignancy in at-risk women.

management.step: Treat anaemia and exclude red flags
management.detail: Iron for anaemia; investigate/refer postmenopausal or high-risk bleeding.
Levonorgestrel intrauterine system is first-line; tranexamic acid/NSAIDs for acute heavy bleeding; hormonal options as alternatives.
Endometrial ablation or surgery (myomectomy/hysterectomy) for refractory disease or structural causes.

references.label: NICE heavy menstrual bleeding guideline; FIGO PALM-COEIN

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia
presentation: Rapid onset of fatigue, pallor and breathlessness (anaemia), bleeding/bruising (thrombocytopenia) and infections (neutropenia).
Bone pain, gum infiltration; usually older adults.
Often blasts on the peripheral blood film.
redFlags: Severe bleeding / DIC (especially acute promyelocytic leukaemia).
Leukostasis (very high blast count) with breathlessness/confusion.

diagnostics.rationale: Cytopenias with circulating blasts suggest acute leukaemia.
Confirms diagnosis, subtype and risk for treatment planning.

management.detail: Refer immediately; treat neutropenic sepsis and DIC as emergencies.
Transfusion, infection prophylaxis/treatment, tumour-lysis prevention with hydration and allopurinol/rasburicase.
Intensive chemotherapy +/- stem cell transplant; all-trans retinoic acid for acute promyelocytic leukaemia (specialist-led).

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
presentation: Fatigue, pallor, bleeding/bruising, recurrent infection and bone pain, most commonly in children.
Lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly; sometimes a mediastinal mass (T-cell).
Circulating blasts on the film.

diagnostics.test: FBC, film and bone marrow with immunophenotyping

diagnostics.rationale: Assess CNS disease and risk stratification.

management.detail: Immediate haematology/oncology referral; manage sepsis and tumour lysis.
Prolonged risk-adapted chemotherapy with CNS-directed therapy; excellent cure rates in children.
Stem cell transplant or targeted agents in high-risk/relapsed disease (specialist-led).

title: Chronic myeloid leukaemia
presentation: Often incidental leucocytosis; fatigue, weight loss, sweats and abdominal fullness from splenomegaly.
Massive splenomegaly is characteristic.
Defined by the Philadelphia chromosome / BCR-ABL1 fusion.
redFlags: Very high white count with leukostasis.

diagnostics.rationale: Leucocytosis with the full spectrum of myeloid cells; basophilia.
Confirms the diagnosis and provides a marker for monitoring response.

management.detail: A BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase inhibitor (e.g. imatinib) is the cornerstone, giving excellent long-term control.
Serial BCR-ABL1 PCR to track molecular response and detect resistance.
Switch TKI or consider transplant for resistance/blast crisis (specialist-led).

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia
presentation: Often asymptomatic lymphocytosis found incidentally in older adults.
Lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, fatigue and recurrent infections as it progresses.
Smear cells on the blood film.
redFlags: Richter transformation (rapid nodal growth, B symptoms).
Recurrent severe infection from immune dysfunction.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms a clonal B-cell lymphocytosis with the characteristic phenotype.
Clinical staging (Rai/Binet) and genetics guide management timing.

management.detail: Many early-stage asymptomatic patients are simply monitored ('watch and wait').
Targeted therapy (BTK/BCL-2 inhibitors) +/- anti-CD20 antibody for progressive/symptomatic disease (specialist-led).
Vaccination and prompt treatment of infections; manage autoimmune cytopenias.

title: Hodgkin lymphoma
presentation: Painless, often cervical, lymphadenopathy in a young adult (bimodal age distribution).
B symptoms: fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss; pruritus; alcohol-induced node pain.
Reed-Sternberg cells on biopsy.

diagnostics.rationale: Determines stage and guides treatment and response assessment.

management.detail: Refer for staging and combined-modality treatment.
Curable in most with combination chemotherapy, with radiotherapy in selected cases.
Monitor for late effects (second cancers, cardiac, fertility) given the young population and high cure rate.

title: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma
presentation: Painless lymphadenopathy, which may be widespread; extranodal disease is common.
B symptoms, fatigue; presentation varies from indolent to aggressive.
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the commonest aggressive type.
redFlags: Aggressive lymphoma with rapid growth, organ compromise or tumour lysis.

diagnostics.rationale: Histology and immunophenotyping define the subtype, which drives treatment.

management.detail: Indolent lymphomas may be observed; aggressive types treated with immunochemotherapy (e.g. R-CHOP) — specialist-led.
Tumour-lysis prevention, infection management, growth-factor support.
Restaging by PET-CT; manage relapse with further lines/transplant/CAR-T as appropriate.

title: Multiple myeloma
presentation: The CRAB features: hyperCalcaemia, Renal impairment, Anaemia and Bone lesions/pain.
Bone pain (especially back), pathological fractures, recurrent infections.
Older adults; monoclonal paraprotein on electrophoresis.
redFlags: Spinal cord compression from vertebral disease.
Hypercalcaemic crisis and acute kidney injury.

diagnostics.test: Serum/urine protein electrophoresis and free light chains
diagnostics.rationale: Detects and quantifies the monoclonal protein.

diagnostics.test: Bone marrow, calcium, renal function and skeletal imaging
diagnostics.rationale: Confirms plasma-cell infiltration and end-organ (CRAB) damage.

management.detail: Treat hypercalcaemia, AKI and cord compression urgently.
Combination therapy (proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulators, anti-CD38, steroids) +/- autologous transplant (specialist-led).
Bisphosphonates for bone disease, infection prophylaxis/vaccination, thromboprophylaxis with immunomodulators, analgesia.

title: Beta-thalassaemia
presentation: Thalassaemia major: severe transfusion-dependent anaemia from infancy, failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly and skeletal changes.
Thalassaemia minor (trait): mild microcytic anaemia, often asymptomatic.
Common in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, South and Southeast Asian populations.
redFlags: Iron overload from transfusions (cardiac, hepatic, endocrine).

diagnostics.rationale: Microcytic anaemia with raised HbA2/HbF confirms beta-thalassaemia.
Distinguish from iron deficiency and monitor transfusional iron overload.

management.detail: Regular transfusion to maintain haemoglobin and suppress ineffective erythropoiesis.
Chelation (e.g. desferrioxamine or oral chelators) to prevent and treat iron overload.
Folic acid, manage endocrine/cardiac complications, genetic counselling; consider transplant in selected children.

title: Haemophilia A and B
presentation: Excessive or spontaneous bleeding: haemarthroses, deep muscle haematomas, prolonged bleeding after trauma/surgery.
X-linked recessive — affects males; factor VIII (A) or IX (B) deficiency.
Severity correlates with factor level.

diagnostics.rationale: Prolonged APTT with reduced factor VIII or IX confirms the type and severity.
Detects antibodies that neutralise replacement factor.

management.detail: Replace the deficient factor for bleeds and around procedures; prophylaxis in severe disease.
Desmopressin for mild haemophilia A; tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeding; avoid IM injections and antiplatelet/anticoagulant drugs.
Manage through a haemophilia centre; address inhibitors and joint health.

references.label: WFH guidelines for the management of haemophilia

title: Von Willebrand disease
presentation: Mucocutaneous bleeding: epistaxis, easy bruising, heavy menstrual bleeding, bleeding after dental work/surgery.
The commonest inherited bleeding disorder; usually autosomal dominant.
Family history of bleeding is common.

diagnostics.test: von Willebrand factor antigen and activity, factor VIII

diagnostics.rationale: Assess overall haemostasis; platelets are usually normal.

management.detail: Raises vWF/factor VIII in type 1 disease for minor bleeds/procedures (test responsiveness first).
For type 3, severe bleeding, or major surgery.
Tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeding; hormonal control of heavy menstrual bleeding; avoid antiplatelet drugs.

title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
presentation: Fatigue, pallor and jaundice with dark urine from haemolysis.
Warm (IgG, commonest) or cold (IgM) types; may be idiopathic or secondary (CLL, lupus, infection, drugs).
Splenomegaly may be present.

diagnostics.rationale: Positive DAT confirms immune-mediated haemolysis and the antibody type.

diagnostics.test: Haemolysis markers (reticulocytes, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin) and film
diagnostics.rationale: Confirm active haemolysis; spherocytes/agglutination on film.

management.detail: Warm AIHA: corticosteroids first-line +/- rituximab; cold AIHA: keep warm, treat the underlying cause, rituximab; address secondary causes.
Transfuse for severe anaemia (with specialist guidance on cross-matching difficulties).
Folic acid; thromboprophylaxis in active haemolysis; second-line therapy/splenectomy for refractory warm AIHA.

references.label: BSH guideline on the management of autoimmune haemolytic anaemia

title: Alcohol-related hepatitis
presentation: Recent heavy alcohol use with rapid-onset jaundice, tender hepatomegaly and malaise.
Fever, anorexia; may have features of decompensated liver disease (ascites, encephalopathy).
Often a background of chronic liver disease.

diagnostics.rationale: Characteristic pattern; bilirubin and INR drive severity scores.
Exclude infection and biliary obstruction; assess the liver.

management.detail: Alcohol cessation with withdrawal management, nutrition (including thiamine), and treat infection/AKI.
Use Maddrey discriminant function/MELD to identify severe disease.
Consider corticosteroids for severe alcoholic hepatitis without contraindication; monitor response (Lille score).

references.label: EASL/AASLD guidance on alcohol-related liver disease

title: Autoimmune hepatitis
presentation: Fatigue, jaundice and abnormal liver enzymes, often in women.
May present acutely or as chronic hepatitis/cirrhosis; associated with other autoimmune diseases.
Raised IgG and autoantibodies.

diagnostics.rationale: Support the diagnosis when other causes are excluded.
Confirms interface hepatitis and assesses fibrosis.

management.detail: Corticosteroids to induce remission, with azathioprine as a steroid-sparing maintenance agent.
Track LFTs and IgG to guide therapy; bone protection on steroids.
Screen for varices and hepatocellular carcinoma; consider transplant for end-stage disease.

title: Primary biliary cholangitis
presentation: Fatigue and pruritus, often in middle-aged women.
Cholestatic liver enzymes (raised ALP); may be asymptomatic at diagnosis.
Associated with other autoimmune conditions; later jaundice and cirrhosis.
redFlags: Features of overlap with autoimmune hepatitis.

diagnostics.rationale: AMA positivity with cholestatic LFTs is highly suggestive.
Exclude biliary obstruction; biopsy if diagnosis unclear or overlap suspected.

management.detail: First-line therapy that improves liver biochemistry and outcomes; assess biochemical response.
Add obeticholic acid or fibrates for inadequate response (specialist-led).
Treat pruritus (e.g. colestyramine), fatigue and osteoporosis; surveillance for cirrhosis complications.

title: Hereditary haemochromatosis
presentation: Fatigue, arthralgia, and 'bronze' skin pigmentation from iron overload.
May present with diabetes, liver disease, cardiomyopathy or hypogonadism.
Usually due to HFE gene mutations; often detected on raised ferritin/transferrin saturation.

diagnostics.rationale: Raised values prompt evaluation for iron overload.
Confirms the diagnosis; assess hepatic iron/fibrosis (MRI, sometimes biopsy).

management.detail: Regular venesection to deplete iron stores is the mainstay, then maintenance phlebotomy.
Chelation where venesection is not tolerated/feasible.
Treat diabetes/cardiac/endocrine effects; surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhosis; family screening.

title: Wilson disease
presentation: Hepatic (hepatitis, cirrhosis, acute liver failure) and/or neuropsychiatric features (tremor, dystonia, dysarthria, mood/behaviour change) in a young person.
Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp examination.
Autosomal recessive copper accumulation (ATP7B mutations).
redFlags: Acute liver failure with Coombs-negative haemolysis (often needs transplant).

diagnostics.rationale: Low caeruloplasmin with high urinary copper supports the diagnosis.
Kayser-Fleischer rings, ATP7B testing and hepatic copper confirm.

management.detail: Lifelong chelation (penicillamine or trientine) to remove copper; introduce carefully (neurological worsening can occur).
Zinc to block intestinal copper absorption (maintenance); avoid copper-rich foods.
Liver transplant for acute liver failure/decompensation; screen relatives.

title: Achalasia
presentation: Progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids.
Regurgitation of undigested food, chest pain and weight loss.
Caused by failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation and absent peristalsis.
redFlags: Rapidly progressive symptoms in older adults (exclude pseudoachalasia/malignancy).

diagnostics.rationale: Gold standard — shows absent peristalsis and impaired LES relaxation.

management.detail: Pneumatic dilatation or laparoscopic Heller myotomy (or POEM) relieve obstruction durably.
Botulinum toxin injection or nitrates/calcium-channel blockers for poor surgical candidates.
Monitor symptoms and nutrition; surveillance for the small long-term cancer risk.

title: Chronic pancreatitis
presentation: Recurrent or persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back, often relieved by sitting forward.
Features of exocrine insufficiency (steatorrhoea, weight loss) and endocrine insufficiency (diabetes).
Most commonly related to alcohol; pancreatic calcification may be seen.
redFlags: New pancreatic mass / weight loss (exclude pancreatic cancer).
Complications: pseudocyst, biliary/duodenal obstruction, GI bleeding.

diagnostics.rationale: Shows ductal changes, calcification and complications.

management.detail: Alcohol and smoking cessation; analgesia (step-wise), addressing neuropathic component.
Pancreatic enzyme replacement and fat-soluble vitamins for exocrine insufficiency; manage diabetes.
Endoscopic/surgical therapy for obstructing ductal disease, pseudocysts or refractory pain.

title: Acute anterior uveitis (iritis)
presentation: Painful red eye with photophobia and blurred vision, usually unilateral.
Circumcorneal (ciliary) redness, a small or irregular pupil, and cells/flare in the anterior chamber.
May be idiopathic or associated with HLA-B27 conditions, sarcoidosis or infection.
redFlags: Marked visual loss, hypopyon, or raised intraocular pressure.
Features suggesting infective or posterior uveitis.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms anterior-chamber inflammation (cells and flare) and complications.

diagnostics.test: Targeted systemic workup for recurrent cases

management.detail: Refer for slit-lamp assessment and treatment.
Topical corticosteroids reduce inflammation; a cycloplegic (e.g. cyclopentolate) relieves pain and prevents synechiae.
Address systemic associations; monitor intraocular pressure on steroids.

references.label: Royal College of Ophthalmologists — uveitis guidance

title: Retinal detachment
presentation: Sudden onset of floaters and flashes (photopsia), followed by a 'curtain' or shadow across the visual field.
Painless progressive visual field loss; reduced acuity if the macula is involved.
Risk factors: myopia, prior cataract surgery, trauma, family history.
redFlags: Macula-threatening or macula-off detachment — sight-threatening, needs urgent surgery.
Sudden shower of floaters with flashes.

diagnostics.rationale: Visualises the detached retina and any tears.
Detects detachment when the fundus cannot be seen.

management.detail: Refer immediately; macula-on detachment is a surgical emergency to preserve central vision.
Positioning advice per ophthalmology while awaiting surgery.
Vitrectomy, scleral buckle or pneumatic retinopexy depending on type; laser/cryotherapy for tears without detachment.

references.label: Royal College of Ophthalmologists — retinal detachment guidance

title: Chemical eye injury (ocular burn)
presentation: Pain, redness, tearing and blurred vision after a chemical splash.
Alkali burns (e.g. cement, ammonia) penetrate deeply and are more dangerous than acids.
Corneal haze and conjunctival/limbal blanching indicate severity.

diagnostics.rationale: Guides duration of irrigation; continue until pH normalises (~7).

diagnostics.test: Visual acuity and slit-lamp after irrigation

management.detail: Irrigate the eye with water/saline for at least 15–30 minutes BEFORE anything else — do not delay for examination; remove particulate matter.

management.step: Check and re-irrigate to neutral pH
management.detail: Recheck pH and continue irrigation until normalised.
Refer urgently; treat with lubricants, topical steroids/antibiotics and IOP control per specialist.

references.label: Royal College of Ophthalmologists — chemical eye injury guidance

title: Age-related macular degeneration
presentation: Gradual central vision loss and distortion (straight lines appear wavy) in an older adult (dry AMD).
Sudden central visual loss/distortion suggests neovascular (wet) AMD.
Drusen and pigmentary changes at the macula.
redFlags: Sudden distortion/central scotoma — possible wet AMD needing urgent anti-VEGF.

diagnostics.rationale: Identifies drusen/macular changes; Amsler detects distortion.
Detects fluid/neovascular membrane and guides treatment.

management.detail: Suspected wet AMD needs rapid referral for intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy to preserve vision.
Smoking cessation, dietary advice and AREDS-type supplements for intermediate disease.
Visual aids and rehabilitation; monitor with Amsler grid for conversion to wet AMD.

references.label: Royal College of Ophthalmologists — AMD guidance

title: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
presentation: Progressive non-bilious projectile vomiting in an infant, typically 2–8 weeks old.
Hungry after vomiting; weight loss and dehydration.
A palpable 'olive' mass and visible gastric peristalsis.

diagnostics.rationale: Detect the characteristic hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis to correct before surgery.

management.detail: Pyloric stenosis is a MEDICAL emergency before a surgical one — rehydrate and correct alkalosis/electrolytes first.
Ramstedt pyloromyotomy once the infant is biochemically stable.
Reintroduce feeds and monitor; excellent prognosis.

references.label: Paediatric surgical guidance on pyloric stenosis

title: Hepatocellular carcinoma
presentation: Often arises in chronic liver disease/cirrhosis (hepatitis B/C, alcohol, NAFLD).
Weight loss, RUQ pain, decompensation of previously stable cirrhosis, or detected on surveillance.
Raised alpha-fetoprotein in some cases.

diagnostics.test: Multiphase CT or MRI of the liver
diagnostics.rationale: Characteristic arterial enhancement with washout can be diagnostic in cirrhosis without biopsy.
Supports diagnosis and assesses hepatic reserve.

management.detail: 6-monthly ultrasound (+/- AFP) in at-risk cirrhosis enables curative treatment.
Resection, ablation or transplantation for early-stage disease with adequate liver function.
TACE for intermediate disease; systemic therapy (e.g. immunotherapy combinations) for advanced disease (MDT-led).

title: Aortic stenosis
presentation: Exertional dyspnoea, angina and syncope (the classic triad) as stenosis becomes severe.
An ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, with a slow-rising pulse.
Often degenerative (elderly) or from a bicuspid valve (younger).
redFlags: Syncope, heart failure or angina — symptomatic severe AS has a poor prognosis without intervention.
Severe stenosis with low gradient and reduced ejection fraction.

diagnostics.rationale: Grades severity (valve area, gradient) and assesses LV function.
Detects LV hypertrophy and guides timing of referral.

management.detail: Refer symptomatic or severe AS to cardiology; avoid vasodilators that can cause hypotension.
Surgical (SAVR) or transcatheter (TAVI) aortic valve replacement is the definitive treatment for severe symptomatic disease.
Serial echocardiography; manage cardiovascular risk factors.

title: Mitral regurgitation
presentation: Exertional dyspnoea, fatigue and palpitations; may be asymptomatic for years.
A pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla.
Causes: degenerative (prolapse), functional, rheumatic, ischaemic, endocarditis.
redFlags: Acute severe MR (e.g. papillary muscle rupture) with pulmonary oedema/shock — surgical emergency.

diagnostics.rationale: Defines mechanism and severity and assesses LV size/function.

management.detail: Standard heart-failure therapy and rate/rhythm and anticoagulation for AF.
Refer severe primary MR (especially with symptoms or LV dysfunction) for valve repair/replacement; transcatheter options in selected patients.
Serial echocardiography to time intervention before irreversible LV damage.

title: Dilated cardiomyopathy
presentation: Heart failure symptoms: breathlessness, orthopnoea, oedema and fatigue.
Left ventricular dilatation and systolic dysfunction not explained by loading/coronary disease.
Causes: genetic, viral, alcohol, peripartum, toxins.
redFlags: Ventricular arrhythmia or syncope (sudden death risk).

diagnostics.rationale: Shows a dilated, poorly contracting left ventricle.
Identify reversible causes; cardiac MRI for aetiology.

management.detail: ACE inhibitor/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor improve outcomes; diuretics for congestion.
Consider ICD/CRT for selected patients; treat arrhythmia and thromboembolism risk.
Abstinence in alcoholic/peripartum types; manage reversible causes; advanced therapies for refractory disease.

title: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
presentation: Exertional breathlessness, chest pain, palpitations or syncope; may be asymptomatic.
An ejection murmur that increases with Valsalva (dynamic LV outflow obstruction).
Commonest cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes; often autosomal dominant.
redFlags: Exertional syncope or family history of sudden death.

diagnostics.rationale: Demonstrates asymmetric LV hypertrophy and outflow obstruction.
Detect arrhythmia and assess sudden-death risk; cardiac MRI and genetics as indicated.

management.detail: Beta-blockers or rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers; avoid dehydration and vasodilators that worsen obstruction.
ICD for high-risk patients; activity advice; family screening.
Septal reduction (myectomy or alcohol ablation) for severe symptomatic obstruction; cardiac myosin inhibitors in selected patients.

title: Atrial flutter
presentation: Palpitations, breathlessness, chest discomfort or fatigue; may be asymptomatic.
Regular tachycardia, classically around 150 bpm (2:1 block) with sawtooth flutter waves.
Shares thromboembolic risk with atrial fibrillation.
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability — needs urgent synchronised cardioversion.

diagnostics.rationale: Sawtooth flutter waves, especially in the inferior leads.
Assess structural disease and stroke risk (CHA2DS2-VASc).

management.detail: Rate control (beta-blocker/diltiazem) or cardioversion; flutter often responds well to DC cardioversion.
Stroke prevention per CHA2DS2-VASc, as for atrial fibrillation.
Cavotricuspid isthmus ablation is highly effective and curative for typical flutter.

title: Ventricular tachycardia
presentation: Palpitations, presyncope, syncope, chest pain or cardiac arrest.
A broad-complex tachycardia; assume VT in any broad-complex tachycardia until proven otherwise, especially with structural heart disease.
May be monomorphic (scar-related) or polymorphic (ischaemia, long QT).
redFlags: Pulseless VT — cardiac arrest, defibrillate immediately.

diagnostics.test: Electrolytes, troponin and assessment for structural/ischaemic cause

management.detail: Pulseless VT → defibrillation and CPR. Unstable VT with a pulse → synchronised cardioversion.
Antiarrhythmic (e.g. amiodarone) and correct electrolytes/ischaemia; magnesium for torsades.
Treat underlying disease; ICD and/or ablation for recurrent VT (specialist-led).

references.label: Resuscitation Council ALS; ESC ventricular arrhythmia guidelines

title: Bronchiectasis
presentation: Chronic productive cough with large volumes of purulent sputum.
Recurrent chest infections, breathlessness and sometimes haemoptysis.
Causes: post-infective, cystic fibrosis, immune deficiency, ABPA, idiopathic.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnostic — shows dilated, thick-walled bronchi (signet-ring sign).

management.detail: Daily chest physiotherapy and mucoactive measures are the cornerstone.
Prolonged antibiotic courses targeted to sputum organisms; consider long-term macrolide for frequent exacerbations.
Address underlying cause, vaccinate, pulmonary rehabilitation; manage haemoptysis.

title: Obstructive sleep apnoea
presentation: Loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas and daytime sleepiness.
Morning headaches, poor concentration, and refractory hypertension.
Risk factors: obesity, large neck circumference, retrognathia.

diagnostics.rationale: Quantifies apnoea-hypopnoea index to confirm and grade severity.
Assesses daytime sleepiness and treatment need.

management.detail: Weight loss, reduce alcohol/sedatives, sleep position; treat nasal obstruction.
Continuous positive airway pressure is first-line for moderate-severe disease and improves symptoms and cardiovascular risk.
Mandibular advancement devices for milder disease; advise on driving safety per regulations.

title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
presentation: Progressive exertional breathlessness and a persistent dry cough in an older adult.
Fine bibasal end-inspiratory 'velcro' crackles and finger clubbing.
A diagnosis of exclusion among the interstitial lung diseases.
redFlags: Acute exacerbation with rapid respiratory deterioration (high mortality).

diagnostics.rationale: A usual interstitial pneumonia pattern (subpleural reticulation, honeycombing) supports the diagnosis.
Restrictive pattern with reduced transfer factor; track progression.

management.detail: Pirfenidone or nintedanib slow decline in lung function (specialist-initiated).
Oxygen for hypoxia, pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination, and treat reflux/comorbidities.
Lung transplantation in suitable patients; early palliative input for symptom control.

title: Sarcoidosis
presentation: Often asymptomatic bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on imaging; cough and breathlessness.
Extrapulmonary features: erythema nodosum, uveitis, arthralgia, skin lesions, hypercalcaemia.
Löfgren syndrome (fever, hilar nodes, erythema nodosum, arthralgia) has a good prognosis.
redFlags: Severe hypercalcaemia or progressive pulmonary fibrosis.

diagnostics.rationale: Non-caseating granulomas confirm; exclude TB and lymphoma.

management.detail: Many cases (e.g. Löfgren) resolve spontaneously and need only monitoring.
For significant pulmonary, cardiac, neurological, ocular or hypercalcaemic disease; steroid-sparing agents for chronic disease.
Cardiology/ophthalmology/neurology input for those organ involvements; monitor for relapse.

title: Lower gastrointestinal bleeding
presentation: Fresh red or maroon blood per rectum, or clots.
Causes: diverticular disease, angiodysplasia, haemorrhoids, colitis, malignancy.
Brisk upper GI bleeding can also present as rectal bleeding.
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability or ongoing heavy bleeding.
Features suggesting malignancy or ischaemic colitis.

diagnostics.rationale: FBC, coagulation, group & save/crossmatch; assess severity.
Localises and may treat the source; CT angiography for active brisk bleeding.

management.detail: IV access, fluids/transfusion as needed, correct coagulopathy; most lower GI bleeds settle spontaneously.
Endoscopic therapy, angiographic embolisation, or surgery for refractory bleeding; exclude upper GI source if unstable.
Colonic evaluation to exclude malignancy; review antithrombotic drugs.

title: Gastric cancer (diagnostic pathway)
presentation: Dyspepsia, early satiety, weight loss, anorexia and epigastric pain.
Iron-deficiency anaemia, dysphagia, or a palpable mass in advanced disease.
Risk factors: H. pylori, smoking, diet, atrophic gastritis.
redFlags: Alarm features: weight loss, dysphagia, GI bleeding, vomiting, anaemia, mass — urgent referral.

diagnostics.rationale: Direct visualisation and histology for diagnosis.

management.detail: Refer alarm symptoms on a suspected-cancer pathway for prompt endoscopy.
Surgery with perioperative chemotherapy for resectable disease; chemotherapy/targeted therapy for advanced disease (MDT-led).
Nutrition, manage obstruction/bleeding, palliative care as needed.

title: Pancreatic cancer (diagnostic pathway)
presentation: Painless obstructive jaundice (head of pancreas), or epigastric/back pain and weight loss (body/tail).
New-onset diabetes, steatorrhoea, and non-specific symptoms causing late presentation.
Often advanced at diagnosis.
redFlags: New diabetes with weight loss in an older adult.

diagnostics.rationale: Assesses the primary tumour, vascular involvement and metastases.
Supports diagnosis and provides tissue; ERCP for biliary obstruction.

management.detail: Refer suspected cases promptly; relieve biliary obstruction (stenting) as needed.
Surgical resection (Whipple) for the minority with resectable disease; chemotherapy for advanced disease (MDT-led).
Pancreatic enzyme replacement, pain control, nutrition and early palliative care.

title: Bladder cancer (diagnostic pathway)
presentation: Painless visible haematuria is the hallmark presentation.
Irritative urinary symptoms; risk factors include smoking and occupational exposures.
Usually urothelial carcinoma.
redFlags: Visible haematuria at any age (urgent referral).

diagnostics.rationale: Direct visualisation and biopsy of bladder lesions.
Assess the upper tracts and stage disease.

management.detail: Refer visible (and unexplained non-visible) haematuria on a suspected-cancer pathway.
Transurethral resection +/- intravesical BCG/chemotherapy with surveillance.
Radical cystectomy or radiotherapy +/- chemotherapy; systemic therapy for metastatic disease (MDT-led).

title: Renal cell carcinoma
presentation: Often incidental on imaging; the classic triad (flank pain, haematuria, mass) is uncommon and late.
Constitutional symptoms, anaemia or paraneoplastic features (hypercalcaemia, polycythaemia).
A left varicocele may indicate renal vein involvement.

diagnostics.rationale: Characterises the renal mass and stages disease.

management.detail: Partial or radical nephrectomy for localised disease; active surveillance for small tumours in selected patients.
Targeted therapy (TKIs) and immunotherapy for metastatic disease (MDT-led).
Surveillance imaging; monitor renal function.

title: IgA nephropathy
presentation: Episodic visible haematuria, classically within days of an upper respiratory infection ('synpharyngitic').
Often persistent microscopic haematuria and proteinuria found incidentally.
The commonest primary glomerulonephritis worldwide.

diagnostics.test: Urinalysis, protein quantification and renal function
diagnostics.rationale: Detect haematuria/proteinuria and assess kidney function.
Confirms mesangial IgA deposition and grades disease.

management.detail: Blood-pressure control with ACE inhibitor/ARB and proteinuria reduction; lifestyle and cardiovascular risk management.
Consider in progressive disease despite optimised supportive care (specialist-led).
Track proteinuria and renal function; treat rapidly progressive disease urgently.

title: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
presentation: Progressive bilateral renal cysts causing flank/abdominal pain, haematuria and hypertension.
Family history of kidney disease; progression to chronic kidney failure.
Associated liver cysts and intracranial aneurysms.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms the diagnosis in an at-risk individual.
Monitor progression; consider aneurysm screening in selected patients.

management.detail: Rigorous BP control (ACE inhibitor/ARB) to slow progression.
Tolvaptan for selected adults at risk of rapid progression; ensure adequate hydration.
Treat cyst infection/haemorrhage and stones; prepare for renal replacement therapy; genetic counselling.

title: Motor neurone disease (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis)
presentation: Progressive painless weakness with mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs.
Limb weakness, bulbar symptoms (dysarthria, dysphagia), fasciculations and wasting; cognition usually preserved.
No sensory loss.
redFlags: Respiratory muscle weakness (breathlessness, orthopnoea) — needs ventilatory assessment.

diagnostics.rationale: Demonstrates widespread denervation; diagnosis is clinical with supportive EMG.

diagnostics.test: MRI and bloods to exclude mimics
diagnostics.rationale: Rule out structural and treatable conditions.

management.detail: Specialist MND team: physiotherapy, OT, speech and language, dietitian and respiratory support.
Riluzole modestly prolongs survival; manage spasticity, sialorrhoea, cramps and mood.
Non-invasive ventilation for respiratory failure; nutrition (gastrostomy); early advance care planning and palliative care.

title: Peripheral neuropathy
presentation: Distal symmetrical sensory symptoms: numbness, tingling, burning pain in a 'glove and stocking' distribution.
Weakness and reduced reflexes in motor involvement; gait imbalance.
Common causes: diabetes, alcohol, B12 deficiency, drugs, renal failure.
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or ascending weakness (consider Guillain-Barré).

diagnostics.rationale: Glucose/HbA1c, B12, renal/liver/thyroid function and others to find a treatable cause.
Characterise the neuropathy and guide further workup.

management.detail: Optimise glycaemic control, correct deficiencies, remove offending drugs/alcohol.
First-line agents include amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin.
Foot care to prevent ulceration, falls prevention, physiotherapy.

title: Hypoparathyroidism
presentation: Symptoms of hypocalcaemia: paraesthesia, cramps, tetany and, if severe, seizures.
Commonest cause is post-surgical (after thyroid/parathyroid surgery).
Low calcium with inappropriately low/normal PTH and high phosphate.

diagnostics.rationale: Low calcium with low/normal PTH confirms; correct magnesium.

management.detail: IV calcium gluconate for severe/symptomatic cases with cardiac monitoring.
Oral calcium and active vitamin D (alfacalcidol/calcitriol); monitor to avoid hypercalciuria.
Periodic calcium, phosphate and renal function; correct magnesium.

title: Hypernatraemia
presentation: Thirst, lethargy, irritability and confusion; seizures and coma if severe.
Usually reflects a water deficit (inadequate intake, GI/renal losses, diabetes insipidus).
Common in the elderly, infants and patients who cannot access water.

diagnostics.test: Serum sodium, glucose and volume assessment
diagnostics.rationale: Confirms hypernatraemia and guides cause/fluid choice.
Distinguishes renal water loss (e.g. diabetes insipidus) from extrarenal losses.

management.detail: Treat shock with isotonic fluid first, then correct the free-water deficit, usually orally or with hypotonic IV fluids.
Lower sodium gradually (about 10 mmol/L per 24 h) to avoid cerebral oedema.
Address diabetes insipidus, GI losses or inadequate intake; monitor sodium frequently.

title: Psoriatic arthritis
presentation: Inflammatory joint pain and stiffness in a person with psoriasis (skin/nail disease).
Patterns: oligoarticular, polyarticular, distal interphalangeal, spondylitis; dactylitis ('sausage digit') and enthesitis.
Nail pitting/onycholysis is a clue.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical; markers may be normal or raised; rheumatoid factor usually negative.
Detects erosions, new bone formation and enthesitis.

management.detail: For mild peripheral disease and symptom relief; treat skin disease.
Methotrexate or other DMARDs for persistent disease; biologics (TNF/IL-17/IL-23 inhibitors) for inadequate response (specialist-led).
Joint dermatology-rheumatology management; treat comorbidities and cardiovascular risk.

title: Cutaneous melanoma
presentation: A new or changing pigmented lesion: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variation, Diameter >6 mm, Evolution (ABCDE).
An 'ugly duckling' lesion differing from the patient's other moles.
May arise de novo or in a pre-existing naevus.

diagnostics.rationale: Full-thickness excision biopsy provides diagnosis and Breslow thickness (key prognostic factor).
Sentinel node biopsy/imaging guided by tumour thickness.

management.detail: Refer suspicious lesions urgently; wide local excision with margins based on Breslow depth.
Sentinel node biopsy in selected cases; immunotherapy/targeted therapy for advanced disease (MDT-led).
Sun protection, skin self-examination and follow-up; screen for recurrence/new primaries.

title: Non-melanoma skin cancer (basal and squamous cell carcinoma)
presentation: Basal cell carcinoma: a slow-growing pearly papule with telangiectasia, sometimes with a rolled ulcerated edge, on sun-exposed skin.
Squamous cell carcinoma: a keratotic or ulcerated nodule that may grow rapidly; can metastasise.
Risk factors: cumulative sun exposure, fair skin, immunosuppression.
redFlags: Rapid growth, ulceration or a lesion on the lip/ear (higher-risk SCC).

diagnostics.rationale: Site, size, differentiation and immune status determine management.

management.detail: Complete excision is the mainstay; Mohs surgery for high-risk/facial lesions.
Topical therapy/cryotherapy for superficial BCC; radiotherapy where surgery is unsuitable.
Sun protection and skin surveillance, especially in immunosuppressed patients.

title: Undescended testis (cryptorchidism)
presentation: An empty or poorly developed scrotum with a testis not palpable in the scrotum.
May be palpable in the inguinal canal or impalpable.
Identified at newborn or routine child health checks.
redFlags: Bilateral impalpable testes (assess for disorder of sex development / endocrine evaluation).
Acutely painful groin/scrotum (exclude torsion of an undescended testis).

diagnostics.rationale: Determines whether the testis is palpable, retractile or impalpable; imaging is generally unhelpful.

diagnostics.test: Specialist/endocrine assessment for bilateral impalpable testes
diagnostics.rationale: Exclude DSD and assess gonadal function.

management.detail: Many descend by 3–6 months; refer if still undescended to arrange surgery.
Surgical fixation, ideally by 12–18 months, to improve fertility potential and aid cancer surveillance.
Advise on the small increased risk of testicular cancer and importance of self-examination later in life.

references.label: Paediatric urology guidance on undescended testis

title: Cervical cancer
presentation: Abnormal vaginal bleeding (postcoital, intermenstrual or postmenopausal).
Offensive vaginal discharge.
Advanced disease: pelvic pain, leg oedema, ureteric obstruction, weight loss.
redFlags: Visible friable cervical lesion on speculum exam.

diagnostics.test: MRI pelvis and examination under anaesthesia

management.detail: Refer to gynaecological oncology for FIGO staging and multidisciplinary planning.
Surgery (radical hysterectomy) or chemoradiotherapy for early-stage disease.
Concurrent cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy.
HPV vaccination and screening programmes prevent most cases.

references.label: WHO guideline for screening and treatment of cervical pre-cancer lesions

title: Endometrial cancer
presentation: Postmenopausal bleeding (the cardinal symptom).
Abnormal premenopausal uterine bleeding.
Risk factors: obesity, unopposed oestrogen, tamoxifen, PCOS, nulliparity.
redFlags: Any postmenopausal bleeding requires urgent investigation.

management.detail: Urgent referral to gynaecological oncology.
Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is the mainstay.
Radiotherapy/chemotherapy based on stage and grade.

title: Ovarian cancer
presentation: Persistent bloating, early satiety, abdominal/pelvic pain.
Increased urinary urgency/frequency.
Often presents late with ascites or an abdominal mass.

diagnostics.rationale: Risk of Malignancy Index guides referral.

management.detail: Gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team.
Maximal debulking improves outcomes.
Platinum/taxane-based chemotherapy; consider PARP inhibitors and genetic testing (BRCA).

references.label: ESMO clinical practice guidelines: ovarian cancer

title: Thyroid cancer
presentation: Painless thyroid nodule or enlarging neck mass.
Hoarseness or dysphagia in advanced disease.
Cervical lymphadenopathy.
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging hard fixed mass (consider anaplastic carcinoma).

management.detail: Endocrine surgery/oncology multidisciplinary team.
Thyroidectomy (+/- lymph node dissection) for differentiated carcinoma.
Radioiodine ablation and TSH-suppressive levothyroxine for differentiated cancers.

references.label: American Thyroid Association management guidelines for thyroid nodules and differentiated thyroid cancer

title: Oral and head & neck cancer
presentation: Non-healing oral ulcer or white/red patch lasting >3 weeks.
Persistent hoarseness, sore throat, or dysphagia.
Neck lump; risk factors tobacco, alcohol, betel/areca nut, HPV.
redFlags: Unilateral neck mass in an adult.

management.detail: Head and neck cancer multidisciplinary team.
Surgery and/or radiotherapy +/- chemotherapy by site and stage.
Smoking and alcohol cessation; dental assessment before radiotherapy.

references.label: NICE guideline NG36: cancer of the upper aerodigestive tract

title: Testicular cancer
presentation: Painless unilateral testicular lump or swelling.
Dull ache or heaviness in the scrotum.
Most common solid malignancy in men aged 15-35.

management.detail: Urology; do NOT perform trans-scrotal biopsy.
Radical inguinal orchidectomy is diagnostic and therapeutic.
Surveillance, chemotherapy or radiotherapy by histology and stage; highly curable.

title: Brain tumour (CNS neoplasm)
presentation: Progressive headache, often worse in the morning or on lying down.
New focal neurological deficit or seizures.
Personality/cognitive change; nausea and vomiting.
redFlags: Headache with papilloedema or vomiting (raised intracranial pressure).
New focal deficit or first seizure in an adult.

diagnostics.rationale: Imaging of choice to characterise lesions.

management.detail: Dexamethasone for symptomatic oedema; urgent neurosurgical referral.
Surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy as guided by tumour type.
Antiepileptic for those with seizures (not routine prophylaxis).

references.label: NICE guideline NG99: brain tumours and metastases

title: Laryngeal cancer
presentation: Persistent hoarseness lasting more than 3 weeks.
Throat pain, dysphagia, referred otalgia.
Stridor in advanced disease; smoking/alcohol risk factors.
redFlags: Persistent hoarseness >3 weeks in a smoker.

management.detail: Head and neck multidisciplinary team.
Radiotherapy or transoral laser surgery preserving voice.
Chemoradiotherapy or total laryngectomy.

references.label: NICE guideline NG36: cancer of the upper aerodigestive tract

title: Mitral stenosis
presentation: Exertional dyspnoea, fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance.
Haemoptysis, palpitations (atrial fibrillation).
Most often rheumatic in origin; loud S1 and mid-diastolic rumble.
redFlags: Acute pulmonary oedema, especially during pregnancy or tachyarrhythmia.
Systemic embolism from left atrial thrombus.

diagnostics.rationale: Detects atrial fibrillation and left atrial enlargement.

management.detail: Beta-blocker for rate; anticoagulate if AF or prior embolism.
Relieve pulmonary congestion.
Percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty or surgery for severe symptomatic disease.
Penicillin prophylaxis if rheumatic.

references.label: ESC/EACTS guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease

title: Aortic regurgitation
presentation: Exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, palpitations.
Wide pulse pressure, collapsing pulse, early diastolic murmur.
Causes: bicuspid valve, rheumatic disease, aortic root dilatation, endocarditis.
redFlags: Acute severe AR (endocarditis or dissection) causing cardiogenic shock.

diagnostics.rationale: Grades regurgitation and assesses LV size/function.

management.detail: Manage endocarditis, dissection or root disease.
Vasodilators (ACE inhibitor/dihydropyridine) for hypertension or symptoms if surgery deferred.
Aortic valve replacement/repair for symptomatic severe AR or LV dysfunction/dilatation.

references.label: ESC/EACTS guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease

title: Tricuspid valve disease
presentation: Fatigue, peripheral oedema, ascites and raised JVP with prominent v wave.
Pulsatile hepatomegaly; pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge.
Usually secondary to right ventricular/pulmonary disease.
redFlags: Progressive right heart failure with hepatic congestion.

diagnostics.rationale: Grades regurgitation and assesses RV and pulmonary pressures.

management.detail: Address left heart disease/pulmonary hypertension driving secondary TR.
Relieve venous congestion.
Repair/replacement considered, often during left-sided valve surgery.

references.label: ESC/EACTS guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease

title: Constrictive pericarditis
presentation: Progressive right heart failure: oedema, ascites, raised JVP.
Kussmaul sign and pericardial knock.
Causes include TB (common in endemic areas), prior cardiac surgery, radiation.

diagnostics.rationale: Demonstrates septal bounce and ventricular interdependence.
Common reversible cause in endemic regions.

management.detail: Anti-tuberculous therapy if TB pericarditis.
Cautious diuresis for congestion.
Definitive treatment for chronic constriction.

references.label: ESC guidelines on the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases

title: Infective endocarditis prophylaxis
presentation: Risk-management topic for patients with high-risk cardiac conditions undergoing high-risk procedures.
Highest risk: prosthetic valves, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease.
redFlags: New murmur, fever or embolic phenomena after a procedure (suspect established endocarditis).

diagnostics.rationale: Identify high-risk cardiac lesions and high-risk dental procedures.

management.detail: Good oral hygiene and regular dental review reduce risk more than antibiotics.
Single-dose amoxicillin (or clindamycin if penicillin-allergic) before high-risk dental procedures in high-risk patients.
Advise patients to seek care for unexplained fever.

references.label: ESC guidelines for the management of infective endocarditis

title: Peripartum cardiomyopathy
presentation: Heart failure developing in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months postpartum.
Dyspnoea, orthopnoea, oedema and fatigue with reduced LV ejection fraction.
No other identifiable cause of heart failure.
redFlags: Acute pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock.

management.detail: Diuretics, beta-blockers; ACE inhibitors/ARBs postpartum (avoid antenatally), hydralazine/nitrates antenatally.
Consider for very low EF given thromboembolic risk.
Cardio-obstetric team; counsel against subsequent pregnancy if LV recovery incomplete.

references.label: ESC position statement on peripartum cardiomyopathy

title: Long QT syndrome
presentation: Syncope, seizures or palpitations, often triggered by exertion, emotion or noise.
Family history of sudden cardiac death.
Prolonged QTc on ECG; may be congenital or acquired (drugs, electrolytes).
redFlags: Aborted cardiac arrest or recurrent syncope.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms congenital subtype and guides family screening.

management.detail: Stop QT-prolonging drugs; correct hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia.
First-line for congenital LQTS (e.g. nadolol/propranolol).
For survivors of cardiac arrest or high-risk patients; treat torsades with IV magnesium.

references.label: ESC guidelines for the management of patients with ventricular arrhythmias and the prevention of sudden cardiac death

title: Brugada syndrome
presentation: Syncope or nocturnal agonal breathing; may present with sudden cardiac arrest.
Often unmasked by fever, sodium-channel-blocking drugs or vagal tone.
Coved ST elevation in V1-V2 (type 1 Brugada pattern).
redFlags: Aborted sudden cardiac death or documented ventricular fibrillation.

diagnostics.rationale: Unmasks pattern and guides family screening.

management.detail: Aggressive fever treatment with paracetamol; avoid provoking drugs (see brugadadrugs.org).
For those with cardiac arrest or arrhythmic syncope.
For electrical storm or as adjunct.

references.label: ESC guidelines on ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death

title: AV nodal re-entry tachycardia
presentation: Sudden-onset, regular, rapid palpitations with abrupt termination.
Associated chest discomfort, dyspnoea, dizziness; may have neck pounding.
Narrow-complex regular tachycardia (typically 150-250 bpm).
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability (hypotension, chest pain, reduced consciousness).
Pre-excitation/wide complex raising concern for alternative diagnosis.

diagnostics.rationale: Shows narrow-complex regular SVT; pseudo-R' in V1.

management.detail: Synchronised DC cardioversion.
Vagal manoeuvres (modified Valsalva), then IV adenosine.
Beta-blocker/verapamil for prevention; catheter ablation is curative.

references.label: ESC guidelines for the management of supraventricular tachycardia

title: Cardiac arrest — reversible causes (4Hs and 4Ts)
presentation: Cardiac arrest during resuscitation where a treatable cause should be sought.
Framework: Hypoxia, Hypovolaemia, Hypo/hyperkalaemia & metabolic, Hypothermia; Thrombosis (coronary/pulmonary), Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins.
redFlags: Refractory arrest without addressing reversible causes.
PEA arrest (frequently has a reversible cause).

diagnostics.test: Point-of-care ultrasound, blood gas and electrolytes

management.detail: Minimise interruptions; treat shockable rhythms with defibrillation.
Oxygenate, fluids, calcium/insulin-dextrose for hyperkalaemia, rewarm, thrombolysis for PE, needle/finger decompression for tension pneumothorax, pericardiocentesis for tamponade.
Targeted temperature management and treat the underlying cause.

title: Occupational asthma
presentation: Asthma symptoms (wheeze, cough, breathlessness) related to workplace exposures.
Improvement away from work (weekends, holidays).
Sensitisers include isocyanates, flour, latex, animal proteins.
redFlags: Ongoing high-level exposure to a known sensitiser.

diagnostics.test: Serial peak flow at and away from work

management.detail: Avoidance of the causative agent is the key intervention; involve occupational health.
Inhaled corticosteroid +/- bronchodilator per asthma guidelines.
Notify as an occupational disease where applicable.

references.label: BTS/SIGN British guideline on the management of asthma

title: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
presentation: Cough and breathlessness after exposure to organic antigens (e.g. mouldy hay, birds).
Acute form: flu-like illness hours after exposure.
Chronic form: progressive fibrosis and weight loss.

management.detail: Cornerstone of management; remove from exposure.
For acute severe or progressive disease.
Antifibrotic therapy and transplant assessment in progressive fibrotic phenotype.

references.label: ATS/JRS/ALAT clinical practice guideline: hypersensitivity pneumonitis

title: Pulmonary hypertension
presentation: Progressive exertional dyspnoea and fatigue.
Exertional syncope, chest pain, signs of right heart failure.
Loud P2, raised JVP, peripheral oedema.

diagnostics.rationale: Estimates pulmonary pressures and RV function.
Confirms diagnosis (mean PAP threshold) and classifies.

management.detail: Group 1-5 classification directs therapy; treat left heart, lung disease, or CTEPH.
Endothelin antagonists, PDE5 inhibitors, prostacyclins in expert centres for group 1.
Diuretics, oxygen, anticoagulation in selected patients; avoid pregnancy.

references.label: ESC/ERS guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary hypertension

title: Lung abscess
presentation: Subacute fever, productive cough with foul-smelling sputum, weight loss.
Risk factors: aspiration, poor dentition, alcohol, reduced consciousness.
Cavitating lesion with air-fluid level on imaging.

management.detail: Cover anaerobes and oral flora (e.g. amoxicillin-clavulanate or clindamycin) for several weeks.
Postural drainage; percutaneous/surgical drainage if no improvement.
Dental care, swallow assessment.

references.label: BTS guidelines for the management of community acquired pneumonia / pleural infection

title: Pleural empyema
presentation: Pleuritic chest pain, fever and dyspnoea, often complicating pneumonia.
Failure to improve on antibiotics for pneumonia.
Pus or organisms on pleural fluid sampling.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms infected fluid (low pH, pus, organisms).

management.detail: Cover community/aspiration organisms; prolonged course.
Intercostal drain for empyema/complicated effusion; consider intrapleural fibrinolytics.
VATS/decortication if drainage fails.

references.label: BTS pleural disease guideline: management of pleural infection

title: Pleural mesothelioma
presentation: Progressive breathlessness and chest pain, often with pleural effusion.
Weight loss; history of asbestos exposure (long latency).
Pleural thickening on imaging.

management.detail: Lung cancer/mesothelioma multidisciplinary team.
Pleurodesis or indwelling pleural catheter for effusion; analgesia.
Chemotherapy/immunotherapy; consider trials; advise on compensation.

references.label: NICE guideline NG12 / BTS mesothelioma statement

title: Foreign body aspiration
presentation: Sudden choking, coughing or stridor, often in a young child.
Unilateral wheeze or reduced air entry.
May present late with persistent cough or recurrent pneumonia.

diagnostics.rationale: May show air trapping or radio-opaque object; can be normal.

management.detail: Back blows/abdominal thrusts (age-appropriate); call for help.
Rigid bronchoscopy for retrieval.
Antibiotics for post-obstructive infection.

title: Ischaemic colitis
presentation: Sudden crampy abdominal pain followed by bloody diarrhoea.
Typically older patients with vascular risk factors.
Often affects watershed areas (splenic flexure).

diagnostics.rationale: Shows colonic wall thickening/ischaemia and excludes other causes.

management.detail: Bowel rest, IV fluids, optimise perfusion; most mild cases resolve.
For moderate-severe disease.
Resection for gangrene, perforation or stricture.

references.label: ACG clinical guideline: epidemiology, risk factors, patterns of presentation, diagnosis, and management of colon ischemia

title: Microscopic colitis
presentation: Chronic watery non-bloody diarrhoea, often in middle-aged/older women.
Normal or near-normal colonoscopy appearance.
Associations: NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs, coeliac disease.
redFlags: Weight loss or nocturnal symptoms prompting exclusion of other pathology.

diagnostics.rationale: Histology shows collagenous or lymphocytic colitis.

management.detail: Review NSAIDs/PPIs/SSRIs.
Oral budesonide is first-line and effective.
Loperamide for mild symptoms.

references.label: BSG guidelines on the management of microscopic colitis

title: Barrett's oesophagus
presentation: Often asymptomatic, found on endoscopy for chronic reflux.
Long-standing GORD symptoms.
Columnar-lined oesophagus on endoscopy with intestinal metaplasia.
redFlags: Dysphagia, weight loss or anaemia (exclude adenocarcinoma).

diagnostics.test: Upper GI endoscopy with biopsies (Seattle protocol)

management.detail: Long-term PPI to control reflux.
Endoscopic surveillance at intervals based on segment length and dysplasia.
Endoscopic eradication (RFA/EMR) for high-grade dysplasia or early cancer.

references.label: BSG guidelines on the diagnosis and management of Barrett's oesophagus

title: Eosinophilic oesophagitis
presentation: Dysphagia for solids and food bolus impaction, often in young atopic males.
Heartburn unresponsive to PPI.
History of atopy (asthma, eczema, allergies).
redFlags: Significant weight loss/failure to thrive in children.

management.detail: Trial of high-dose PPI.
Swallowed budesonide/fluticasone.
Elimination diet; endoscopic dilation for strictures.

references.label: AGA/joint task force guidelines on eosinophilic esophagitis

title: Intestinal pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome)
presentation: Marked abdominal distension with features of obstruction but no mechanical cause.
Often in unwell, immobile or post-operative patients.
Massive colonic dilatation on imaging (acute colonic pseudo-obstruction).
redFlags: Peritonism / signs of ischaemia or perforation.

management.detail: NG decompression, correct electrolytes, stop opioids/anticholinergics, mobilise.
For acute colonic pseudo-obstruction not responding to conservative measures (with cardiac monitoring).
Colonoscopic decompression or surgery if refractory or ischaemic.

references.label: ASGE/ACG guidance on acute colonic pseudo-obstruction

title: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD/NASH)
presentation: Usually asymptomatic; incidental raised transaminases or fatty liver on imaging.
Associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome.
May progress to steatohepatitis, fibrosis and cirrhosis.
redFlags: Features of decompensated cirrhosis (ascites, varices, encephalopathy).

management.detail: Weight loss (>=7-10%), diet and exercise are the cornerstone.
Optimise diabetes, lipids and blood pressure; statins are safe.
For advanced fibrosis; consider pharmacotherapy in NASH.

references.label: EASL-EASD-EASO clinical practice guidelines for the management of NAFLD

title: Alcohol-related cirrhosis
presentation: Stigmata of chronic liver disease in a heavy alcohol user.
Jaundice, ascites, variceal bleeding or encephalopathy when decompensated.
Spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia.

management.detail: The single most important intervention; offer assisted withdrawal and support.
Beta-blocker/banding for varices, diuretics/paracentesis for ascites, lactulose for encephalopathy.
HCC surveillance ultrasound; nutrition; transplant assessment if abstinent.

references.label: EASL clinical practice guidelines: management of alcohol-related liver disease

title: Portal vein thrombosis
presentation: Abdominal pain, distension; may be incidental.
Acute: pain, fever; chronic: portal hypertension with varices.
Associated with cirrhosis, malignancy or prothrombotic states.

diagnostics.test: Doppler ultrasound / CT or MR venography

management.detail: Anticoagulate acute non-cirrhotic PVT and selected cirrhotic patients to promote recanalisation.
Variceal screening and prophylaxis.
Address malignancy/prothrombotic disorder.

references.label: EASL clinical practice guidelines on vascular diseases of the liver

title: Hepatic hydrothorax
presentation: Pleural effusion (usually right-sided) in a patient with cirrhosis and portal hypertension.
Dyspnoea; may occur with or without ascites.
Transudative fluid on sampling.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms transudate and excludes infection/other causes.

management.detail: As for ascites management.
For symptomatic relief; avoid chest drains (risk of complications).
TIPS or transplant assessment in refractory cases.

references.label: AASLD practice guidance on ascites and hepatic hydrothorax in cirrhosis

title: Small bowel obstruction
presentation: Colicky central abdominal pain, vomiting, distension and absolute constipation.
Adhesions (prior surgery) are the commonest cause; also hernias and tumours.
Tinkling or absent bowel sounds; dilated loops on imaging.
redFlags: Signs of strangulation/ischaemia (constant pain, peritonism, fever, lactic acidosis).

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms obstruction, level, cause and ischaemia.

management.detail: NG decompression, IV fluids, correct electrolytes, analgesia.
For adhesional SBO without ischaemia; water-soluble contrast may be therapeutic/prognostic.
For strangulation, closed loop, or failure to resolve.

references.label: WSES guidelines on adhesive small bowel obstruction

title: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
presentation: Rapid decline in renal function over days to weeks.
Haematuria, proteinuria, red cell casts, oliguria.
May have pulmonary haemorrhage (pulmonary-renal syndrome).
redFlags: Severe AKI with hyperkalaemia or fluid overload.

diagnostics.rationale: Shows crescentic GN and guides immunosuppression.
Differentiates pauci-immune, anti-GBM and immune-complex disease.

management.detail: Treat as emergency to preserve renal function.
High-dose corticosteroids with cyclophosphamide or rituximab; plasma exchange for anti-GBM/severe disease.
Manage AKI, hyperkalaemia, and dialysis if needed.

references.label: KDIGO clinical practice guideline for glomerular diseases

title: Lupus nephritis
presentation: Renal involvement in systemic lupus erythematosus.
Proteinuria, haematuria, hypertension, renal impairment.
Other lupus features (rash, arthritis, serositis).

diagnostics.rationale: Classifies ISN/RPS class and guides therapy.

management.detail: Corticosteroids plus mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide for proliferative classes.
Mycophenolate or azathioprine; hydroxychloroquine for all.
RAAS blockade for proteinuria, blood pressure control.

title: Diabetic nephropathy
presentation: Progressive albuminuria and declining eGFR in long-standing diabetes.
Often coexists with retinopathy.
May progress to nephrotic syndrome and ESRD.
redFlags: Rapidly rising creatinine or active sediment (suggests alternative diagnosis).

management.detail: Tight control slows progression.
ACE inhibitor or ARB for albuminuria.
Add for renal and cardiovascular protection; consider finerenone.

references.label: KDIGO clinical practice guideline for diabetes management in CKD

title: Membranous nephropathy
presentation: Nephrotic syndrome: oedema, heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia.
Commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in non-diabetic adults.
Primary (anti-PLA2R) or secondary (malignancy, infections, drugs, lupus).
redFlags: Venous thromboembolism (high risk in nephrotic syndrome).

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms diagnosis and distinguishes primary disease.

management.detail: RAAS blockade, salt restriction, diuretics, statin; anticoagulation if high thrombotic risk.
Rituximab or calcineurin inhibitor/cyclophosphamide for high-risk or progressive disease.
Address malignancy/infection if identified.

references.label: KDIGO clinical practice guideline for glomerular diseases

title: Acute interstitial nephritis
presentation: AKI with a temporal link to a drug, infection or autoimmune disease.
Classic triad (fever, rash, eosinophilia) is uncommon.
Drugs: NSAIDs, PPIs, antibiotics.
redFlags: Severe AKI with uraemia or hyperkalaemia.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms interstitial infiltrate when diagnosis uncertain.

management.detail: Key intervention; review NSAIDs/PPIs/antibiotics.
Considered for drug-induced AIN with no recovery after withdrawal.
Fluid balance, treat hyperkalaemia.

references.label: KDIGO clinical practice guideline for acute kidney injury

title: Urinary incontinence (stress and urge)
presentation: Stress: leakage on coughing, sneezing, exertion.
Urge: sudden compelling need to void with leakage (overactive bladder).
Mixed pictures common, especially in older women.

management.detail: Pelvic floor exercises (stress), bladder training (urge), weight loss, caffeine reduction.
Antimuscarinic or mirabegron for urge incontinence.
Surgery (e.g. mid-urethral sling) for refractory stress incontinence.

references.label: NICE guideline NG123: urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women

title: Urethral stricture
presentation: Weak/spraying urinary stream, straining, incomplete emptying.
Recurrent UTI; history of trauma, instrumentation or infection.
Mostly affects men.
redFlags: Bladder stones or upper tract dilatation.

management.detail: Catheterise (suprapubic if urethral access fails).
For short strictures; high recurrence.
Definitive reconstruction for recurrent/long strictures.

title: Hydrocele
presentation: Painless scrotal swelling that transilluminates.
May be congenital (communicating) in infants or acquired in adults.
Testis often impalpable within a tense hydrocele.
redFlags: Underlying testicular tumour or infection (do scrotal ultrasound if testis not palpable).

diagnostics.rationale: Excludes tumour and confirms diagnosis when testis impalpable.

management.detail: Most infantile hydroceles resolve by 1-2 years.
Hydrocelectomy for persistent/symptomatic adult hydroceles; herniotomy approach for communicating type in children.
Address infection or filariasis where relevant.

title: Varicocele
presentation: Scrotal 'bag of worms' swelling, usually left-sided, more prominent on standing.
Dull aching scrotal discomfort.
May be associated with subfertility.
redFlags: Acute-onset, right-sided or non-reducing varicocele (consider retroperitoneal mass/IVC obstruction).

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms reflux and assesses testicular volume.

management.detail: Reassurance and scrotal support for mild symptoms.
Varicocele repair (surgical or embolisation) for pain, testicular growth arrest, or selected subfertility.

title: Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis
presentation: Painful, tender thyroid following a viral upper respiratory infection.
Transient thyrotoxicosis then hypothyroidism, often self-limiting.
Fever and malaise; raised inflammatory markers.

management.detail: NSAIDs first-line; corticosteroids for severe pain.
For thyrotoxic symptoms (no antithyroid drugs needed).
Recheck TFTs as most recover; some develop permanent hypothyroidism.

references.label: ATA guidelines for the diagnosis and management of thyrotoxicosis

title: Hashimoto thyroiditis
presentation: Autoimmune hypothyroidism with a firm, painless goitre.
Fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation.
Positive anti-TPO antibodies; commonest cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-replete areas.

management.detail: Replace to normalise TSH; titrate by symptoms and TSH.
Higher requirements; check TFTs each trimester.
Other autoimmune disease (e.g. coeliac, T1DM).

references.label: ATA guidelines for treatment of hypothyroidism

title: Thyroid nodule and goitre
presentation: Palpable thyroid nodule or diffuse/nodular goitre.
Usually euthyroid; may cause compressive symptoms.
Most nodules are benign.
redFlags: Rapid growth, hard fixed nodule, hoarseness, cervical nodes (malignancy).

diagnostics.rationale: Assesses function and stratifies malignancy risk.

management.detail: Ultrasound risk scoring directs need for FNA.
Manage hyper-/hypothyroidism if present.
For malignancy, compressive goitre, or significant cosmetic concern.

references.label: ATA management guidelines for thyroid nodules

title: Hypopituitarism
presentation: Symptoms reflecting deficient pituitary hormones (fatigue, hypogonadism, growth failure, hypothyroid, adrenal insufficiency).
Causes: tumour, surgery, radiotherapy, Sheehan syndrome, trauma.
May present acutely with adrenal crisis.

management.detail: Glucocorticoid first (before levothyroxine), then thyroid, sex steroids, growth hormone as indicated.
Educate on stress dosing of steroids and emergency card/injection.
Surgery/radiotherapy for tumours.

references.label: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline on hormonal replacement in hypopituitarism

title: Prolactinoma
presentation: Galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea/oligomenorrhoea, infertility in women.
Reduced libido and erectile dysfunction in men.
Macroadenomas: headache and visual field defects.

diagnostics.rationale: Defines tumour size and mass effect.

management.detail: Cabergoline first-line; shrinks tumour and normalises prolactin.
Prolactin and MRI; manage in pregnancy with specialist input.
Trans-sphenoidal surgery if intolerant/resistant or for apoplexy.

references.label: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline: diagnosis and treatment of hyperprolactinemia

title: Carcinoid syndrome
presentation: Episodic flushing, secretory diarrhoea, wheeze.
Usually from a metastatic neuroendocrine tumour (often small bowel).
Right-sided valvular heart disease in advanced disease.
redFlags: Carcinoid crisis (profound flushing, hypotension, bronchospasm), often triggered by procedures.

management.detail: Octreotide/lanreotide controls symptoms and tumour growth; cover procedures to prevent crisis.
Surgery, liver-directed therapy, PRRT in specialist centres.
Echocardiographic surveillance and valve surgery as needed.

references.label: ENETS consensus guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours

title: Gynaecomastia
presentation: Benign proliferation of glandular breast tissue in males.
Concentric, often tender, subareolar firmness.
Physiological in puberty/elderly; drugs and hormonal disorders are common causes.
redFlags: Hard, eccentric, fixed mass or nipple discharge (exclude male breast cancer).
Rapid progression with systemic features (consider tumour).

management.detail: Stop offending drugs; manage hypogonadism/hyperthyroidism/liver disease.
Physiological pubertal gynaecomastia usually resolves.
Persistent symptomatic cases for medical/surgical options.

references.label: Clinical practice guidance on evaluation and management of gynaecomastia

title: Hirsutism
presentation: Excess terminal hair in a male pattern in women.
Most commonly due to polycystic ovary syndrome.
May be accompanied by acne and menstrual irregularity.
redFlags: Rapid-onset/severe virilisation (clitoromegaly, voice deepening) suggesting androgen-secreting tumour.

management.detail: Eflornithine, depilation, laser.
Combined oral contraceptive +/- anti-androgen (e.g. spironolactone).
Weight loss for PCOS; address underlying disorder.

references.label: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline: evaluation and treatment of hirsutism in premenopausal women

title: Essential tremor
presentation: Bilateral postural/action tremor of the hands, often with head/voice involvement.
Improves with alcohol; positive family history common.
No bradykinesia or rigidity (unlike Parkinson disease).
redFlags: Asymmetry, rest tremor or other parkinsonian features.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical; exclude drugs/thyroid disease.

management.detail: No treatment if not bothersome.
Propranolol or primidone.
Consider DBS or focused ultrasound in specialist centres.

references.label: Movement Disorder Society consensus on tremor classification

title: Restless legs syndrome
presentation: Urge to move the legs with uncomfortable sensations, worse at rest and in the evening.
Relieved by movement; disrupts sleep.
Associations: iron deficiency, pregnancy, renal failure.
redFlags: Severe sleep disruption or augmentation on dopaminergic therapy.

diagnostics.rationale: Iron deficiency is a common, treatable contributor.

management.detail: Iron replacement if ferritin low.
Reduce caffeine/alcohol; review aggravating drugs.
Alpha-2-delta ligands (gabapentin/pregabalin) preferred; dopamine agonists with caution (augmentation risk).

references.label: AASM clinical practice guideline for restless legs syndrome

title: Normal pressure hydrocephalus
presentation: Triad of gait apraxia, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline.
Magnetic, broad-based shuffling gait often the earliest feature.
Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy.
redFlags: Features suggesting alternative cause of dementia.

management.detail: CSF tap test or external drainage trial.
Ventriculoperitoneal shunt can improve gait, especially when treated early.

references.label: Guidelines on the diagnosis and management of idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus

title: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
presentation: Headache with visual obscurations and pulsatile tinnitus.
Typically in young women with obesity.
Papilloedema; may have sixth nerve palsy.

diagnostics.rationale: Detect papilloedema and monitor for visual loss.

diagnostics.test: MRI/MRV brain then LP with opening pressure
diagnostics.rationale: Exclude mass/venous thrombosis; confirm raised pressure with normal CSF.

management.detail: Sustained weight reduction is disease-modifying.
Reduces CSF production; first-line medical therapy.
Urgent CSF diversion or optic nerve sheath fenestration for fulminant visual loss.

references.label: Consensus guidelines on the management of idiopathic intracranial hypertension

title: Lumbar radiculopathy (sciatica)
presentation: Radiating leg pain in a dermatomal distribution, often from disc herniation.
May have sensory disturbance, weakness or reflex loss.
Pain often worse on coughing/straining; positive straight leg raise.
redFlags: Cauda equina features (bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction).

diagnostics.rationale: For red flags or persistent/severe symptoms before intervention.

management.detail: Emergency MRI and surgery if suspected.
Stay active, analgesia, physiotherapy; most improve.
Consider epidural injection or surgery for refractory/progressive deficit.

references.label: NICE guideline NG59: low back pain and sciatica

title: Cervical radiculopathy
presentation: Neck pain radiating into the arm in a dermatomal pattern.
Arm paraesthesia, weakness or reflex changes.
Often from disc herniation or spondylosis.

diagnostics.rationale: Localises the root and screens for myelopathy.

management.detail: Analgesia, physiotherapy; most resolve in weeks.
Surgery for myelopathy or progressive/refractory radiculopathy.

references.label: Guidelines on the management of cervical radiculopathy from degenerative disorders

title: Carpal tunnel syndrome
presentation: Numbness/tingling in the thumb, index, middle and radial half of ring finger.
Worse at night; relieved by shaking the hand.
Thenar wasting in chronic cases.
redFlags: Thenar muscle wasting/persistent weakness (consider urgent decompression).

diagnostics.rationale: Confirm and grade severity when uncertain or pre-surgery.

management.detail: Nocturnal wrist splints; treat contributing conditions.
Local corticosteroid for moderate symptoms.
Carpal tunnel release for severe/persistent symptoms or motor loss.

references.label: AAOS clinical practice guideline on carpal tunnel syndrome

title: Viral meningitis
presentation: Headache, fever, neck stiffness and photophobia, usually less toxic than bacterial.
Enteroviruses are the commonest cause.
Generally self-limiting.
redFlags: Altered consciousness, seizures or focal signs (suspect encephalitis/bacterial cause).

diagnostics.rationale: Lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, negative Gram stain.

management.detail: Empirical antibiotics +/- aciclovir until excluded.
Analgesia, antipyretics, hydration; most recover fully.
If HSV meningoencephalitis suspected.

references.label: UK joint specialist societies guideline on viral meningitis

title: Reactive arthritis
